Afternoon Session,
'I'uesday, October 9th, A. L. 5906.
'!'he Grand Lodge was called on at two o'clock, the Grand
Master presiding.
'!'he Grand Master then delivered his Annual Address to
the Grand Lodge, as follows:Brethren of the Grand"todge:
One year ago, as we gathered together in this beautiful city, the
metropolis of the Pacific Coast, teeming with industry and prosperity, we little thought of the change which would be effected i~ so
short a time.; but we can all give thanks to Him who does all thrngs
well that in our hour of need the Grand Jurisdictions of the world
' forth their relief quickly and generously, and that m
. our
poured
State we had the necessary men of courage, honesty and ability to
handle the relief matters in a most satisfactory manner, but, better
still, they had the tenacity and unity of purpose to determine to
rebuild our demolished and burned sections of the State better and
more substantial than before.
Brethren, you who have not visited the stricken sections of our
State prior to the convening of our Grand Lodge can have no ~oncep­
tion of the bravery of our citizens, when, i=ediately followmg the
disaster and fire of April 18th, last, the men of California, with the
pioneer spirit of '49, determined· that the California: of the future
should be far better, more solid and substantial than before. What
has been accomplished . to date speaks volumes for these men _of courage, and from .my observations I believ~, and I am sure y?u will agree
with me that in a short period of time our metropolis and other
injured ~ities near by will soon be a credit and joy to all Californiap.s.
The relief work incident to the disaster of April 18th last having
been such an important matter, and involving so many different
points, I have deemed it best to submit to the Grand Lodge an

,

Our Grand Jurisdiction has suffered severely during the past year
in the loss of two of our Past Grand Masters: M.:. W.-. William
Johnston, who was Grand Master in 1891, entered into rest November
14, 1905. The Grand Lodge was specially convened at Sacramento,
November 18th, and the last and solemn duties to our dead Brother
were performed by the Grand Lodge, with Past Grand Master Edmund C. Atkinson in charge of the ceremonies.
M.'. W.'. Hiram N. Rucker, who was Grand Master in 1887,
passed to the Great Beyond December 13, 1905. The Grand Lodge
was specially convened at Merced, December 16th, and before the
largest concourse of citizens ever ·gathered in .that city the beautiful
ceremonies of our Order were conducted by R. :. W. '.. Edward H. Hart,
Deputy Grand Master.
Both of these Brethren will be greatly missed at our Grand Lodge,
but their kindly faces, their genial words of greeting and their able
advice on all important questions will live in our memories until time
shall be no more. The very sudden and unfortunate accident which
befell Brother Past Grand Master Rucker and caused his untimely
death was a decided loss to our Widows' and Orphans' Home, over
which institution he was Superintendent, and the able and entirely
satisfactory manner i.n which our Brother performed his duties
makes the loss to our Fraternity doubly hard.
I have taken the liberty to appoint as a Special Memorial Committee on the death. of Past Grand Masters Johnston and Rucker
Brothers Past Grand Masters Edmund C. Atkinson, ~'rank M. Angellotti and James A. Foshay, and recommend that a special hour be set
apart for "the reading of the Report of this Committee.
Owing to the destruction of our entire Grand Lodge records, and,
in fact, all papers connected with the Grand Secretary's office, it is
not possible to give the full list of deaths of the Grand Officers of
other Grand Jurisdictions, except those received subsequent to April
18th last. It is greatly to be regretted that proper tribute and respect
cannot ~e shown in this Address to the honored dead of other Grand
Jurisdictions, but probably that can be corrected next year, when
notifications from our other bodies have been received. We mourn
with our Sister Jurisdictions the loss of the following Brethren:

Condition of Our Jurisdiction.
It is with pleasure that I am able to report to you that, notwithstanding the unfortunate casualties of a · few months since, the
general condition of Masonry within our Jurisdiction is most satisfactory in every respect. The returns for last year show a membership, on July 31, 1905, of 31,561; the returns for this year show a
membership of 33,769, a net gain of 2,208.
Lodges located at points most seriously injured· have undoubtedly
felt the effect of the disaster, and I have in a number of cases
authorized Lodges to return the fees of petitioners where the appli·
cants had presented their petitions for degrees prior to April 18th,
last, and which petitions were to be acted upon at the meeting subsequent to April 18th, and where it further appeared that the petitioners
or applicants required the amount of the fees for the support of
themselves or their families, and were in no financial condition to
lose the eost of the fees or to take the degrees. While I acted without
legal authority in these eases, it was in the interest of charity and
humanity.

192

Immediately following the disaster of April 18th last I called upon
the Master of each Lodge in the district which suffered on that fateful morning, asking ·for full and ·complete reports of their condition.
I found that in a large number of instances Masonic Temples and
places of meeting had been badly injuted to such an extent that meetings could not be held therein. I issued instructions for the Masters
to make the best possible arrangements under the circumstances, fol·
lowing as closely as possible to our Constitution and General Regulations, and if necessary temporarily change the meeting nights until
such time as the normal conditions would be resumed. It was a matter
that required immediate action; hence I acted promptly in every case
and was naturally compelled in a 'large extent to rely upon the wisdom
and the judgment of the Masters of the various Lodges.

•

Amendments to By-Laws have been presented in a number of cases
for approval, and of such amendments which have been approved by
me I presume have been lost with the records of the Grand Secretary's
office, but no amendment has been approved until said amendment
conformed in every respect to the uniform Code of By-Laws. It is
certainly to be regretted that many of our Secretaries are not familiar
with our regulations. It has been necessary for me to return, some·
times two and three times, these proposed amendments for correction.
Charters.
Many Charters were burned or destroyed in April last, and it has
not been possible as yet to renew them. I have therefore authorized
all Lodges which did not have charters at this time to continue to act
and work as if the charters were in their possession. Just as soon as
the Lithographing company can renew our Charters duplicates should
be issued to all the Lodges requiring the same.
Regalia.
I will state for the benefit of the members of the Grand Lodge
that this body owned two sets of regalia; one of which was used for
ceremonies taking place outside of San Francisco and the other being
the new regalia recently purchased for use at our Annual Communications. Both of these magnificent . sets of regalia were consu.med in
the fire of April last, but fortunately the Grand Secretary in his wis·
dom had one thousand dollars insurance on the same and by my direc·
tion he has undertaken to replace one of the sets which the manu·
facturer has promised for use at this Annual Communication.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
Mruionic Board of Relief of Los Aµgeles.

Brother C. W. Bush, a member of the Fraternity residing in Los
Angeles, California, died some eighteen months since, leaving a portion of his estate to the Masonic Board of Relief of Los Angeles.
Owing to the peculiar laws of this State, it was thought at one time
that the Board of Relief of Los Angeles would not be able to secure
this property, but by the active and energetic efforts of Brother
Samuel Prager, President of the Board, and Brother August Wackerbarth executor of the estate, said Masonic Board of Relief, to thorough!~ protect itself and to protect the interests of the ~'raternity,
duly incorporated under the laws of the State of California, and on
August 1st came into possession of the property, consisting of a
two-story brick building at the corner of Los Angeles and Market
streets, in Los Angeles City, of the appraised value of $33,000.00;
also two unimproved pieces of property in Los Angeles City of the
app;aised value of $12,196.99, making the total appraised value of
the estate turned over to the Masonic Board of Relief of Los Angeles
$45,196.99.
The present income of this property is two hundred and. twenty
dollars per month. Unfortunately, a few' days after the Board came
into possession of the property a fire occurred in the building at Los
Angeles and Market streets, causing a damage of several hundred
dollars. This, however, was covered by insurance, which will probably
fully protect the Board. In order that the Fraternity will be protected in years to come, it will be necessary for this Board to place
the property on an income basis, which will undoubte'.11y necessitate
the selling of the unimproved property and the ma.king of further
improvements in the building ~t Los Angel~s and Market streets~ ~he
balance to be invested in other income-bea.nng proper~y or secunties.
Consequently, this Grand Body will probably be called upon to make
its usual contribution to the Masonic Board of Relief of Los Angeles
for the coming year, and after that, when their property is placed
upon an ineome-producing basis, or within. o'ne year, the n?cessary
contribution to said Masonic Board of Rehef can be matenally reduced.
Masonic Employment Bureau of Los Angeles.
After a connection of nearly ten years with the Masonic Board of
Relief of Los Angeles, and a thorough study of the situation, I felt
that as California is the Mecca of thousands of people from the
Eas{ who visit our Golden State by reason of its mild climate or in
sear;h of health, many of . our Brethren from the Eastern Jurisdic-

...

195

tions arrive here ~thout funds, and frequently with families entirely
dependent, but with the hope of securing employment; and in hundreds of cases worthy Brethren have visited this State and positively
refused to accept financial assistance, and, in fact, declined charity.
All they desired was an opportunity to secure honest employment.
Believ.ing that our Fraternity could set a good example in this
way, I prevailed upon the Scottish Rite Bodies, Chapters and Command~ry of L~s Angeles to make monthly donations for one year to
ope~ a Masonic Employment Bureau. This Bureau was opened for
business November 15, 1905. A regular office is maintained in the
Masonic Temple in Los Angeles, which is open from 9 a. m. to 12,
noon, and is in charge of a competent Secretary, whose duty it is to
secure written applications from worthy Masons and their dependents
desiring employment, and then each afternoon to visit all employers
and endeavor to place our deserving Brethren in positions. The
results have been more than satisfactory, and I am pleased to state
that the Masonic Employment Bureau of Los Angeles, during the ten
months of its operation, has made a most magnificent showing as the
following Report from the Secretary of said Bureau will sho~:

Secretary to place our unemployed Craftsmen in positions whereby
they can support themselves and families, and thereby be indepen-

For all human ties that bind us,
l!'or all tasks our God assigneq us,
For the bright hopes yet to find us,
And the good that we can do."
Respectfully submitted by yours truly and fraternally,

The following Brethren were present at the meeting called by
me May 19th last: E. H. Hart, Deputy Grand Master; George M.
Perine, Senior Grand Warden; R. H. Lloyd, Junior Grand Warden;
E. Coleman, Grand Treasurer; George Johnson, Granll Secretary;
F. M. Angellotti, E. C. Atkinson, C. L. Patton, Thomas Flint, 0. S.
Henderson, J. B. Stevens, Past Grand Masters; J. H. Neff, Past
Junior Grand Warden; J. W. Anderson, Past Grand Lecturer; W.
Frank Pierce, B. P. Flint, Henry L. Davis, F. W. Van Sicklen and J.
Tonningsen; and, after careful, thorough and exhaustive discussion,
it was decided by more than a majority present that it was for the
best interest of the Grand Lodge that the property at Post and Montgomery streets of this city be sold at a price not less than seven
hundred and fifty thousand dollars.

Within the past sixty days Brother Reuben H. Lloyd secured a
buyer for this property at the figure of seven hundred and fifty thou•
sand dollars, and on behalf of the Grand Lodge I signed the necessary
papers to dispose of the Grand Lodge stock of 5,881 shares, out of a
total of 25,000 shares, which action has been concurred in by everybody holding stock in the corporation.

K. ··'· ········' ·' ···············...

There can be no question but that lor many reasons it would have
been a splendid and magnificent monument to Masonry to erect a
first-class steel-frame building on the old site; but conditions after
the :fire ch.anged the situation very materially in San Francisco, and
it is my judgment that the action in selling the property at the price
given was a decided advantage to the Fraternity. The Committee in
charge, representing the stockholden of this corporatio.n, have been
.requested by me to hold the mo,ney intact as long as .poss.i ble, or until
after this Gr.and Body should meet, .in order that ~mmediate action
could be taken W~!Jr!Jby a 'l'emple,. a credit to Maso~ry and to this

Grand Lodge, recommended as follows:
''Omit therefrom the rosters of the various Lodges, and insert in
lieu thereof tabulated statement showing the number and name of each
Lodge, together with the names of the Master and Secretary thereof
and the date and place of meeting.''
In my judgment, after careful and mature deliberation and after
investigation of the work of the various Relief Boards incident to the
disaster of April 18th last, it is a serious mistake not to publish the
names of the members of our Grand Jurisdiction in good standing. I
do not maintain that it is necessary that the same should be in the
proceedings of the Grand Lodge, but it is my idea that at the annual
meetings of the various Lodges of this Jurisdiction held during December of each year there is a general overhauling of the records and
delinquent members are suspended; hence, on January let of each year
practically all of the Lodges of this J .u riediction have accurate and
complete rolls of their members, a~d as the election takes place in all
Lodges during December it is my judgment that it is wise and expedient to publish early in January a complete roster of each and every
L!)dge of this Grand Jurisdiction showing newly elected and appointive officers and members in good standing, and have the same properly
distributed to each constituent Lodge of this Grand Jurisdiction.

GRA.ND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA..

207

"Has a Lodge, or the Worshipful Master thereof, the right to
create a salaried office not mentioned or enumerated in the By-Laws of
the Lodgef Is such an appointment lawfuU"
This quest~on was brought out by a resolution adopted by "Dorie"
Lodge as follows:
"That the Master be empowered to appoint an instructor, said instructor must be a member of ''Doric'' Lodge, for the purpose of
assisting candidates in the lectures of the first and second degrees.
Said instructor to receive a compensation of :five dollars for each
candidate instructed by him. ''
In the Uniform Code of By-Laws adopted by this Grand Lodge
there is no provision for the !1-Ppointment of such an officer as an
Instructor. Under our Constitution it is provided that no Lodge shall
advance an Entered Apprentice or a Fellow Craft to a higher degree
until after a strict examination in open Lodge he shall have given
satisfactory evidence that he is entirely proficient and well qualified
in that or those he has already taken; thus being clearly noted that it
is the duty of the candidate to be properly prepared. There is no
doubt as to the i;ight of the Master, without the coment of the Lodge,
to appoint a brother to instruct a candidate; the real question is as
to the right to pay for such service from the Lodge funds. It appears
that when the resolution was adopted by "Doric" Lodge many can·
didates were appearing for examination, and hardly two had the same
work. It is undoubtedly at times a hardship on the Master of a
Lodge and on the Brethren to be required to teach a candidate the
lectures of the Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft degrees. After
a thorough and mature deliberation it is my opinion, as our laws now
•xist, that Lodge funds cannot be used for the purpose of paying an
lastructor, but the question as to whether or not it would be a ma·
terial advantage to our Fraternity if all candidates were taught the
work uniform!,. and might not materially reduce the work imposed
upon some of our Brethren in Lodges which are increasing rapidly in
IJembership by having a paid instructor should be given careful <:on·
lideration. Hence, I have not decided the question, but refer it to the
Grand Lodge for a decision as to the expediency of creating such an
office and having it paid by the Lodge if deemed best by any Lodge
of this Jurisdiction to do so, or to amend our uniform Code of By·
Laws to cover all points involved in the question presented.

My answer to this letter was .dated December 9th, and was as
follows:
·
"Referring to your favor of the 4th regarding life membership in
your Lodge, also referring to the copy of By-Laws of your Lodge and
calling my attention to Article VIII, Sec. 3, which provides how life
memberships may be established in your Lodge, permit me to call
your attention to the fact that the copy of By-Laws as submitted was
apparently revised November 12, 1903. If that be a fact, I can not
understand why this Section regarding life memberships should be
.in your by-Laws. Please note Section 928, Anderson's Manual, read·
ing as follows:
" 'Sec. 928. No Lodge under the .Jurisdiction of the Grand
Lodge of California can establish life memberships by resolution or
in any other manner.'
''This was approved by the Grand Lodge in Session of 1901. Same
was not apparently understood by all Lodges, as you will note by
reading Sections 936 and 937, which are as follows:
'' 'Sec. 936. Several Lodges in the .Jurisdiction have contended
that the decision of the Grand Lodge at the Annual Communication of
1900, relative to Life Membership, did not prevent them from issu·
ing life memberships where ·a standing resolution or by-law passed
prior to and in force at the time of the decision so provided. I have
decided that a life membership is not established by the mere passing
of a resolution providing for it, but that the act of receiving the
money and issuing the certificate constitutes or establishes the life.
membership, and that, since said decision, it is improper and illegal
to issue or grant any life membership or receive any money therefor,
and any and all resolutions or by-laws providing therefor should be
immediately repealed by the Lodge.
" 'Sec. 937. Where a Lodge, prior to the decision of 1900, has,
by resolution or otherwise, granted a life membership, agreed that
a Brother should be a life member, and enrolled him as such in
accordance with the agreement, or in any manner created and granted
such life membership, it is then an executed contract between him
and the Lodge, and ~an not be set aside or rescinded without the
consent of both, and such life memberships must stand.'
"This was adopted and approved by the Grand Lodge in Session
of 1902, consequently why should the revised copy_of your By-Lawll

"This part I must confess I was not aware of or being so, it must.

.
"Nevertheless the ruling of the Grand Lodge has been strictly

troubling you that you may so enlighten us that we may proceed without further errors.''

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

:Masonic Home, Decoto.

It was my intention when I assumed the position as Grand Master
to give the Masonic Home considerable attention, but, unfortunately,
other matters of serious importance have prevented, but recently I
had an opportunity of visiting our splendid institution and going
over it very carefully. In my judgment, the Home is well and eco·
nomically conducted; the Brethren, their wives and the widows who are
domiciled there are certainly well taken care of in every particular.
It was very pleasing to note the neat and healthy appearance of all
the children, and I cannot speak too highly' of the excellent care and
motherly devotion of our Matron, Mrs. Rucker, whose heart is undoubtedly wrapped up in the welfare of the children, young and old,
under her charge. It is my opinion that the Trustees are handling
the business of the Home in the best possible manner, and I cannot
see how any great saving can be made. We have erected this magnificent institutioll, and must conduct it so that it will be a credit to
our Fraternity, and I feel positive that our Trustees are doing everything in their power to follow the teachings of our beloved Order
and looking carefully after the interests of the Grand Lodge. It has
been suggested that it would be more satisfactory to some of the
Lodges if we followed the method adopted by the Southern California Home; that is, to require each Lodge which may place an
adult or a child in the Home to pay for their maintenance, and for
the Grand I.i::·i~e to provide for the fixed charges, such as expend,iture!
for help, Superintendent, Matron, taxes and other charges that must be
maintained to keep ;J.p the institution, but the cost of food and
supplies given to each inmate shall be paid by the respective Lodges
whom they are charged against. This question was brought up in
Los Angeles, where .one Lodge of three hundred and forty members
pays annually three hundred and forty dollars towards the Masonic
Home, and has· never had any direct benefits from it, whereas another
Lodge of equal size has had a Brother and his wife as inmates for
several years; hence, as a suggestion, it might be well to investigate
the propriety of changing the system, following the lines, as before
stated, of the California Masonic Home Association at San Gabriel.
I have also had the pleasure of visiting the California :Masonic
Home Association, and find that they have a magnificent propetty, and

'' 'Admission to the Home will be made by the Board of Directors,

certified by the proper officers and under seal. Admission may be
had on the nomination of individual Masons, their widows or orphans
i:p good standing in other Masonic Jurisdictions who are able to
defray their entire expenses, at the discretion of the Board of
Directors.'
"You will note that the Grand Lodge instructions are that this
money donated is 'to be used by said Association in the care and
maintenance of sick and distressed Brother Master Masons, their
widows and orphans,' whereas, your rules, apparently, apply simply
to those in Southern California. Before your acceptance of this
d mation it is my duty as Grand Master to call your attention to
these important points, and to request that before this money is used
by you that you consent and agree to the resolution adopted by tho
Grand Lodge, which, in my judgment, provides for the care and maintenance of ·sick and distressed Brother Master Masons, their widows
and orphans, Qf the entire California Jurisdiction.''

Financial Statement.
December 1, 1905, cash on hand .............. . .. . ........ $ 5,049 92
Collected from all sources since................ . ......... 7,079 07

This is larger than it will be next year; while the. table expenses
and help will be more, water, insuranee, printing and sundries will be
much less.
The net cost of table board has been $15 per month, which will be
reduced as the family becomes larger. We have had some twenty·
four in the Home, but now have twelve regular inmates, a happy,
contented family. There are other applicants who will soon be admitted.
The Board of Directors all have the interests of our Home at
heart and are now planning for a large increase in the general interest
of the Fraternity-which will increase our income. The Institution
is entirely free from debt and the assets at present are:

Our Home is supported by gratuous donations, together with membership fees of $1.00 per year, or $25 for Life.
We were exceedingly fortunate in securing Mrs. Ora E. Aikin as
our Matron, who has for the last twelve months given entire satisfaction. She has at present two women as houaekeepers, who also keep
the dining-room, and one woman as cook. At present only one man
cares for the grounds aud cow. The men in the Home are assisting
in the· care of the grounds. Our pay-roll for help is $130 per month;
as soon as cold w:eather begins this will be increased to $155 per
month.

Philippine Islands. Papers were in P!Oper form, with the exception
that Certificate of Quali:fi.cation from a Master of a Lodge was not

Among the papers asking for this Dispensation is the approval

and report to this .Grand .Body at this Session.

now recall several cases where certain Lodges have arbitrarily refused
to grant recommendations for new Lodges, which facts I should be
glad to give to the Committee of Jurisprudence at any time, makes it
incumbent upon me to respectfully but urgently recommend the
Constitution be so amended that the Grand Master have the power
in case the nearest or most convenient Lod·g e shall refuse a recommendation for the organization of a new Lodge, to investigate the
necessity and issue a Dispensation if it is, in hie judgi:nent, considered
best and proper. This recommendation has not been made hurriedly,
but after deep thought and, to my mind, will result in great benefit to
our Grand Jurisdiction.
Conclusion.
Finally, my Brethren, in closing my Report, I desire to thank you
one and all for the kindness and courtesy extended to me during the
past Masonic year. I commenced my year's work with the best
intentions in the world, intending it to be one long to be remembered
in Masonic history, for I anticipated visiting practically all the Lodges
in the State, but my personal business, my health, and the relief work
has prevented. I have, however, been errabled to visit a large number
of our Lodges· and have been received with fraternal kindness,
and I assure -you that the memory of the cordial greeting, the hearty
hand-clasp, and the words of welcome from our Brethren will never
be forgotten. Not being gifted with the flow of words required by
our orators, I have not attempted to make speeches during my numerous visits, but have endeavored to impress upon all the Fraternity that
this was to have been a business administration, and if I have succeeded to your satisfaction it will be a source of great pleasure to me.
In visiting different portions of the State I have observed a great
deal of discussion regarding "Superior California," "Northern California,'' ''Central California,'' and ''Southern California.'' My
.tlrethren, we have in this great State but one California, and that is
the whole and the entire State. If there is any time in our history
when we require united effort it is now, and by this united effort we
can rebuild and make the portion of our State requiring our assistance
far better than before, and I ask you now, one and all, to forget
everything but that one great word, ''California.'' It will require
the highest type of Jitizenehip to continue California 'e reputation
and steady advancement, and nothing can do more in up-building this
great State than to ·have each and every Lodge in California assisting
in the splendid work.
Respectfully and fraternally submitted,
MOTLEY HEWES FLINT,

The Grand Master then presented a detailed report of
the General Masonic Relief Fund as follows:

GRf\ND Mf\STER'S RELIEF
REFORT
Los ANGELES, CAL.
October 1, 1906.
Brethren of the Grand Lodge

On the morning of April 18th last as! was about to leave my home to attend
to my business engagements the telephone operator at my office called mf' up
and stated that she had just received a message from the train dispatcher
of the Southern Pacific Railway informing her that there had been a severe
earthquake in San Francisco and a number of people had been killed. Of
course I little realized that the disaster would prove. so serious, but on reaching the center of the city I ascertained that the newspapers were preparing
to issue extras and then it dawned upon me that the casualty was much more
serious than first appeared. I immediately called upon the telegraph companies 11.nd the railway authorities for full information biit unfortunately
the wires out of San Francisco were ei~her seriously damaged or not working
satisfactorily and but little information could be secured more than the fact
that the loss of life had been appalling and the city of San Francisco was
burning. Notwithstanding the fact that my physical condition was not all
that could be desired I deemed it my duty to go to San Francisco at once
and within a short time Brother Oscar Lawler, Grand Orator, telephoned and
volunteered his assistance and agreed to go with me by first train. We left
Los Angeles at the first opportunity and on reaching Oakland the next morning found the streets crowded with panic stricken people from San francisco
practically all ~f whom had lost all their earthly possessions and were simply
striving for an opportunity to get away from the scene of the terrible disastef
and the conflagration which was fast destroying the metropolis of the Pacific coast. After inquiries I ascertained that a meeting of Masons had been
called for April 20th at the &:Ma.sonic Temple and I 'attended this meeting
and found that it had been called by Doctor R. W. Meek, he acting as tern~

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

226

227

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

porary Ch:>irman. It was found that the first matter of importance was t.he
securing of funds to meet the immediate necessities. Every bank in Oakland and surrounding points was closed. I finally, by giving proper guarantees, was accommodated by Brother Samuel J. Taylor, Secretary of the Realty
Syndicate, with a loan of one thousand dollars in gold, and at this time I desire to express to Brother Taylor my deep and sincere appreciation of his
kindness in our hour of need. Finding that it was not possible to secure further
funds I telegraphed to Los Angeles and instructed that three thousand dollars
in postal money orders be ·sent me from my personal funds !\S I was satisfied
that I could secure the necessary amoi,mt through thepost-office. I will add
that for many days all the available funds I secured was through post-office
money orders sent me from Los Angeles which were promptly cashed through
the courtesy of the Postmasters of Oakland and San "Francisco. This method
immediately relieved the financial situation. Dr. R. W. Meek was elected
President of the Masonic Relief Bureau and appointed the following brethren
members of the Executive Committee. Alfred William Burrell, David
Rutherford, George Roeth, Adam Francis GunnandJosephFountainClui.ndler.
The Masonic Temple at Oakland was immediately opened and lodging given
hundreds in the different rooms in the building. Hot meals were prepared
and no person was refused lod~g or meals. A splendid organization was
effected and to our beloved brethren of Oakland Masonry is surely greatly
indebted. While I do not know the names of many of the volunteers who
gave up their time for the splendid wo~k, still I have their likenesses in my
heart and I can but express in this feeble manner the appreciation which is
due to them from all the Masons of the world. Eighteen large wagons were
secured and through the efforts of the General Relief Committee at Oakland
and the Oakland Board of Trade, both of which organizations were most
kind and generous at !ill times, sufficient provisions were secured to fill the
eighteen wagons and they started the next morning, by first boat for San
Francisco. I personally used a carriage which we loaded with bread and
canned beef, and on arriving in the stricken city food stations were established at manY points, Brother Lawler and myself distributing the provisions
we had to the people on the streets whom we met as we drove to the different
refugee carnps.
Certainly oni:i of the saddest sights I have ever seen wasduring the first
day of our relief work in San Francisco. Mothers called to us as we drove through
the streets begging for bread for their children and milk for their babies, but·
I am very glad to state that it was only on the first day of our work that we
found "the conditions to be so serious for on the following day the food had
arrived in such quantities that all cases of serious distress could be promptly
relieved.
For your information .let me detail in a few words the work of one day
in connection with the Oakland Masonic Relief Bureau and that of your
Grand Master and Grand Orator who spent the entire day for fourteen consecutive days in the strick~n city. In Oakland each night the eighteen wag-

It took some few hours for our brethren in San Francisco to fully realize
their position. Many were dazed by the disaster but it was not many hours
before they came bravely to the front and determined that the Masonic relief
should .stand out boldly. A meeting was promptly called at King Solomon's
Temple, presided over by Worshipful W. Frank Pier.ca, details of organization
perfected and Worshipful Brother Harry J. Lask placed in charge as Secretary.
After discussion the following were elecj;ed permanent officers of the organization: Worshipful Brother William Frank Pierce, President; Worshipful
Brother Harry Joseph Lask, Secretary; Worshipful Brother Harry Davis
Loveland, Vice-President, (Brother Loveland, on account of illness, soon after
resigned and his place was filled by the appointment of Worshipful Brother
Brilsford Pease Flint.) Worshipful Brother Otto Frank Westphal, Treasurer.
This organization developed into what I consider one of the most substantial
and satisfactory relief boards ever gotten together. I have several times examined the business methods adopted and have the highest praise for the
manner in which the work has been carried on from its inception. Complaint
was made to me that the Masters of the lodges of S~n Francisco were not giving the attention necessary to relieve the distre!!B0d and I therefore issued

Immediately after the dire calamity which befel our city on April 18th19th-20th last, and recognizing the importance and necessity of concerted
action for those who were sufferers by the earthquake and fire, a number of
Craftsmen in this city assembled _a nd determined on at least, distributing
food to those who might be in want of it. To this end the directors of King
Solomon's Temple, 1745 Fillmore St., lent assistance and gratuitously placed
their main . rotunda at the disposal of a few zealous Craftsmen, who started
• out immediately to procure eatables. Stores from the general commissary
~ment of the United States Government were obtained. Chairs, tables,
cutting knives, axes and other implements necessary to work with were boriowed, and thus equipped, the iron gates were thrown open and the task o
feeding the hungry began. At first it was only intended that the ·Masons and
their kindred should be supplied, but as supplication after supplication was ·

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

266

267

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

made, almost begging for food, the portals were opened wide, and the distributing station started by Masons for Masons was in reality a veritable
"Gates Ajar".On the first day of the voluntary giving out food, upwards of
seven-thousand persons of both sexes, of all ages, of every nationality and
irrespective of creed or religion were supplied. From that on, and for nearly
nine days thereafter, at least six-thousand rations a day were given out, and .
the fervent "God bless you", the silent thanks and the humble gratitude of
all was more than payment for the trying and strenuous work of the little band of Master Masons who worked day and night, early and late . The
good, big-hearted Craftsmen of Oakland and Alameda County, hearing of the
work that was being done, came to the aid of those in charge by supplying
food in such quantities that at times it was a puzzle where it could be stored.
In the whole world's history covering calamities which have befel cities,
countries and nations, (and none have been handed down in any equalling
that which overcame our cherished city) , is there any record of the feeding
sans cost to any one, as was the case on the many days succeeding the second
and third_ days of the disaster. In a population of over 500,000 persons, and
allowing that 100,000 of them fled the city, there is yet to be heard of one
single instance where anyone went hungry. Arrangement had been made,
and was made for everyone, and it will always be a remembrance, never to
be forgotten, of the millionare standing in front or behind the poorest soul in
the "Bread-line" (Prince and Pauper) awaiting his chance to obtain something, no matter how little or what he might be given, to appease his and his
family's hunger. Conditions were unalterably changed, and "one touch of
nature made the whole world kin". As disasterous and sorrowful as was the
calamity, it had its good effect in rµaking all as one family and binding the
tie· of brotherly love and fraternity stronger. It knew no station in life,
all, like the teachings of Masonry, were of an equality; they met upon the level
and parted on the square - such a square as had never before dawned on
men - not even Craftsmen who suffered, to realize the full meaning and
intent of that teaching, Moreover, it brought an old and sacred Order
. to the front rank of respect and esteem. The profane opened their eyes in
wonderment, and their very looks indicated that Masonry amounted to something .after all, unless how could they who were members of it, succor those
who had belittled and defiled it, and treat all as if of their own fold. The
parable of the good Samaritan was brought home to ·them, as it never was
before; and while our Craft needs no commendation, no thanks, nor testimonial, it is gratifying to know that its principles and teachings have found favor
with many who heretofore have abhorred what they term "Secret Societies" ..
Willingly day after day, with joyful mien, the little band of workers - the
gleaners in the Lord's vineyard of help and assistance,- toiled without murmur, and it was only when it was found that storage for food became the
question, that it was decided to limit the distribution to Masons and their
families oilly. As previously stated, our good brethren of Oakland and Alameda County were supplying us with untold quantities of food of every

Sub-~tations were established, committees were appointed, and the real
work of the Board commenced. The name chosen was:
GENERAL MASONIC RELIEF BOARD
As a compliment to you (moreover deserved) you were induced to
accept the Honorary Chairmanship.
At date of Thursday, April 26th, due and timely notice having been
given a meeting was held at 9.30 o'clock in the morning, at whi?h there were ·
prese~t the officers as before named an? a .majority o~ the el~ct1ve officers of
the several branches of Maaonry in this city. At this meetmg, the officers
elected at the preliminary meeting of April 23rd were made permanent; and
words of commendation for what had already been done, was t~e key-~ote of
all who spok~. Further and more amplified means of extending relief was
discussed and dete:nnined upon, and with every assurance by yourse~ that
ample funds were at the command of the Board, for any and all calls, it was
ordered that a general assemblage of all Master Masons ~e r~qu~ted to meet
and confer with the Board on Monday, April 30th, at which trme it was hoped
every Master Mason in this city would lend a hand to aid the distressed and
those requiring relief.
"Blest be the tie that binds."
On that date, at 9.30 o'clock hi the morning, the meeting took place, and a
more enthusiastic gathering of Masons n~ver assembled. All seemed to be
imbued with the one thought of helping those who were in need of assistan~e,
and the attendance was so large, that many had to content themselves ~th
remaining int.he lobby, and catching here and there a word of what was ta.king
.place in the meeting room. Volunteers ~ere call~d for 1'.<> take cb.arge of
districts in the unburned portions of the city, and 1Il less .trme t~an it ta~es
to record this over two hundred brethren had offered their services to assISt
the Board in
~ork. Districts were outlined, all points were covered, and
a general plan adopted whereby none should be ov:erlooked who needed help.
It was also resolved that the Masters and Wardens of all the blue lodges,
as well as the first three officers of every branch of Maso~, the wom?n relatives of members of the fraternity, should form an adv1~ory co~1tte~ to
this Board, and that meetings should be hdd every morrung, at which trme
the general work of the day should be determined upon, an~ ways and ~e~ns
adopted for carrying into effect a~d the best meth~s of carmg for and aiding
the distressed and homeless. This advjsory committee met for several .weeks
and did much to carry out the noble work outlined by yourself. Durmg ?'11
this time, the officers held frequent meetings and e?1arged the scope of its

its

labors.
It was believed that the addition of two well known Craftsmen as offi~rs
of this Board, and to serve with it in an advisory capacity, would extend its

'

269

sphere of usefullne1;1s, and in consonance with this, R . W. Bro. Jacob Hart
Neff, Past Junior Grand Warden and Bro. Charles Lord Field were made a
part of its executive. The question of employment being brought to the
attention of the Board, it was decided to call a general meeting of the Craft
for Sunday morning, May 13th, and on that date at 10 o'clock, a monster
meeting was held when the immediate necessity of providing situations for
those of our brethren who had lost their employment was brought up, and
sub-committees were appointed to report to the Board any employment that
could be had for those in need of places, and more especially to visit those
members of the Craft requiring help, and acquaint them with the fact that
many of the brethren were in need of employment, and if possible, to give
Masons a preference in engaging help. That meeting was the means of
placing many a Craftsman on his feet, and giving him an opportunity of supporting himself and family, as well as relieveing this Board of much of its
work. Hundreds of positions were found for our brethren, and while scores
of the places accepted were not equal to those held by them previously, still
there was not a murmur of discontent from any one, but on the contrary,
words of thanks for being able to earn a living, were heard on all sides. All
this time, food was being distributed three times a day, and clothing, blankets
and other necessaries and comforts of life bountifully given. The best of
feeling prevailed, and happy, smiling countenances, not withstanding the
terrible ordeal through which they had passed, were the rule and not the
exception.
"And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor
and though I give my body to be burned,
And have not charity, it profiteth me nothing."
The Board also from its inception was furnishing transportation to all
part.a of the world to those who solicited it. It was the policy of the Board not
to give transportation to any able bodied man whose home was in this city
who desired the chance of going to some distant state or country, either for
recreation or to get'away. The need of our men remaining here became more
apparent daily, and it was only to those who had been sojourning here that
such free transportation was given, but no objection to granting it was made
women and children, as they were better off out of the city than in it. The
several railroad and steamship companies gave this Board half-rate fares,
and to them our thanks are more than due
The quarters of the provision department proving inadequate on
account of the great amount of food being distributed it became necessary
to move to a larger place, as well~a.B ask for more volunteers to help in distributing the food. As time wore on, a better system of food distribution
was put into effect. Regular hours of giving out supplies were established
and orders were required from each person applying for the food, an apportionment on the lines of government rations being applied, thereby giving to each
person enough, and still not that over-abundance which might create waste.

Our brethren in charge of this department worked with a will, sometimes
remaining on duty as long as eighteen hours a day, still putting in their time
cheerfully and with never a murmur of discontent. They wanted to please
as well as help their brethren and families and succeeded so well as to ea.rn the
gratitude of ell. ~ j ~
The general offices of the Board were also found to be too s~all and
cramped to efficiently conduct the relief business, which was growing instead
of les.sening, and accepting the generous offer of R. W. Bro. Jac~b Hart Neff
to occupy the splendidly arranged and fitted lower floor of his home, on
Monday, May 7th, the hee.dque.rteis of the Board were moved to 1154 O'Fa.rrell Street, where it has remained &ver since. The word "generous" .is used
above in speaking of the offer from Bro. Neff. It is but a mild adjective, as
·R. W. Bro. Neff has steadily declined to accept remuneration of any kind, and
has even when extra necessities were needed, ·paid for the same himself, and
positively declined reimbursement. The provision department was also
moved, notwithstanding the fact that the location was away from the "maddening crowd", the demands upon us.were even greater than ever. Our hel~rs
were equal to the occasion and no matter how large the number, or pressmg
the demand, all were served, and bountifully at that. Carloads · of c:1moked
and canned meats were sent to us; tons of California's most luscious and
succulent fruit, flour, coffee, canned goods and thousands of loaves of bread
handled, and everything that heart could wish for was donated by our thoughtful and beloved brethren in all parts of our country and state. Dainty boxes
of cooked meats and eggs, together with fruits and canned goods were sent by
the wholesale.
As many of our brethren were destitute of clothing and bedding (inchiding their families) and a.s it became apparent that the external ~ well
as the internal part of their body must. be cared for, the women relatives of
our brethren were pressed into service and by courtesy of Pastor J. Fuendeling of St. Mark's German Evangelical Lutheran Church, the spacious basement of his "House of the Lord" was given for our use, and in it was stocked
a plentifcl supply of every kind of clothing, including outer and underclothing,
not excepting warm comforters and necessities for the baby, as well as the
aged. The Red Cross Society donated upwards of fifteen hundred dollars
worth of f§Pvernment shoes, besides tents, mattresses, blankets and woolens.
The women were placed in full charge of the clothing department and the
requirements of all of our fraternity who applied were supplied. This establishment wa.s maintained until August 1st, when it was deemed best to concentrate the entire work of the Boe.rd under the direct supervision of its
officers, and the department was moved to a large storeroom near our offices
and marui.ged directly from this office ·
"Never sitting down conten~ed w:hile o~ ~el}.ow creatures
a.round us are in want, especially when it 1s m our power
to relieve them."

271

During the first number of weeks of the inception of the Boe.rd, many
thousands of dollars were advanced both to lodges and individuals, who did
not desire our offering, but only asked for an accomodation in the shape of
a loan until such a time as the banks should reopen, or their business so
arranged as to permit them to obtain what was really and justly theirs.
Bank accounts were cashed, cheques paid, money advanced on insurance
policies, the stipendiaries of lodges and the local Boa.rd of Relief taken ca.re
of and the bills and other urgent acco\.Jnts due by lodges paid. All advances
were me.de at their face value, no discounts were taken and no profit attempted, as it was the policy of the Board to assist all of the Craft needing help to
the fullest extent of the meaning of the word "ASSIST". Nearly every loan
or advance so me.de has been repaid, and in many cases the Board was asked
to accept a profit, but in each case the proffer was declined with thanks.
":aenew our ho:i}e, inspire our faith."
Telegrams of offers of help in. the shape of money came in daily and before
a reply could be sent accepting the same, package after package of coin and
currency was being delivered into our Treasurer's hands. Our distant breth~
ren were not slow in showing and proving the metal of their great big-heartedness. Action followed words, and tangible action at that·, and at no time from
the commencement of the work of relief was there· a moment but what ample
funds were at hand to meet any and all exigencies that might arise. The
Board received inspiration at all times· from you, Most Worshipful Sir and
Brother, as every letter and telegram sent by you gave us to understand
that your heart and influence was with us in our work, and you desired the
broadest and most liberal charity shown. Such words as those kept us
filled with a love for the labor we were engaged in, and while we heard nothing
but pitiful stories and saw nothing but sorrow and helplessness, we were
imbued with a spirit to keep on and work the harder for our poor distressed
brethren who had suffered so keenly from the calamity that had befallen us.
In this we were nobly aided by hundreds of our brethren, each of whom
volunteered to share part of our work at any and all times, day or night.
We were in the midst of most trying times, but never undaunted, and our
motto was Nil desperandum. Our only thoughts were to try and alleviate
suffering. and how well we succeeded remains for those assisted to say.
"Charity extends beyond the grave through the
boundless realms of eternity.'
Besides the work of feeding the hungry, clothing those bereft of almost
everything, supplying beds and bedding, furniture, stoves, cooking utensils,
crockery and cutlery, and temporarily assisting others by finding employment for them, and a hundred and one other things to lighten the burden of
their woes, we have cared for and visited the sick, administered to the dying,
buried the dead, traced and recovered lost ones, returned children to their
parents, effected reconciliations, and have thrown the strong protecting arm
of Masonry around many, some of whom would have had injustice done them

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

272

27a

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

and what little they ·had taken from them if not for our intercession.
Through our influence the amounts due from fire insurance companies on
losses have· been obtained, appraisements on losses have been increased at
least twenty per cent, and as high as fifty, and proportionate payments made
on fire insurance matters,· and proofs of loss have been prepared. We have
cashed claims due from the City Relief Finance Committee and Red Cross
Funds, and have drawn legal documents, including agreements, leases,
powers of attorney and other papers. In fact, this Board has performed
and accomplished more than is known, and has even conducted women and
children to the steamers and railroad trains, moved their personal effects
and belongings, assisted them in leaving the city, and attending to their
every want, so that their departure might not only be safe, but s~ gua~?d
as to prevent any confusion or accident arising. We have assisted m rep~1r­
ing dwellings and chimneys, and making houses habitable, as well as rentmg
houses and rooms for many and finding places of abode. The members of
the Board have been at the call of any and every unfortunate, night and.
day, even at "low twelve'', and every case requiring attention has be.en given
immediate help, our motto being "Quick action and needful assISta~ce" ·
Many have been the hurried and wild automobile rides in the dead of rught,
to care for the sick or dying. Physicians have been called, nurses engaged
and hospital se,rvice attended to as quickly as v.ehicles could carry, and often
it has been an all night watch of care and solicitude, but in the end a labor of
love - errands of mercy - with results which fully repaid us.
It has been the endeavor of the Board to keep the expense account as
low as possible. No money has been squandered or _frittered aw~y; nothing
has been purchased in the way of office or other supplies not essentially _ne~es­
sary and the salaries have been fair but not exorbitant. At the begmrung
of 0 :U labors and for some weeks thereafter. it was imperative that some of
our helpers be paid, as they had families to support, and having themselves ·
lost everything by fire and being in the same unfortunate position as thousands of other sufferers and their loved ones having to be fed, clothed and
housed it was no more than right that some small return be given them. Had it
not b~n that we were able to employ them, we must of necessity have relieved them out of the funds at our command, and by giving them something
to do and reasonably compensating them, we saved an amount of money
which otherwise we would have had to doimte, and at the same time, made
them independent. They earned all they recived, in fact they did not receive
enough, but considering what we were constituted for, we did not d~~m it
fair to give them their full worth in pay and they felt as well that it was
incumbent on themselves to give part of their time and services for those who
were in a more unfortunate position than they.

It was decided by the Board after it had been in existence but a short
while, to conduct its affairs as practicable as possible and in aiding those who
might seek our assistance, to apply what is known as practical charity .to our

J

donations, that is, so far as could be applied. To this end it was decided
that true charity consists in helping people to help themselves. From ex:perience it was known that to give an applicant any sum of money at one time
and not try to help him so thii.t he could help himself would be no charity
or assistance to him whatever, but would rather make him a dependent, and
as our Craftsmen hesitated to accept anything that might be termed "Charity",
we gave all to understand that they were only receiving what was their
rights as pledged by each and all by evi!ry tie which binds us together as
Free-masons. To make this RIGHT more effective and pronounced, we
decided on restoring people so far as we could, to the positio1'l occupied by
them prior to the calamity and we have given sewing machines, irons, pressing boards, shears, etc. to those who were tailors, so that they again might
resume their usual avocation. Instruments have been furnished to dentists,
together with dental chairs and machinery necessary to resume their profession; instruments and books to physicians and surgeons; tools to carpenters,
. machinists and all kinds of mechanics ; sewing machines to women who are
dressmakers and for ·household purposes; wagons and horses to laundry
wagon drivers; and to other tradesmen; instruments and charts to seafaring
men; pianos and other musical instruments to music teachers, performers
and vocalists ; photographic supplies and cameras to artists and photographers; electrical appliances to those engaged in the electrical business and to
apprentices learning that, as well as other trades. No profession, art or
calling has been neglected and while as previously noted, we did not attempt
to overdo it, we have given good and plenty and to use . a common term
"have endeavored to put them on their feet again". Even to attorneys and
counselors-at-law have legal books been given, and it may be surprisinp; to
many, when it is known that of all who have sufferei the most through losses
from the fire, professional men and women take the the front rank. Not
only did many of them lose their valuable instruments, reference books and
tllectro-machinery, but their clients and patients scattered, and their business
since then has been such as to barely give them a living.
"Acting with our neighbor upon the square, rendering
him every kind office which justice or mercy may
require, and relieve his distress and soothe his affliction."
Our influence - the strength of Masonry - has been used in more than
one way. It has been successfully carried out in intercessions with the civil
and military authorities. Our letters have been honored in nearly every
instance, and much good has come to many of our brethren and their families through the influence of letters sent by this board to those high in authroity, oft-times not members of the Fraternity, but who recognizing its strength
and well defined principles which are known to the profane as well as to thoEe
initiated into its mysteries.
Nothing that could be thought of for the welfare of our brethren has been
left undone,. and our every thought bas been to devise means to make all a1
happy as could be under the trying times and to give them all the ·succor, help ·

and aid possible. Our only regret at times has been that we_ may not have
done enough for some, but when second thoughts of tha~ kmd came u_pon
us, we have hunted them up and ·made amends for any httle shortcommgs
that may have occured as an error on our part.

The business of the office of the Board has been enormous. When it
is realized what it means to receive thousands of communications, telegrams
and inquiries, and every communication, letter, telegram, postal card and
inquiry an,swered without delay, then some little idea may be formed of
a small part of our work. We have endeavored to conduct our affairs on
strict business lines, not forgetting that Fraternity was coupled with the
busin~ in hand, and to each and a~l, whether by written or verbal commun' cation, it bas been our endeavor to answer every communication, not alone
eqiectitiously, but in an intelligent manner, and to give as fully as possible
the informat.ion desired. Our accounts, data and vouchers are in perfect
shape, and although an audit has been had and everything found to be correct,
the intent of Masonry, one of its most sacred tenets that its
charities must be unostentatious and that the left hand must not, know
what the right hand doeth - has been more than strictly adhered to, and
88 will be further seen by examining the schedules of relief extended, neither
the name of the person assisted nor the lodges of which they claim membership are given, and none outside of yoUrAelf and the members of this Bo~rd
are cognizant of who as indi~duals have been relieved, or as to whether this
lodge or that lodge or other body· of Masonry has received ·more or less than
the other. While it has been essentially necessary for the Board. to have the
names of applicants and lodges, their numbers and locations, in order to keep
its records straight, and its finances clear so that the Board of Audit, (a Committee of the Grand Lodge of this jurisdiction), can intelligently pass on all
vouchers of expenditures; no one but thoRe before mentioned have any definite
information of those aided, and under your instructions, never will. The
vouchers after approval, will have been destroyed and thus an effectual
silence of Masonic law and custom faithfully adhered to.
We believe that with the foregoing a synopsis of our labor has been
reported, and we now present to you Rtatistical, financial and other tables
which will show in detail the full workings of the Board.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Provision Department.
All told when this branch of our work was at the highest point, there
were fully forty of our brethren who assisted in the distribution of food.
This number finally gave way to six, who had all they could attend to for
many days. They worked tirelessly and without complaint, and were the
means of bringing comfort to the hungry and needy. Connected with this
department were four drays and six wagons, each of which made innumerable
trips daily, obtaining cases of food, clothing and bedding at depots, etc., and
distributing orders to those unable to come to us, by reason of infirmity and
old age. When we discontinued our provision department (June 2nd) we
turned over to the Salvation Army about six tons of provisions, consisting
of hams, bacon, canned meats, canned fruits, cereals, etc

able by individual effort and our influence to supply our brethren or their
kin with a few positions, as a.re more fully enumerated in the following excerpt •
from our records. We could have accomplished more in thie; particular line
had those of our brethren in a,ffluent circumstances requiring help come to ·
our assistance and informed us of their wants, giving us the preference· in
supplyinl them with ~hose of our applicants who wanted postions. We
. trust that l)re long such brethren will affiliate with us and make this Boa.rd
the nucleus of an employment bureau which will prove far better for those
needing our care, than the mere giving of alms and other assistance. It will
make many of our applicants self-supporting and be more compatable with
their own self respect and the digriity of the Craft

Conclusion.
"He looketh on the earth, and it trembleth,
He toucheth the hills, and they smoke."
Psalm civ, 32.
And now Most Worshipful Sir and Br~ther, we have placed before you
the record of our labors. We appreciate, as officers of this Board, the great honor
you have conferred :upon us by confiding to our care the noble work which we
have endeavored to carry out. It is a distinction to be proud of, in trying
to help humanity and our brethren. St. James declared that true and undefiled religion before God arid the Father is in visiting the widows and orphans
in their affliction and keeping one's self uD.st>otted from the world. Surely
to relieve the distressed and aid all in affliction and to cheer th'em with sympathy is the divinest work in which man can be engaged. Our obligations
of gratitude to all our brethreen who have in any way assisted us, whether
Jjnancially or by their help, or by their good and ~iQ.d suggestions and ready
JeBponse to our appeal for their advice and assistance can never be expressed
and much less recompensed. Words in such a case are but empty thoughts,
their reward must come hereafter, and from a higher power.
This report would indeed be incomplete_without some little recognitio
by name of several of our brethren who have given so freely of their time and
labor and have so unselfishly devoted the best efforts of their hearts to ai
us and our unfortunate in the severest and most urgent cases. To our Bro.
George Henry Boskowitz, M. D., of Doric Loqge No. 216, mode~t and unostentatious, no words are adequate to render to him our gratitude and that o
all the Fraternity for his many acts of professional kindness. Day and night,
always at our command, leaving his large pra~tice to be of service to o~r
sick and dying, he has gratuitously given his skill, and we would be truly
iangra.teful did we not here mention him as an example of all that is Masonic
and noble.
Our Bro. Roland English Hartley, M. D., Past Ma8ter of King Solomon's
Lodge No. 260, is also here placed on our roll of honour, for always and ever
ready to visit and care for the sick, following· his every obligation to aid his
brethren whenever and wherever in distress.
To Bro. James William Ward, M. D., of Crock~tt Lodge No. 139, we are
under the deepest obligation. Occupying the position of President o f
the board of Health of this City and County, it has been our good fortune
to have him as a member of the Fraternity and to personally know him as
a man and physician: All the influence at his command has been freel
.granted to us. Position after position has he given those of qur brethren
qualified .to fill the same. In such places where he needed men, e,nd th e
hospitals under his control have been the haven of many. a poor unfortunate
demanding his attention, with the best of care and skill given them to restore
health and happiness.
·Others too numerous to mention, of the same profession, have served us
or offered their ·services and to all .we can truly say THANKS.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

We cannot conclude this report without mentioning what in our opinion
is the present condition of unfortunate and distressed members of the Craft
and their families in this City. At the present time we firmly believe that
all who suffered either physically or financially, or both, from the earthquake
and fire, to be in fairly good condition, that is so far as immediate wants and
necessities are concerned. All their wants have been met as fully and as to
their needs as has been possible, and while we admit that there may be some
whose wants may not have been made known to us, those who have applied
or been sought, have had · everything done for them that could be, and
that all of these are comfortably situated at present and are nearly above want
of anything. That, for the past and present, but the future is ':vhat is troubling us. We grieve to say that we fear .for the future. We are fearful of the
approaching winter. This may seem pessimistic, but to be truthful, we must
say so, although we should have preferred to have taken the other view, and
would have done so, had we the slightest belief in the roseate word -<>ptimi.&tic.. While the people of this city are to be give~ every credit, and which is
no more than deserving, for their fortitude in the hour of affliction, and their

the aid of us or from any other source. W~ hope and pray for the best, but

every human being and our purpose is to learn how to use the materials to

of the Great Architect of the Universe."

The earth's crust was shaking, quivering, .wrenching to the right and left
and in other opposite directions and it seemed that nothing could survive the

of the wounded and dying ceased, those who had escaped unharmed stood

It aeemed like a tomb in the open streets. Not a thing of life seemed to
move or breathe. The seriousness of the situation could n,ot at first be grasped.
From all eections of San Francisco .there could be plainly seen the glare of
light on the leaden sky cast by the fires which had sprung up in a hundi:ed
different directions almost simultaneously. The dread cry that water was
not available with which to fight the flames was passe.d from lip to lip and not
unlike Nero at the destruction· of the beautiful city of :Rome, the homeless
eettled down to witness the scenes .of desolation .and ruin.
It was not for long, however, for soon· every available able-bodied man
was preseed into service in the attempt to stay the flames which were fast deYouring l>uildings and property which had survived the tremblor. As the
men fought fast and hard, the women and children were hurriedly carrying
away the belongings from their doomed homes. Many pitiful sights were
witnelllled, many acts of charity were done and through it all the residents
llbowed a spirit of bravery and unconcern IJ).atchless in every particular.
Hardly had the last severe shock subsided before Mayor Schmitz and
other officials of San Francisco were at work attempting to quiet a bewildered
almtitude, and the l!Oldiery-the men· of blue who know not what fear is-the men of blue of both the army and the police force-were soon patrolling

the streets to prevent looting and the wanton destruction of property. The
commanders located at the Presidio on that verge of land kissed by the first
waters which fl.ow and ebb from the yawning mouth of the Golden Gate, did
wondrous things on behalf of tlie sufferers. They brought order out of chaos,
stilled the fear which seemed to close the throats of strong men and dependent ·
women and in tens of thousands of ways assisted in the work of caring for
thos~ who had lost their all in the earthquake and fire, ·
Some of the scenes enacted during the first hours of the burning of the
city beggar description. The hospitals and homes for the wretched were
turned into mad houses. Patients who were unable to care for themselves
groaned and cried out with feelings of helplessness, and, the stronger ones,-:those on the way to recovery-ran about like one possessed. Fainting women,
praying men and bewildered children could be seen on every hand and the
work of removing the sick, tlie crippled and the otherwise afflicted to the general hospital at the Presidio was by no mealli! a small undertaking. There
were many nurses, who, from a feeling of duty had worked themselves beyond
the power of human endurance and fell fainting to the floor. This:added to
the already long list of sufferers and for a time confusion reigned supreme.
As the flames, stealthily at times, then noisily and with a roar of defiance
swept their way along the principal streets, many lives were snuffed out. The
dead and dying were tenderly cared for, but those who were in positions to
know agree that San Francisco's death roll would be long in calling provided
everybody had been recovered. The flames and resulting ruins have carefully and completely hidden from human sight all that remains of many who
were once prosperous citizens and beloved members of now grieving families.
For a time it appeared that there would be much illness in the city by
the Golden Gate and that there would be a famine, but these things happily
did not occur owing to the liberality and promptness of the outside cities providing food and clothing and Oakland was by no means the last to come to
the aid of her sister city :which was so sorely stricken. In fact it was through
the efforts of the generous citizens, worthy officials and lodges and churches of
Oakland that San Francisco was not left to suffer and hold out her scorched
and withered hands for succor one moment longer than was absolutely necessary.
After days and nights of bitter strife with the flames which had greedily
consumed millions of dolla!'S worth of property, it appeared that they were
under control, and hundreds, yes thousands of workers, both civilian and of
the army, who had kept the city in a roar with exploding dynamite, the use
of axes and wrecking paraphernalia, sank from utter exhaustion and in their
tum needed the care of thor;ie for whom they had risked their lives that a portion at least of the city's homes might be spared.

it all seemed like a dream~ that nothing so overwhelmingly disastrous, it. ap-

Through all this terrible disaster by which every hotel, bank, every large

thousands more who were left without the means of livelihood, was admirable. There was very little panic and no serious disorder. The rations, tents,
and blankets on hand at the army posts adjacent to the city were dealt out
to the sufferers with no account of the responsibility involved; and within
two days, relief supplies from n~ighboring states and cities and army supplies
from Tarious army posts had begun to arrive and were being distributed.

Within a few hours after the disaster, there was not a member of the
Masonic organization on either side of the bay who had not been cared for
in one way or another. This refers to those in want. All those who had
•caped without loss in any direction, gladly joined with the working forces
and gave their aid in relieving the suffering which had existed in every direction.
As a first step in the direction of relief, the Masonic Relief Bureau on the
aecond day following the disaster sent eighteen wagons drawn by two horse,,
each, filled with provisions to the stricken city. At a low estimate one hundred
and fifty tons of provisions were. sent to San Francisco, the most of it being
furnished at the expense of the Masons. True it is that a portion of this
amount was given by the Oakland Chamber of Commerce.
For over a week the brethren worked like slaves in San Francisco and
did not complete all their work in Oakland for months after the disaster.
The headquarters in Oakland were in the Masonic Temple at Twelfth and
'Washington streets and there were stations established in SanFranciscoat
llwenty-third and Mission streets, at the Stanyan street entrance to the Park,
one in King Solomon's Hall on Fillmore street, one at North Beach and another
one at 3584 Clay street. Besides' these there was a head. distributing point
and office in the ferry building. The amount of business transacted in these
quarters was enormous. At the ferry station there was a force of men con1tantly preparing sandwiches which were carried off in teams for distribution.
At least $15 a day was paid out for each of these wagons by the Masons and
•fterthey had distributed the food, they picked uP'refugees' trunks and baggage
on their return trip. A regular checking system was established and many
arti_cies were carried to headquarters for the refugees regardless of sex, race,
color or to which fraternal organization, if any, they~belonged. And besides
the food which was freely distributed to the needy in San Francisco, over
35,000 meals were supplied the refugees in the Oakland Temple. Money
was sent in liberally from all quarters of the United States and this with what
had been given locally, resulted in an immense relief fund at the' disposal of
the Masonic fraternity.
The executive committee of the order ~as most generously treated by
the Santa Fe and Southern Pacific Railroad companies. In many instances,
money was advanced for transport_a tion and besides this the companies never
refused an~ tmnsp~rtation to worthy and deserving people. In all the relief
work done m the city of Oakland and surrounding communities the railroad
IJlfPilizations aided materially, and had it not ·been for their conscientious
effort on behalf of those doing relief work, but little headway could have been
made. The Masonic fraternity are particularly thankful to the companies

At the time'of the arrival of the.advance guard of the Masonic fraternity,
Market. street was full of excited, anxious people who were gazing horrified
at the ruins as the result of the various fires which had been merged into one
great conflagration. The presence of the members of this order with flying
badges had an instantly reassuring effect on all awe-inspired persons. They
knew the quality of the men wearing the badges and not in· one instance did
anyone of those in the streets apply for aid that it waa not granted.
The thing that at this time made the greatest impresiiiori on the working lodge men was the strange and unearthly silence. · There was no talking,
no apparent excitement among the near-by spectators; while from the great
and dying. city lying at their feet there came not a single unusual sound. No
one seemed to be greatly concerned over material possessions and each was
to the' other as a brother. San Francisco had indeed been taught a hard lesson
and a lesson that softened in some distinct manner the instincts of the sufferers or their more fortunate brothers and sisters.· Not that charity and
self-denialhadnoeager followers before that memorable .time, but the terrific
disaster set more people to thinking of the bible's teachings than could all
the sermons ever preached from the pulpits of high or lowly houses of worship.

hither and thither, caring not for dress, for jewels, for nothing but safety.
