It has been stated that in all the overwhelming calamity that befell San
Francisco during the three days' and nights' conflagration that followed the
earthquake, one of the supreme tragic moments was reached that Wednesday morning when the firemen, rushing with their engines and hose carts to
the various points of alarm, found themselves standing helpleBB bef?re the
spreading flames beside empty hydrant!l. But there ":'ere more _tragic moments than that. One of them was when Chief of the Firemen Sullivan was at
death's door by an injury sustained at the time qf the earth~ua}ce. But _the
supreme tragic moment, the one that appealed to everyone m San Francisco
and outside points was, "what can be done with the hundreds of thousands
who are homeless and penniless?" The earthquake and fire were the acts
of God. The care for the poor, bewildered and destitute were the acts of.
humanity. And from where was the first step toward relief to come? The
officials and the soldiery were active, but what of them in the case of those
who were flocking into the city of Oakland by the thousands- yes- tens of
thousands? They came unclothed-they came hungry, destitute, weary ~nd
with hearts and minds heavy and numb because of the ordeal through which
they had just passed. This was the supreme moment and it is fortunate that
there were men in the city of Oakland who were equal to the emergency and
a goodly number of them wore the insi&nia of the Masonic fraternity.
On the Oakland side of San Francisco bay, it was like taking command
of a battle after it had been turned into a rout. The effectual fire fighting
in San Francisco was on the part of brave men who had the endurance or
permi88ion to stay in threatened buildings, in fact it was of their own ch~ice,
but the ca.ce of the wanderers, the putting of life into the stomachs ~nd mmds
of the wretched and depressed, the clothing of the naked, the feedmg o_f the
destitute, fell into the hands of just as brave men as those who had nsked.
their lives in the attempt with dynamite and battering rams to stop the spread
of the flames. For is it not an act of bravery and stout-heartedness to feed
and clothe restless thousands when it took determined effort to find either
clothing or food, to find places in which the wretched could lay_ their heads,
to find blankets with which to cover their shivering forms? Is it not an act
of bravery to abandon one's business, to go without necessary sleep and to
labor by the light of the sun and throughout the dark~t hours on ?ehalf of
those unfortunates with whom you have no acquamtance or ties of relationship? Is it not bravery to risk your own lives to save those who hold
out hands of want to you for assistance? And these things and more were
done by the o·akland Masonic Relief Bureau.
.
Befor~ going into detail ·as to work done in the city of ~akland by the
Masonic Relief Bureau after the arrival of the refugees here, it may be well
to give some reasons as to the necessity for su?h a c~aotic condi~ion of affairs from the scientific side of it. Alexander G. McAd1e of the Umted Sta~es
Weather Bureau situated in San Francisco has said, "that not the leas~ mteresting feature of the great earthquake was the record made at va~ous
points on the earth's surface, showing the displacement of the earth particle, ·

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

311

or in other words, the indication of the passing earth tremors and waves.
The instrument by which earthquake motion is determined is called a seis1nograph, and the particular type of instrument most favored today is the
9e1ich-Omori horizontal pendulum seismograph. The instrument obtains
its name from an eminent investigator Bosch; and an equally eminent Jap-anese iavestigator- Dr. F. Omori, Professor of Seismology in the Tokyo Imperial University and member of the Imperial Earthquake . Investigation
eeromittee. Ten or more of these instruments are installed at different points
around the globe, and doubtless very full records have been attained, the diseuBBion of which will materially increase our knowledge of the way in which
the earth's surface transmits the jar occasioned by any great slip or dislocation of strata, commonly called an earthquake.
"Europe seems far away from the Pacific Coast and yet within twenty
minutes from the time the earthquake began in San Francisco these horizontal and vertical Micro-Seismographs were busy recording, as best they could,
the different sets of wave motions traversing the United States, speeding
across the Atlantic and hurrying throughout Europe. Japan iB our neighbor
to the West. but not a close neighbor. Within eleven and one-half minutes
the seismographs in Tokyo were recording the beginning of the shock in San
Francisco. · It was then about 10:30 Wednesday night in Japan-Japan
standard time. Without delay Prof. Omori could tell by means of the record
given on the seismograph the.t a severe earthquake had occurred on the American side of the Pacific at 5:13:05 A. M. -our time. The record of the earthquake at Washington, D. C., in the weather bure~u laboratory obtained by
Prof. Charles Marvin, with a large Omori seismograph, told' him before the
news had yet arrived from San Francisco that a severe dislocation of the
earth's crust had occurred about 2450 miles away from Washington. It was
then 8:19 in the morning, Washington time. The actual displacement of
the ground at Washington, D. C., was nearly one-half inch each side of a point
of rest. The movement was so slow, however, that only a seismograph could
detect it.
"At Tokyo the movement was a little less and equally slow. In San
Francisco if a record of the movement could have been obtained, perhaps an
inch or more each side of the neutral point would have been recorded· but
executed in an extremely short time. These displacements, continuin~ for
about forty seconds, from west to east and back again, and up and down,
constitute the heavy, racking and twisting motions known to 311 of us.
"One of the most interesting features of the seismograph record is the
duration of the so-called preliminary tremors. These small waves travel
through the body of the earth at the rate of about six or seven miles a second. They precede the larger waves, which apparently move on the earth's
surface and travel at a rate of about two mile.s a second. Knowing the interval between the beginning of the preliminary tremors and the beginning
of the surface waves, we can determine approximately the point or line of

origin of the earthquake. Thus at Washington the preliminary tremo~ la~ted
six minutes. At Tokyo, nme minutes and forty-nine seconds. At Brrmmgham, Engiand, they lasted twenty-five minuU:S. Somet~me in the future
when seismographs will be in use in San FranclBCO, we will be able to note
the beginning of a sma)l earthquake, and by comp11.ring o~~ seismograph
with those made elsewhere, determine the center or line of ongm.
''At 'a point exactly midway around the wotld from San Francisco _the
tremors would have lasted twenty-eight minutes. It is not merely to satisfy
scientific curiosity that such records are made. Far from it. The welfare
of mankind is the objective. Judging from the history of disturbanoes in .
this kindly land, the present generation will probably not be called upon to .
again undergo such experiences as those of April 18th. Mankind fortunately
recovers quickly and as quickly forgets. A certain few, however, more de- '
-voted than ever to their labors, will follow the trail with a doggedness and
persistence tha t can only spell achievement, measuring earth movements
for the welfare of all men."

The brothers sent to San Francisco received much praise at the hands
of their superi.o rs for the splendid results they obtained and the general good
work done there. It was no easy task to climb about the brick-filled st reets
and through hot debris .to reach the side of those in trouble; it was no easy
task to convince many that it would be safe to cross San Francisco bay to
Oakland as they had been informed that Oakland was as bad off as San Francisco if not worse. As soon as they were prevailed to come to Oaklan d, how
ever, they were glad of the chance to get somewhere where they knew that
they would be provided for in every way. They were clothed, fed, housed,
cive.Q money, provided with transportation and sympathy at the hands of
the Masonic Relief Bureau and many of those so aided had no connection
JVhatever with the Masons or any member of the Masonic fraternity. Yet
this ha d no effect on the attention given them. The Masonic records of the
p at andoverwhelmingdisast er show that numerous utter strangers to Mallru"Yor the crafth 1d the bestofatt.ention and a t no cost to themselves. Hunlllredsof women and likewisemenwho hadnoplacetogoandwhowere in need of
food, were taken in by the committees and properly attended. No worthy
Jllllbject, and in fact many unworthy ones were lifted upon their feet by those
who had willingly given their time and attention to the helpless who came
to Oakland in droves.
A slight idea of the enormous amount of work and good done by the Ma1<>nic Relief Bureau can be gleaned from minutes held by the members of
.the bureau and of the Executive Committee. The first meeting, as has been
told, was held on the twentieth day of April, a time when it was seen that every
~e.nization, church and individual must put forth their best efforts to.care .
for the thousands of refugees who were flocking to the Oakland side of the
bay. At that meeting, necessary committees were appointed and steps were
taken for obtaining and distributing information badges that there should
be no hitch ~n efficient service. It was at this meeting that the Grand Lodge
and the entire order of the state promised their support in the work. During the evening of the same day the wives of the members.of the various lodges
were called in.to take a hand and right well did they do the work laid down
for them. The executive committee was appointed during this meeting
and many brothers volun~ered their services in any capacity. In fact there
were so many wishing to give their aid, that no work could be found for them
to do. There was not a member of the order found who was not willing and
even anXious to get in line with the workers.
On a called meeting for April 28th, it being called to order by Chairman
R. W. Meek, it was agreed to transfer the work of the committee to the secretary. In consequence the chairman was empowered to employ a. competent
pen~m who gave his entire time to the relief work. This was a great saving
of tu:ne to the committee which was working night and day to keep things
l'Unnmg smoothly and to see that all the wants of the refugees were attended
to. It was agreed at this meeting that the Executive Committee should
rneet nightly, until the st ress of trouble was over, and it was also agreed thRt.

work bard and those who believe that relief work from standpoint of this committee is not difficult and trying work, he or she try it. Here and there and
there and here for something for the needy to rest a weary head. A hunt
foracot,asearchfora bedand when thedayis done and although hundreds have
been provided for in this direction, there are hundreds more waiting for a
f'petition of the work that has gone before. And the Train Committee.
Those who have fought their way through large crowds just for the purpose
of finding a relative or friend, can realize what the members of such a committee must have to contend with. At the time just following the earthquake there were thousands hurrying to Oakland. It was the duty of the
members of this committee to locate the deserving refugees and see to it that
they were properly cared for, and it was a gigantic undertaking.
Then we have the Housing committee. The members of this committee

were obliged to go from place to place in se~rch of rooms and other accommo-

dations for those who were arriving in Oakland faster than they could be
provided for byall the relief committees, lodges, churches and other like asso'Ciations. The Housing committee worked day and night in Oakland to get
~ms for those who depended upon them in this direction. Every house
1Il Oakland was visited with the hopes that a vacant room could be found.
They were successful in many instances but in a great majority of cases, the
'tranderers were sent to the refugee camps or to tents provided for them.
Bvery cot available to the Masons was pressed into service regardless of race,

These first one hundred applications are included in this report with the
object in view of showing the various requirements of the refugees and to
illustrate how many different lodges had members who were rendered entirely destitute by flame and earthquake.
Some wanted one thing and some another. There were petitions for
transportation, food, clothing, cooking utensils, tents, cots and bedding and
numerous other articles needless to mention. The largest number probably
asked for transportation as they were anxious to get near friends or reln.t.ives.
But hundreds .were clothed and fed during the days of stress a11d discontent
following the disaster. In the Masonic Temple there was an unusually busy
scene. Those without pl.8.ces to sleep and those without f~ or shelter were
all provided for and it is safe to say that the members of the Masonic fraternities were as heavy losers as those connected with any like organizatio1!.

•

And the members of the Oakland Masonic Relief Bureau did not stop
to look into their own losses when they saw the thousands or homeless flock~.
ing in Oakland. They at once prepared to meet the emergency and most
well did they do the work. They worked hand in hand with the Oakland
Relief C-0mmittee and outside lodges and also did much individual and collective relief work. Had it not been for the Oakland Masonic Relief Bureau ·
in Oakland there would have been much unnecessary suffering and want.
The .Mason~,~ has been said before, did iiot only care for Masons, but out
of the generosity of their own hearts and pockets, prepared most generously
and aided greatly in the general relief work which was going on. ~n f~ct
the Oakland Masonic Bureau considered itself a part of a great orgamzatton
of relief committeell, lodges and churches which were working toward one
end-the care of the. de9titute and the protection of the helpless.
The exact details of the· work can never be tabulated. So much good
was done and quickly forgotten because of something else to do, that no record
was kept of every act, but the general aid given and the charity extended,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

321

will not be forg~tten long after the city of San Francisco has cleared away
her debris and nsen anew, one of the grandest cities of our United States.
And she will not forget that Oakland willingly and unselfishly held out a helping hand to the ~wildered San Franciscans who called loudly for aid.
Those who worked with and assisted the Oakland Masonic Relief Bureau, have ~ot looked. for nor did they expect that they would receive any
words of praise for their many worthy acts, but to give succor to the hungry,
to hunt ou~ homes ~or th_e needy and to do other such deeds of valor, place
111clt men side by side with those who have made history "through times of
war and troublous periods. The man who will assist another man and neglect his own affairs and relatives to do so, is a man, every inch of him. And
the world knows it, knows that Oakland produced more real men than has
been the fortune of any other city within the confines of the Umted States.
For the occasion present;ild itself and those in charge of things, were not found
wanting.
Money was no object to those doing relief work. The pinched drawn
mieerable faces and bodies of. the women and children as well as ~en wh~
came here for succor and relief, were too much a lesson of self denial to allow
any to stop to think of self gain or self sacrifice. Taken from the outset the
the affair was well and most thoroughly handled. While the members of the
Masonic Bureau were doing all in their power to relieve suffering, there were
others in Oakland doing the same. And when the needy were concentrated
in the camps on the Oakland shores of San Francisco bay, the efforts of a.II
were doubled
Nightly meetings of the executive committee were held while the crisis
was on and they were all well attended. Questions of vital moment were
discussed and considered from every view-point and in ·m ost instances were
decided with practical unanimity. And .the financing of this emergency enterprise was no small matter of itself. The money raised in Oakland was
fllpplemented by generous contributions from many outside points. The
difficulty and rather delicate duty of determining the demands made upon
the treasury was carefully and conscientiously performed and a system of
vouchers was devised that saved many dollars for the Masonic Bureau and
paranteed the disbursement of money vyithout fear of favor or mistake.
The ladies who gave such great and willing assistance during the days
'
of trials and troubles following the earthquake and fire, should come in for
m~ch ~rving praise. Their knowledge of humanity and their quick sense
of JUBt1ce, worked much toward the splendid ends attained. They were here,
there and everywhere, looking out for the interests of the affiicted and had
it not been for their hearty co-operation with the ma.le sex, who were alsohard and willing workers, it is more than probable that it would have ta.ken ·
much more time to right affairs than it did.
·
There is one individual whose position was most trying and yet who wa."
never heard to enter a complaint and that person is Robert G." Evans, chief

..

322

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

of the Commissary depa rtment. Although his duties were many and varied,
he attended to them with such exactness and business ability, that there was
no confusion in obtaining and distributing food to the refugees. At one time
shortly after the overwhelming disaster, the banquet hall in the Masonic
Temple proved inadequate for the horde of needy who were served with meals
and a coffee and sandwich line was instituted on the street. For a number
of days there were hundreds who satisfied their appetites in this manner and
the line was done away with only after affairs had become largely settled.
Mr. Evans had much assistance from the ladies in his work and felt thankful
for it.
It might be said again that it would be utterly useless to give a detailed .
statement of the work done or to personally mention each and every one who
had a hand in the work, but they have satisfaction in the fact that their work
was appreciated, it having been done well-extremely well. Those who
toiled in Oakland and thoiie who labored in San Francisco well realize that
if it had not been for united effort on the part of ali concerned, no such worthy
and commendable ·a ctions could have been carried out and no such self-sat isfying results have been obtained. There is hot a man, woman or child,
Mason, or members of other organizations who can help but admit tha t the
liberality of Most Worshipful Motley H. Flint was not excelled by any individual nor can they deny that Dr. R. W. Meek, Chairman of the Executive
committee and President of the Oakland Masonic Relief Association did not ·
do everything in his power to aid the afflicted and to give his assistan ce toe~ry mn.TJ who willingly gave time and attention to the work of relief. Neither
can it be denied that each and every member of any of the committees under
the Masonic order did all within human reason and endurance to carry out
the work laid do'l'l'n for tl;iem. The sick were sent to proper institutions or
to fri·e nds, the naked were given clothing, the hungry were liberally fed, the
strangers were given transportation to their homes and everything was done
that could be done for the welfare of the unfortunate visitors from San Francisco.

Despite the fact that the officers and committeemen as well as many
others did all in their power to give comfort to the needy, they would have
been powerless to act without the aid of those who contributed so liberally
to the relief fund of the Masonic Relief Bureau of Oakland. Money poured
in from every direction and was put to the best of use. Everyt hing was
carried on along strictly business lines and the financial report shows that the
Oakland Masonic Relief Bureau had on hand at the meeting of September
10, 1906, the splendid sum of $11,046.08. As the relief work is to be continued
throughout the year, this money will be used in the general work of relief
and that it will be judiciously distributed, goes without saying.

ALAMEDA RELIEF BOARD.
Alameda, Cal., Sept. 16, '06.
Motley H. Flint,
Most Worshipful Grand Master,
Los Angeles, Cal.
Dear Sir and Brothn:We submit herewith statement of the relief extended by Oak Grove Lodge
No. 215, F. & A. l\J.
On April 19th, 1906, a special meeting was called for the purpose to
provide ways and means to secure aid for the refugees. A motion was made
and seconded that the Master be authorized to spend $500. 00 arid appoint a
committee of fifteen to assist him in caring for them.
The committee was divided into squads of three who worked on all the
local trains coming into our city and turned them over to others who were
in waiting to receive them and conveyed by vehicle to our hall, where they
were fed and made as comfortable as possible.
A quantity of beddin~ was bought, used for making beds for the many
-~fugees, the large hall bemg for fai:nilies and women; the small hall being
used for the men.
A number were permitted to take bedding where shelter could be provided
in different parts of our city.
·
The Temple was thrown open on the morning of April 20 and was kept
open for twenty-four hours per day till Thursday, May 3, 1906, when the dining
room was closed.
No account was kept of the number of meals served.
No one was turned away, no questions asked as to sect or opinion, that a per·
son who came up the steps was in need was sufficient.
Through the aid of the Ladies of the Eastern Star, and others, the dix:tlng
room was handled splendidly, Bowers brightened the tables and the sympathetic ·
touch of these kind hands gladdened the hearts of many a sufferer.
The committee are indebted to many who gave their time and service
and others who refused pay· for service and supplies;·
. ·. .

SAN JOSE RELIEF BOARD.
To Motley H. Flint,
Grand Master F. & A. M., of California.
M. W. Sir and Brother:
The great calamity of April last, occasioned special and immediate
action in doing our ·part toward rendering every kind office that might be
required of the Masonic Fraternity in those trying days.

•

Many thoughtful and kindly acts had already been performed by members of the craft, both as citizens and Masons and by the Masonic Board of
Relief ot San Jose, when a special gathering of Masons took place on
Sunday morning, April 22nd at the Masonic Temple at San ·Jose, called by
the Masters of the Lodges of that city at which I was i;ppointed permanent
chairman. A secretary and two assistants were chosen and arrangements
made for systematic relief work at the railroad depots and elsewhere.
Inside of an hour after adjournment, a large tent had been erected at the S. P.
Depot · and headquarters established there. The trustees of the Unitai:ian
Church kindly tendered the fraternity the use of the church and the edffi'ce
wn.s immediately supplied with cots, blankets etc. for caring for the refugees
from San Francisco.
Books were also at once opened by the Secretaries to reoord the names.
of Masons who had rooms at their homes that might be used for brethem in
need of such and many hundreds were cared for in that manner, thereby
rendering a kindly office as well as spreading the cement of brotherly love
and affection.
This class of work went on for many days, regular changes being made
in the personnel of the members stationed at the depots and el~ewhere.
The headquarters were kept open all night for over a week.
With thankfulness I note that not a death occurred among the members
of the craft in this district, as a result of the catastrophe; though several
members were injured and a great many lost a portion or all their possessions.
The whole-heartedness with which the Masonic fraternity here and
elsewhere entered into the work of relief occasioned not only all the cominendation of members of the Craft, but received the benediction of the people
at large
Thanks is due to the railroad companies for carrying many members .to
and from this city free ~f charge for transportation, some members indeed
being given transportation a great distance .

With great gratitude to those jurisdictions

M. W. Motley H. Flint
Grand Master of Masons of Calif.
Dear Sir and Brother:As requested by you, I attach report showing relief given to San Francisco Fire Sufferers by Sacramento Masonic Board of Relief.
Our Board, whj.ch is composed of the MBBters ~d Wardens of the five
Lodges here, met on the day following the catastrophe to make arrangements
to take care of all who might come this way. At the Board's request, I made
a trip to Oakland and personally offered you our assistance. The Masters
reported to the Board that their Lodges stood ready to assist us financially
as did the Masonie Hall Ass'n, Sacramento Chapter No. 3, R. A. M. and the
Scottish Rite Bodies and also appointed members to act in conjunction with
the Board. Committees were appointed to remain on duty at the Hall, and
INT~gements were made to furnish Board and Lodgings. We did not have as
many cases as we expected, but this was due to the fact that the majority
of those who left San Francisco continued on to Eastern points .
The report shows a balance of $278 . 60 and the Board thinks that if
you decide to allow us to retain this balance, it will, with the amount wc have
in our General Fund, last us through the winter.
Trusting the report meets with your approval, I remain,
Yours fraternally,
F. A. Roblin,.
Secretary.

FRUITVALE RELIEF BOARD.
Fruitvale, August 18, 1906.
Motley H. Flint, M. W. Grand Master of F. & A. M. of Cal.,
Dear Sir and Broth!!1
Your request concerning the relief work done, at hand. At the call of
the Master of Fruitvale Lodge, a meeting of the members convened for the
express purppse of providing some ways and means to take care of refugees,
masons and others who might come from San Francisco
The most feasible plan proposed and adopted as the best, was the establishment of Masonic Headquarters on the main thoroughfare and the appointment of a committee to act i,n conjunction with the officers of the lodge,
to visit San Francisco and also to wait upon the local trains which arrive
every 20 minutes in Fruitvale from San Francisco. To aid and assist refugee
Masons and other · needy persons, the . committee made themselves conspiCuous by the Masonic badges they wore. In this way Masons were easier
identified, located and temporary shelter provided.
At a call meeting of the Lodge on April 30, arrangements were formulated
to have a committee of brethem in the vicinity surrounding their homes
visit their neighbors and ascertain if there were any Masons stopping with
them and whether they could provide room for any refugees. This committee which consisted of thirty-Bix members, made this search on the· day
following and secured places of shelter for a large number of families. A
committee visited the Oakland Masonic Board of Relief and were informed
by that body that. whatever provisions were needed for refugees in Fruitvale
might be obtained from them for the expressing of them to Fruitvale. ·The
expressing was provided for and the provisions· taken to the Fruitvale headquarters and distributed to the needy, although a number-were provided with
provisions in this manner. A great number were taken care of at the homes of
brethem who did not call on the Relief Board for assistance
·•
One hundred and twenty-Beven Masons were taken care of hi tills manner.
Doctors of the Fruitvale Lodge gave their attention to the sick free of
any charge.
.
I only mention the above to have it clear in your mind that the brethem
of Fruitvale Lodge met their obligations without any shirking of their duty.
I will concede to your request regarding the expenses, but with the understanding that Fruitvale Lodge does not wish to be re-imbursed. The brothers
appreciating the fact that they were called upon to help in the hour of need.

as although it is true we have several Brothers on our rolls who will undoubteclly require ~i~tance, we are quite confident that the funds of the Lodge
will be ample for all demands.
We desire to callyourspecial attention to the noble work perform~d· by
·the ladies of Unity Chapter, No. 65, 0. E. S. without whose assistance we could
have accomplished but little. They responded to the call for help instantly
and willingly, and for nine days worked early and late in ministering to the
wants of hundreds of refugees, as well as three companies of soldiers whb
were quartered on us at diff~rent times.
No account was kept of the number of meals served, but a conservative
estimate would. place the number at four t~ousand.
Our main Lodge Room was used as a dormitory by the refugees, and the
large assembly hall on the firstfloorwas placed at the disposal of the s?ldiers.
All who made themselves known as being in any way connected with the
Masonic Fraternity were ~irected to the Masonic Committee's headquarters
at 12th and Washington Sts., where special attention was accorded them.
Several of our members were active participants in the work of this C'-0mmittee
whose endeavors can only be commended in the highest terms, a full account
of which will doubtless be rendered to you from other sources.
Special mention must also be made of the other Fraternal organizatiolll!
who occupy our Lodge room, and who for over three weeks surrendered their
rights without a murmur-neither asking or expeeting any rebate in their
rent, and many of the individual members offering contributions of mon.ey
supplies and ·services.
Thanking you most sincerely for the interest you have displayed in Alcatraz Lodge, I remain,
Fraternally Yours,
H. A. GLINES,·
Secretary.

LOS ANGELES RELIEF BOARD.
To the Most Worshipful
Motley Hewes Flint Grand Master of Masons
State of California:
Dear Sir and ·Brother:Complying with your request of August 16, 1£06, concerning the action
which this Board of Relief took in the matter of the dirnster occasioned by
~quake and fire which befel the Central portion of our glorious State,
on the 18th day of April, 1906, will say:·
. That immediately upon the realization of that awful calamity, a special
meeting of the Masonic Board of R.elief of Los Angeles, was called on April
22nd, 1906, at which meeting I was directed to communicatE: with each Maeonic Body of this City, and request a contribution of One Dollar ($1. 00)
{ler capita, to enable our Board . to relieve the clistJess of the n:embers of the
craft, and those dependent upon them who might take refuge in our City.
This request was promptly complied with, and there came into my hands,
as Secretary, from the various Masonic Bodies of our city, together with
individual contributions; and also from Mount Zion lodge of Troy, N. Y.,
the sum of Three Thousand One Hundred and Seventy-Four Dollars and
Fifty Cents ($3, 174 . 50 ).
Arrangements were made that the Masonic Board of R.elief, should
establish Headquarters at the Masonic Temple, and notices were placed in
all the Newspapers of the City, calling attention to that fact. We secured the
use of the Banquet Room and Kitchen for the purpose of providing meals;
also the Lodge Room recently vacated by the Scottish R.ite Bodies, was filled
with cots and bedding for use of the ladies.
We secured the upper floor of the Lexington Hotel (now the Rosselyn
Hotel ) for the use of the gentlemen.
A cook was hired, aJ?.d with the assistance of the Ladies of the Eastern
Star, meals were provided at the Masonic Temple; committees were appointed,
who met all trains coming from the North, and brought the members of the
flaternity to the temple, and after a bath, a good meal, and a rest, positions
were eecured, as best they could be, for employment.
Those of the unfortunates who were in feeble health, were sent to the
Southern California Masonic Home at San Gabriel, at our expense, and when
they were recovered, they sought employment.
. Quite a number of refugees being aged, and having relatives in other

oit1es, were furnished with transportaiton, as they desired.
It is estimated that at least One Thousand (1000) Meals were furnished
at our expense,

Which report was concurred in, and the brethren therein
named were admitted to seats.
The Grand Lecturer presented his Annual Report to the·
Grand Lodge as follows :
.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Master
and Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
I beg to submit this brief report upon the condition and needs
of the Lodges in the several Masonic Districts of this Grand Jurisdiction.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

367

In August last a circular letter was sent to each District Inspector, which was intended as a sort of guide to them, pointing to
the matters which, as Inspectors, it would be their especial duty to
tnvestigate.
It is gratifying to be -able to say that nearly all the Inspectors
have sent in their repgrts concerning the work they have accomplished and the condition of the Lodges over which they have been
called to exercise supervision and impart the necessary instruction
in the Ritual and Work.
From the reports of the Inspectors, it is found that with few
exceptions the Lodges are in a prosperous condition; that the work
is in accordance with the Ritual and fairly well done; that the books
of secretaries are neatly and correctly kept; that the minutes are
properly transcribed by the secretaries and signed by thew:. M.".
as required by the Grand Lodge; that the dues, though not collected
in advanc~, as required by the Uniform Code of By-Laws, are generally paid at or before the annual election of officers. In tbis connection I might say that the custom of paying dues at the end of
the Masonic year has grown almost into a law.
The Inspectors report that they have been busy in the discharge of their official duties and have visited and instructed the
Lodges of their respective districts at all times when requested
by the Lodges to do so, and more than this, have voluntarily gone
to the Lodges and proffered their assistance.
It is to be regretted, however, that some Lodges, notably those
which are in the greatest need of instruction and assistance, are
the ones that not· only refrain from asking the Inspectors for help,
but also fail to get together when notified by the Inspector in
advance of his coming.
It would be of great benefit if the Grand Lodge should adopt a
regulation providing that where the Inspector is cognizant of a
Lodge in his district that from carelessness or lack of interest is
not able to confer any or all degrees in a creditable and proper
manner, the Inspector be authorized to forbid further work in the
Lodge until the fault be remedied.
I hold that the Inspector is
now so authorized; and I know of an instance where the Inspector,
knowing a certain Lodge in his district was not able to confer the
degree as it should be done, went to the w:. M.". of that Lodge
on the day the · degree was to be given and forbade it, until the
Lodge had been called together and practiced on the work until
the w:. M.". and his officers had acquired the necessary proficiency.
It was a splendid lesson, not only to the Lodge itself, but to the
other Lodges of that district. It was a glorious example of the
stamina of that Inspector and worthy of emulation by other Inspectors.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

It has been apparent to me for several years that it would be
of benefit to the Lodges to require Junior Wardens-elect, before
being installed, to be able to confer the E. A. degree, and that
Senior Wardens be able to confer both E. A. & F. C.
Were this provision embodied in a Regulation, it would not
make it necessary for the Master-elect to cram into his memory in
a short time the entire work of the three degrees.
It would lessen the strain and confusion consequent upon
burdening the mind so much in so short a time, and it would lighten
the task of the lnspect9rs by having them examine the Masterelect only in the Ritual of the Third Degree and the law governing
Masonry in general and his duties as Master in particular. Upon
this question I have sounded the several Inspectors, and through
them the officers of the Lodges, and the result has shown the great
majority of all concerned very much in favor of such a regulation,
and I therefore respectfully suggest that such a regµlation be
adopte<j. by the Grand Lodge.
'

I presume that the Inspectors whose reports have not reached
me have, through business pressure or forgetfulness, neglected this
duty.
I regret that it has been impossible for me to do as much work
during the year as I had hoped and planned to do.
The great cal1amity of last April so much disturbed the whole
State that for several months it seemed impossible to settle· down
to the usual order of everyday business, and later the intense summer heat rendered work in the Lodge-rooms so disagreeable that
it would have been little less than torture for the brethren to assemble.
However, I have done the best that was possible under the
litcumstances.

It is known to the Grand Lodge and the membership throughout the State that at all times since I have held the office of Grand
Lecturer, I have been engaged in professional work in the city of.
San Francisco and could only devote such time to Masonry as
was not occupied in my profession.

reposed in me, and thanking the brethren for the many kindnesses
and courtesies extended me, I am,
Sincerely and fraternally,
WILLIAM H. EDWARDS,
Grand Lecturer.

There seems to be a sentiment among the Lodges that the
time has come when the Grand Lodge of California should have
its Grand Lecturer devote his entire time to the business of lecturing the Lodges, not only in the Ritual and Work of the Fraternity
as used in the conferring of c;legrees and the proper transaction
of the business of a Lodge, but also in the principles and groundwork of this greatest of all societies.
·

Which report was ordered, to be referred to· a Special
Committee of three, and the Grand Master named the following brethren to constitute _such committee-

It is well known many of our brethren know less about the
history and symbolism of Masonry than they should. They· are
eager to learn more. Nothing could be of more benefit to the
Grand Lodge than to have a Lecturer go from Lodge to Lodge,
stirring up interest, awakening enthusiasm and so bringing into
our brotherhood the good and the true of every community in our
glorious State.

370

I cannot close this report without saying something concerning "Anderson's Manual." When the author of that book had completed that most valuable volume and offered it to the Masons of
California, it was a complete compendium of the Constitution,
Regulations, Decisions, and Forms of every kind and character,
clearly and accurately stated and in all up to date in every particular, and it was a source o.f genuine pleasure to know that if one.,
wanted any form for any Masonic purpose, he had only to look in
. "Anderson's Manual," and, like a dear friend, it was there to greet
him. If one wanted to find any Masonic law or decision for Calrfornia, he had only to search "Anderson's Manual" and he found it.
If one sought to establish a new Lodge, every form of procedure
was in it. If a cornerstone was to be laid, the form was there,
and so on throughout, everything could there be found.
But one by one the forms have been dropped out, the decisions
which have been reversed do not now appear, and if we desire t,o
trace through them the rise and progress of Masonry in this State ·
we cannot do h.
I believi- from the comments of the brethren thrnui?:hout the
:State upon the changes and omissions above named that the Grand
Lodge should refer the book to its author tha·t it may be by him
revised, and that all that original volume contained should again
appear between its covers with whatever has since been ordained as
law or decision.

The work of this Board of Relief for the year 1906 has been increased by the unfortunate disaster which befell the City of San
)'rancisco on the 18th day of April; for which reason many unfortunate
6rethren, or their families, sought refuge in our own beautiful city,
and called upon us for aid. However, a word from this Board to ..
the several Lodges of our city, brought a ready, generous response,
and thereby we were enabled to relieve the suffering with little dillieulty; and we believe no worthy brother, or any member of his family,
has suftered for the necessaries of life.
To all who contributed to this Board of Relief for the benefit of
the San Francisco sufferers we extend our fraternal thanks.
MASONIC EMPLOYMENT BUREAU.
Through the efforts of Most Worshipful Grand Master Motley H.
Flint, a Masonic Employment Bureau has been established, through
which several hundred positions have been secured for needy Masons,
their widows or orphans. This we deem · a most worthy charity,
nabling one to become self-supporting.

Dear Sir and B.rotherComplying with your request of August 16th, 1906, concerning the
action which .this Board of Relief took in matter of the disaster occasioned by earthquake and fire, which befell the central portion of our
glorious State, on the 18th day of April, 1906, will say:
That immediately upon the realization of that awful calamity,
a special meeting of the Masonic Board of Relief of Los Angllles was
called, on April 22d, 1906, at which meeting I was ·directed to communicate with each Masonic body of this city, and request a contribu·
tion of One Dollar ($1.00) per capita, to enable our Board to relieve
the cli~tress of tb,e members of t he craft and those dependent upon
them, who might take refuge in our city. This request was promptly
complied 'with, and there came into my hands as Secretary, from the
various MasQnic bodies of our city, together with individual contributions; and also from Mount .Zion Lodge, of Troy, N . Y., the sum
of Three Thousand One Hundred and Seventy-Four Dollars and .Fifty
Cents ($3,174.50).
Arrangements were made that · the Masonic Board of Relief should
establish headquarters at the Masonic Temple, and notices were placed
in all the newspapers of the city, calling attention to that fact.. We
secured the use of the banquet room and kitchen for t he purpose of
providing meals; also the Lodge Room. recently vacated by the Scottish Rite Bodies, was filled with cots and bedding for use of the
ladies.
We. secured the upper floor of the Lexington Hotel (now the
Brooklyn Hotel) for the use of the gentlemen.

402

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE

A cook was hired, an.d with the assistance of the Ladies of the
Eastern Star, meals were provided at the Masonic Temple; committees were appointed, who met all trains coming from the North, and
brought the members of the fraternity to the Temple, and after a
bath, a good meal, and a rest, positions were 11ecured, as best they
could be, for employment.
Those. of the unfortunates who were in feeble health, were sent
to ~he Southern California Masonic ·Home at San Gabriel, at our expense, and when they were recovered, they sought employment.
Quite a number of the refugees being aged, and ha.v ing relatives
in other citie's, were furnished with transportation as they desired.
·
It is estimated that at least One Thousand (1000) Meals were furnished at our expense.

Islands, under the jurisdiction. of the M. W. Grand Lodge of California,
which Lodges hold, as it were, a unique position in American Masonic
history, being the advance of American Freemasonry on territory
under the exclusive control of the United States of America, in the
far orient, and it is fit and proper that a Representative ac<\uainted
with the conditions existing in these islands s.h ould be present at the
Annual Communications of the Grand Lodge; therefore, be it
Besolved, That·"Manila" Lodge, No. 342, petition the M. W. Grand
Lodge of California to refund to it, the amount of one hundred and

The M. :. W. :. Charles L. Patton pre.sented the following:
To the M. W. Grand Lodge of California:
The undersigned, on behalf ·of the· Masonic Hall Association of the
City of San Francisco, and in order that the matter of the sale of the
Temple site may be fully un~erstood by the Granil. Lodge, submits
the following for consideration:

. 409

Upon receipt of this money it is the intention of the Hall Association to obtain an order of Court permitting the distribution of all the
funds on hand among the stockholders and, for the reason that there
is no power in · the Hall Association to acquire a new site under its
Articles of Incorporation, the Directors propose to proceed to disintp0rporate.
The Directors have, however, been advised that nearly all the Masonic Bodies owning stock in this corporation desire to invest all or
nearly all the amount to be received ·from the sale of the Temple site
to build a new Temple on a new site to be selected, are about to
formulate a plan whereby a new hall association shall be incorporated
with a capital stock equal in amount to the price received from the
sale of the Temple 'a nd div1ded into. twenty-five thousand shares oi the
par value of thirty dollars each, so that each stockholder in the
present Hall Association may either receive tlie amount due him on
cUasolution in cash or may receive an equal number of shares of equal
value in the new hall association in lieu of ~hares in the old association.
The fact that the purchase price of the Old Temple site ,has not
yet been paid makes it impossible to furnish the Grand Lodge at this
time with a more detailed statement of the plans for the ereetion of
a new Temple.
As the decision of this Grand Lodge in reference to investing the
funds received from the sale of the Temple site in a new and modern
Temple for the use of the Craft, will have great weight in accomplishing this most desirable purpose it is suggested that a committee
be appointed at this seBBion of the Grand Lodge with power to act for
the Grand Lodge in all matters connected with the consummation of
the sale of the Temple site and with the erection of a new Temule in
Ban Francisco.

To the M. W. Grand Lodge of California:Your committee to whom was referred the address of the M. W.
Grand Master, Motley H. Flint, beg leave to submit the following:
It has been the fortune of Grand Master Flint to serve tliis Grand
Jurisdiction in the most eventful year of its history, and in a capacity
which, for taxing one's powers and resources, has never before fallen

414

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

to the lot of r,.ny Grand Master of this or a:uy other Gran<l Jurisdiction.
The awful calamity which befell the City of San Francisco i;_ April
last was so sudden and appalling that thousands of it~ inhabitants
were not only deprived of their homes; but of the actu'al r.ecessaries
oI life. It required a man · of great executive ability to take charge
of the relief work and organize committees to perform the service
demanded, and Grand Master Flint, by reason of his business experi•
ence, was specially qualified to grasp the situation and render the most
efficient service".
·
We commend his untiring zeal and personal efforts in aiding the
needy, and . heartily approve of his action in helping, not only the
members of the Masonic fraternity and their families, but all wl;io
were in distress in those trying hours.
'•
The generous response of other Grand Jurisdictions, in contributing
so liberally, for, the relief of ·San Francisco and other stricken cities
in our State, shows how universal was the sympathy of our Masonic
brethren and how tru·e and loyal the fraternal spirit when a great
occasion calls it into activity. The funds donated were gratefully
received, worth-ily bestowed and faithfully accounted for, and the
report of the Grand Master on the relief fund, and the record of relief
work as shown by his special report, is a tribute to Masonry throughout the world.
We note with pleasure the gain in membership during the year, and
the satisfactory condition of Masonry in general in this Jurisdiction.
. We recommend that so much of the address of the Grand Master
as deals with decisions be referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence;
that portion which relates to the amendment of the constitution in
regard to granting Dispensations for the formation of new Lodges
upon the recommendation of the Grand .Master where the nearest.
Lodge declines to give its consent, be referred to the same committee;
that portion which relates to Masonic Temple matters in San Francisco be referred to a spec.i al committee for consideration and ·report;
that portion relating to a Dispensation for a new Lodge in the PhilippineA ·be referred to a special eommittee, and that portion relating
to printing a list of members of Lodges be submitted to the Grand
Lodge for its consideration and deeision.

great loss sustained by him in the destruet1im of thP, records of his

417

Upon the trial before the Commissioners, through his counsel,
the accused himself being present, he pleaded guilty to the charges,
and such was the finding of the Commission. In sentencing the
accused to reprimand th'e Commission evidently took into consideration a promise to repay the money in six months, or sooner if possible.
If a · Brother so far forgets his Masonic duty as to appropriate
money of the Lodge, entrusted to him as an official, he should be
ltlbjected to. such discipline as shall, at least, convince the Lodge
that he is penitent for his act, and worthy to mingle with his Masonic
Brethren. While a reprimand may work reform fot small offenses,
the good faith of the Brother will ·be better shown if he is deprived,
for a season, of Masonic rights, and' displays to his Brethren· a bearing th~t will justify them in again receiving him into full fellowship.

Your Committee is not B'atisfied that the sentence is sufficient
or adequate punishment for the offense of w:hich the Brother has
acknowledged himself guilty. Such conduct warrants the severest ·
~nishment1 known to our law, but 'as the tri~l Co=issioners h~ve
shown such great .leniency, and there may be circumstances of which
we are ~ot cognizant, which may be urged in mitigation, we are disposed to recommend a milder judgment.
We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its
·e.doption:
Resolved, That the action of the Trial Commissioners of ''Monterey" Lodge, No. 217, sentencing A. A. Manuel to a reprimand, be,
and the same is, hereby reversed, and that the said A. A. Manuel be,
and he is, hereby suspended from all the rights and privileges of
:Masonry.

Resolved, That the action of tlie several Lodges upon the cases
herein particularly specified be, and the same is, hereby affirmed.

Your Committee, to whom was referred the trial record in the case
of Robert Emil Goeritz, expelled by "Chico" Lodge, No. 111, have,
had the same · under cohsideration, and beg leave to report.
The accused was charged with unmasonic ·conduct in four specifications, but evidence was introduced to the Commission only as to
one, which was that during the month of April or May, 1905, the said
Goeritz came to me (the accused) and said he was in trouble. and

418

419

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

asked me as a Mason to assist him by letting him have some cattle
to tide him over his difficulties, and that in a few days he would pay
me for them without fail. I (the accuser) gave him the assistance
he desired, and he took my cattle and disposed of them,. and took the
money and left the State, and I have no doubt but it was his intention at the time he secured the cattle to rob me of my property.

would not accept of it. If there was dishonesty in procuring the cattle the evidence does not show it. At most, _it shows that in his business he estimated beyond his ability.

At the time that charges were preferred the accused was in Butte,
Montana, and wrote to the Ma~ter, asking an extension of the time
of trial for at least sixty days, which was granted, and at the expiration of that time the trial proceeded and the accused was present.
In his statement to the. Commission he said: "Everybody knows the
way I started in business, and as soon as I made a few dollars, I spent
it in improving my business with :fixtures, etc., and :finally I got married and my expenses were higher and business was pretty good, and
I improved my business, and in one way I made a mistake. I risked
too much, and I thought business was getting better, and it got
worse, prices declined, competition was harder, and I could not meet
my bills; consequently, my family expenses were awfully high, it was
impossible for me to cut them down, which I can prove by my books.
Through this came my family trouble, and I made a mistake by
starting in drinking, and for this I ask forgiveness from my brothers.
I tried to beat nobody out of a cent; that is why I came back and
took charge of the market, where I take only my living expenses,
and I will pay everybody dollar for dollar.''
Upon the trial the only evidence offered was by the accuser, who
testified ''all the charges preferred by me were on the hearsay of
Brothers, except the :first charge, relating to cattle.'.'
The accuser was apparently not even ha.If-hearted in his prosecution, for when asked, ''Where did you get the other information
preferred in charges 7'' answered, from Brother J. D. March; and
when further asked, ''Why did you not get the witnesses here to
prove thaU" answered, ('Because I did not care to." He also stated
that he received a letter from Brother Goeritz offering to square the
first charge, relating to the cattle, but that he wrote him an answer
that he would not do se, as it was too late, and he was advised by
Masonic authority that he could not do so.
The transaction disclosed by the charge gave the accused the
privilege of using the cattle, and in the absence of fra~d, 'such use
would not subject him to censure. The only thing looking towards
fraud is that he went away, but before the compietion of the trial
he returned and went to work, and was only taking his living expenses,
and would pay everybody dollar for dollar. According to the prosecutor he had offered to square his indebtedness, but the prosecutor

The charge of fraud, a serious offense, especially when committed
by a Mason against a Brother, should be fully and clearly substantiated by the testimony. Anderson's Manual, Sec. 203, page 250.
by the testimony. Anderson's Manual, Sec. 203, page 250.
We are not satisfied that the evidence in this case is sufficient to .
justify the finding of the Commissioners.
We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:
Resolved, That the action of "Chico" Lodge, No. 111, expelling
Bol:/ert Emil Goeritz be, and· the same is, hereby reversed and set
aside.

Your Committee, to whom was ~eferred the trial record in the
case of Hugh Kirkman, a member Qf "Lawton" Lodge, No. 75,
located at Lawton, Territory of Oklahoma, tlien residing at Fort
j[cKinley, Rizal, Philippine Islands, expelled by ''Manila'' Lodge,
No. 342, have had the same under consideration; and beg leave to
18port as follows:
The a.ccused, an officer in the United ·s tates Army, was charged
by a member of said "Lawton" Lodge with having .e mbezzled $772.23
of moneys that he had in his possession as such officer.
.

.

The Trial Commissioners were elected March· 31st, 1906, and the
Master named April 5th, 1906, as the time for the first meeting of
the Commissioners, and ordered the Secretary to prepare a summons
to •ccused, which summons was served upon the accused April 1st,
1906. The accused was at the time under arrest by the United States
military authorities, and General Wood refused . to allow him to
appear before the. Commission. This fact was made known to the
llio=is11ion and on motion it adjourned until April 10th, 1906, authorizing a brother to take the deposition of the accused, and to notify
him of his right to be :r:epresented at the trial, ood· also to give him
tufficient time ' to prepare for his defense. Upon April 10th the Commission again met, and •the accused's deposition not being received,
another adjournment was had, until April 14th, 1906, at which · time
no objection was . made to the Commissioners, and the accused filed
an answer, which was witnessed by the accuser and a Brother Lawrence -8. Carson, of "Minrehohn" Lodge, No, 5, of Sioux Falls, South
Dakota, who represented the accused upon the trial. In the answer
the accused admitted the charge, and upon the trial there was evidence
of other witnesses, that justified the action of the Commissioners.
These proceeding11 were not in compliance with our l~w, and if
the 'accused had not 'ppeared by answering and being represented;
the sentence of the Lodge could not stand. Our law is very plain.
(Const., Part VI, Art. IV, Sec. 3.) "If the accused be within the
jurisdiction of the Lodge, the summons and a copy of the charges
shall be issued at least ten. days prior to the day appointed for the
trial, and shall be served personally. by the Tyler, or some other member of the Lodge, authorized by the Master for that purpose, or shall

422

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

be left at his ordinary residence or place of business,'' and we can.
not too seriously commend to our Brethren having trials, that they
closely re.a d and pursue the practice laid out for them in the law
thereby avoiding the 'necessity of reversal.
·
· '
Your Committee, however, are of the opinion that inasmuch as
the accused Brother appe·ared by answer and representative and made
no objection to the character of the service of summo~s, that he
waived any informality that might exist in such service and as
the evidence before the Commission justifies the sentence, 'we offer .
the following resolution and recommend its adoption:
Resol.ved, Th~t the action ~f "Manila" Lodge, No. 342, expelling
Hugh Kirkman from all the nghts and privileges of Masonry be and
the same is, hereby affirmed.

evidences itself ~ot in formulas · or rituals, but in deeds of kindness
done. An ancient sage declared ~hat we should thank God for the evil
as well as for the good, and the philcnmphy of that counsel is evidenced
in the great blessing that flowed from full hearts to the distressed
population 0f our beloved city as an earnest and a proof of the great
goud :Masonry has done for the wodd.

trution. In view of the foregoing, your Commit.tee begs to offer the
following:

We cannot refrain from congratula~ing the Grand Lodge and Ma110nry in general, for the wisdom given us to select such a man for
this highly important and arduous post. The Grand Lodge is peculiarly fortunate in being able to command the services even in part
of one trained for a lifetime in the profession of teaching. One ·to
whom the imparting of knowledge has become practically a second
nature. And when we consider the kindly tact and polished diplomacy
with which this work has been accomplished, we cannot but renew
our congratulations. Brother Edwards has not hesitated to praise
where praise was due, nor has he withheld censure where that was
called for. And it is this fearless administration of the duties of his
high office,_coupled with the kindly manner of his teaching, which has
so endeared him to our hearts, and at the same time brought . the work
to its present high standard of efficiency. Since the adoption of the
new ritual the duties of his office have been greatly augmented, and
all Masons will readily realize what a stupendous task confronted the
Grand Lecturer in bringing about the change all over this vast jurisdiction, and when we see· that it is admitted that the work in these
few short years has been entirely remodeled and brought to a degree
of perfection, where it is' a subject of favorable comment all over the
United States, we can begin feebly to realize ~hat a herculean undertaking the Grand I.ecturer has accomplished and how great should be
our appreciation of his efforts.

Bro. Rodolph W. Meek, from .the Special Committee on
tht Grand Lecturer's report, presented the following-:
To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:Your Committee to whom was referred the report of the Very
Worshipful Wm. Harvey Edwards, Grand Lecturer, beg to submit the
following repor~:
·
·
We feel that we cannot take up the report in detail without, in
passing, at least making a few general co=ents on the admirable and
efficient ma·. iner in whieh the office of Grand Lecturer has been filled
in recent years.

We note with great satisfaction that the large majority of the In11pectors have been faithful and diligent in the discharge of their
duties, but we. also note the deplorable negligence of some Lodges ·in
permitting their work to fall far below. the standai:-d, and failing to
seek the assistance of the Inspectors to the end that this condition
might be remedied.
With regard to the recommendation of the Grand Lecturer that the
Inspectors be vested with the power to suspend the work of any Lodge
nntil the proper degree of _proficiency has been attained, we concur in
the advisability of conferring such authority upon the Inspectors and
re.commend that this portion of the Grand Lecturer's report be referred
to the Committee on Jurisprudence.
We heartily concur in the recommendation of the Grand Lecturer
that the Junior and Senior Wardens-elect be required to perfect
themselves in the Entered Apprentice and Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Degrees· respectively before installation in their respective
offices and recommend that this portion of the report be referred to
the Committee on Jurisprudence.
We eannot but feel that the criticism of the Grand Lectµrer of the
present form o_f Anderson's Manual is well taken1 and _con<:ur ~th

We

note with particular pleasure the sentiments of the 9-rand
Lecturer upon the subject of devoting hie entire time to the work of
this office. It may not be amiss to say in this connection that other
Jurisdictions, notably New York and Missouri, require the whole time
of the Grand Lecturer and pay him a salary commensurate with such
requirements. Masonry has ·reached such a point in California that
such .a requirement on the part of the Grand Lodge seems absolutely
essential if we are to retain our present high standard among the
jurisdictions of the United States. It is not alone instruction in the
ritualistic work which we ought to require of the Grand L .e cturer, but
having a man capable of doing so, it would immensely add to the edu·
cational value of the office, if we could receive from him lectures and
instructions upon the history, principles, ground work, symbolism and
the law and jurisprudence of the Order. But it is totally otit of the
question to expect such ser;vices from our Grand Lecturer unless he
can devote his whole time ·to the office, and if we ask that of him we
must be prepared to pay him a salary in accordance with the demands which we make upon him. We are asking the entire time and
attention of an expert, · and we must be prepared to pay according to
the services which we receive. So while we hesitate to recommend a
figure, for the purpose of bringing the matter in concrete form before
the Grand Lodge, we would recommend that the salary of the Grand
Lecturer be fixed for the ensuing year at Twenty-five Hundred Dollars,
with the usual allowance for traveling expenses.
In conclusion, we would again reiter~te our appreciation which we
.feel confident is concurred in by the Grand Lodge and Masons throughout the ·state, of the magnificent administration of the Grand Lecturer,
and while Brother Edwards in his usual modesty has refrained from
touching upon a greater part of his achievements, a perusal of the
Grand Lodge report, showing the growth of this Order in this State
and our own personal contact with his delightful personality, speak
volumes for him in his work and. as a man and a Mason.
Respectfully submitted,

R. W ." MEEK,
D.R. WELLE,

This being the hour for the special order, as ordered by
the Grand Lodge yesterday, the Grand Or;ttor, the W. :. Bro.
Oscar Lawler, delivered the Annual Oration before the
Grand Lodge, as follows :
' 'God moves in a mysterious way his wonders to perform.''.
Since the Divine fiat was sent forth which . brought the world from
darkness to light, the planet in its course through space has progressed
in :i series of diurnal revolutions, with alternating periods of light
and darkness, and as, in a never-ending circling around the central
sun, it never traverses exactly the same .t rack, but comes almost back
to the. same places, only always a little farther on through the infinite
expanse, so, there often seems to be a corresponding system of progress
in the world of thought and knowledge. .
Man, the creature, is born, passes through the morning, noon and
evo.·ning of life, to vanish into the Great Beyond, whither his fathers
have gone before him; nations are brought into existence, wax great
anu powerful, ultimately to wither and decay, goin·g the way of all
eart hly things; God the Creator, everlasting and perpetual, supervit1·
ing the passing generations, in his infinite wisdom has made each
o~e better than th~ one which went b efore, and in the building of
nations has given us a government of to-day b etter and more benefi·
cent than its predecessor of yesterday.
'T o human eyes the Divine purpose and the manifestations of the
judgments of the Almighty have ofttimes- nay always-been a
mystery. To their dim and restricted v ision. the visitatigns of a socall:id merciful God have been sore afllic:tions, and the course of human
affairs has at times seemed to be one of retrogression rather than of
progress; but, in due course of time, which "healeth all wounds, " the
calamity of yesterday forms the background for the bountiful blessing of to-day-the pestilential visitation to one generation brings
for.th the means of securing health and immunity therefrom to its
successor, and the grossness, passion and vice of one day has turned
man to ''love virtue, for she alone is free,'.' the next.

from

The J ew was led .
the bondage and <;>ppression of Egypt to
the Promised Land, where his genius established and his successors
, have maintained a system of personal conduct and a st andard of
moral character which affords an example susceptible of profitable
imito.tion; and, though for centuries he has been a wanderer on the
faee of the earth, th?ugh (to their shame be it said), he has been
oppressed by ev ery people of ev ery gener ation, and though to~ay the

When the trials and tribulations of the Prince of Peace were ended .

titude, the ·inspiration .and guide of a great portion of the human
race in the path of virtue.
At an early day a great r eligious hierarchy was established hav ing
for its purpose the promulgation of the pr ecepts and exemplification
:;f tl:e practices of the lowly man of Galilee-with the lapse of time
and accumul~t~on of power it assumed control and dominion, not only
over the rehg1ous, but also over the civil and 'governmental affairs
of men and nations. Tpe opposition thus aroused resulted in a controversy without parallel for the cruelty, bitterness, bloodthirstiness and
unbridled a.way of ·animal passion displayed , and in which the characteristic least observable was the Christian virtue professed by all
the participants. Protestant vied with Catholic in devising means of
torturing human beings into false professions-while Alva butchered
Calvi~ burned. If Mary led her victims to the stake, Elizabeth cas~
h~rs. mto foul dungeons, there to starve and rot.
But, while the
'71ctims .of those dreadful times may have felt that the God of Hosts

eo•1rse was one of r etrogression, w e who ar e enjoying the fruits

privileged to exercise our r eligious devotions at such time and in s~ch
manner as an unrestricted conscience may dictate, acknowledging
~tizenship in a country whose sole demand is that we ·be true t o our·

In our own country the Puritan landed at Plymouth and the Catholic in Maryland, both ready and willing to face the privations of the

The progenitors of American independence promulgated the 'doctrme that all men are born free and equal; and yet, when t~e funda·

It -is not unnatural that the possessor of great wealth and the

the toilers of the land should look upon the interference of the law to

A few months ago I stood in the gallery of that Temple where for
"so many years we were wont to assemble-that dear old Temple now
laid in dust and ashes, and as I gazed upon the life-like portraits of
my departed brothers with whom I had associated in this Grand
Lodge, a feeling of sadness came over me that defied my soul 's resistance, and, like the lonely cavalier in Locksley Hall, I seemed to hear
the phantom years whispering, "Never! Never!" Never to hear
their voices again! Never to stand in the living presence and receive
the hearty, fraternal greeting!

Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
As we assemble in Annual Communication to resume our accustomed duties for the benefit of the Craft, and for the exchange of fraternal courtesies, we· are saddened by the appearance of vacant places;
and we note with sorrow the absence of some ·of our most faithful colaborers.

What a mystery is death! Philosophers tell us that God never
gives to man the k ey that opens the golden gate of Eternity until his
time shall come to enter there. The only proof they give us of
i=ortality is that the desire to live again is implanted in every
human breast; that . the sun-browned children of the forest see God in
clouds and dream of happy hunting grounds beyond the star-gemmed
sky; that the polished and imaginative Greek in fancy walks in Hesperian gardens and roams in Elysian fields. This is their conclusion:
It muet be so!

Plato, thou reasonest well,
. Else why this longing !or Immortality?

But, my brethren, our faith requires a firmer foundation. The
philosophy of six thousand years has failed to search the chambers of
the human soul. Reason, unless it .be illumined by inspiration, leaves
us in the cold and chilling atmosphere of uncerta.inty and doubt.
Intellect is not our highest endowment. Imagination is not our crowning faculty, Every form of genius is inferior to conscience, to faith,
to sym.p athy and love. Man became a liv ing soul when God breathed

Infinite life, similar in essence but different in degree. If God is the
Infinite Spirit of Life back of all, from which all comes, then clearly
our life, as individualized spirits, is continually coming from that
Infinite S~urce by_divine inflow.

Our departed brother was born in· Wilkinsburg, Pennsylvania, June
2, 1825. He came from rural parentage and of a long line of tillers of
the ~oil; In youth he labored on hi!J father's farm in summer and
attended the district school in. the winter months. From boyhood he
was a diligent worker, doing with alI°his might what his hands found
to do. So diligent was he in his studies and so rapid was his progress
that at the age of 19 years he became a teacher in the public schools.
The following year he fell a victim to the ''gold fever''; he joined a
large party of neighbors and friends and journeyed across the plains
to California, the El Dora~o of the West. He crossed the snow-capped
Sierras and descending the western slope came into the Sacramento
valley; and at sight of a beautiful spot on the bank of the Sacramento
river he exclaimed, "Here I pitch my tent." His first night's rest
was beneath a giant oak, which in after years shaded his beautiful
dwelling. He secured a tract of land in acc.ordance with his means
and later purchased large outlying tracts until he came into possessio~
of one of the largest and most fruitful farms on the Sacramento river.
He built an elegant r~sidence :ind brought around. it everything that
could conduce to the comforts and enjoyments of home. Peace and
Plenty sat smiling at his door.
It was my privilege to enjoy an. intimate acquaintance with our
brother for more than thirty years. I was often a visitor at his home
and he a guest at mine. For nearly twenty years we met once a week
as directors of a corporation which .was the cutsodian of the poor
man's ·s avings, the widow's mite, and the orphan's heritage. It was
in this relation that I learned to admire our brother for his rigid
adherence to justice and right.

Brother Johnston's every act was the sequence of mature thought.
He made no failure, left nothing undone, improvei;J. every hour, and
every year's effort tended to material prosperity.
He was also a man of public spirit; he did much for the general
sn-osperity of the State, and served in many positions of trust. His
advice was eagerly sought in private and public enterprises. His hand
and heart were ever open to public and private charities.
As a public speaker he aspi~ed to· no ·flights of eloquence, he used
no ~mooth and rounded periods. His words were simple, plain,
ftta1ghtforward, and big with meaning. He held the attention of his
audiences and impressed his hearers with the superiority of his judg·
ment. Many times I listened to his words in the halls of legislation
and observed him in the dignified position of President of the State

Senate. At all times and in all places he acquitted himself with credit
to his name· and honor to the position.
As Grand Master of the Grand Lodge he was ever faithful in the
discharge of his official duties, and zealous in promoting peace and
harmony among the Craft. He appointed the first Trustees of the
Masonic Home, and for years thereafter he was a faithful member
of the Board. His last appearance in this Grand Lodge was at the
Annual Communication of 1904. He had already received the Supreme
Grand Master's warning to gather up his working tools and prepare
to quit earth's field of labor. He had suffered from a stroke of par- ·
alysis, and could with difficulty converse with the brethren. A short
time thereafter a second admonition was given and he entered into
a state of mental decline. He was often oblivious to time and place,
and a guide attended him wherever he went. At last came the third
warning. ''God's finger touched him and he slept.'' On the fourteenth of last November, as the shades of night were gathering round
his beautiful home on the banks of that river which for more than
fifty years had gladdened his heart with its musical cadences, our
brother bade adieu to the scenes of earth and passed into the Silent
Land.

To the M.:. W.:. Grand Lodge of Califomia:It is not often that we ar.e so forcibly reminded of the uncertainty
of human life as we were when, on the 13th day of December, 1905,
our friend 11:nd Brother, the M.:. W.:. Hiram Newton Rucker, Past
Grand Master of this Jurisdiction, was, without a moment's warning,
called f~m a life of usefulness among us to the Grand Lodge above.
He had been in attendance upon a meeting of the Board of Trustees
of our Masonic. Home, of which he was the Superintendent, and 'was
returning to the Home, when the accident occurred which caused
his death. One moment vigorous and strong, filled with enthusiasm
for the work for which he was so well fitted, looking forward to
many years o:f' usefulness and companionship with his Brethren, the
next, he had gone to join the innumerable throng in ''that undiscovered country, from whose bourne no traveler returns.''

I see many new faces befor(J me. My brothers, you, who are here
for the first time, are not expected to enter ful}y into our deep sorrow,
for you did not know our departed brother. But the lessons of this
hour and the influence of this sacred observance should make deep andp
lasting impressions upon your minds and hearts. You have, no doubt,
felt the pangs of separation from friends and brothers and, .even now
you may be cherishing the memory of loved ones lost. Unite then
with us in the comforting assurance that, if our Masonic fli!-ith be not
founded .upon the quicksands-if our hope be not a delusion and a
will-o '-the-wisp, the separation is not final; that when the storms of
. life are past, when the mistakes and discords of time no more annoy,
when the clouds of sorrow and the mists of doubt have rolled a,way,
there will be an unbroken reunion out beyond life's golden sunset
where earth's shadows never fall.

Brother Rucker lived practically his whole life in California; he
was born on September 6th, 1844, at Arrow Rock, in the State of
Missouri, and came to this State with his parents at the age of six
years, and thenceforth continually resided here. His first home here
was in our beautiful Santa Clara Valley, where he was educated in
our public schools and at the University of the Pacific, from which
he graduated (with the first class of the medical department) in the
year 1870. For the following eighteen years he made his home and
practiced his profession in Merced County. He was one of the prominent citizens of the county for many years; and always took a
commendable interest in public affairs. For a long time he served
his fellow citizens in the official capacity of Coroner and Public
Administrator, and was also Chairman of the Democratic County
Central Committee. In the year 1884 he was appointed by the
Governor of the State to be a Director of the State Hospital at Stockton, and in the year 1888 he was elected to the important office
of Superintendent of that institution, which office he held for four
years. In the year 1892 he removed to Oakland, where for the
following nine years he resided and practiced his profession, and was
for a season President of the Board of Health. In the year 1901 he
returned to the scene of his early labors in Merced County, where
he continued to reside until, in 1904, he responded to the insistent
call of his Brethren to take upon himself the duties of Superintendent
of the Masonic Home at Decoto, which office ·he most acceptably
filled ' until the time of his death.

1:our Committee, to whom was referred the resolution offered.by
P. G. M. Patton at the Annual Communication of 1905, relative to the
discontinuance of the Representative system, have had the same under
consideration, and report as follows:
The custom of appointing Representatives to and from other
(;i-rand Lodges is an ancient one, still in force in almost all the Grand
Jurisdiction; some few, however, have discontinued and abolished
same.
We see no· reason at the present time for any change on the p~rt.
of .our Grand Lodge in regard to this matter, and believe it under all
circumstances to be undesirable, and therefore recommend that the
system be continued in force as heretofore.
Your C<_>mmittee, to whom was referred the resolution relative to
the exeI?ption of Masons over seventy years of age from the payment of dues, have had the same under consideration, and report as
follows:
Every Mason, whether old or young, if able, should bear his proportio.n of the burdens of his Lodge and pay his dues; if not able it
becomes the duty of the Lodge to see that his dues are remitted and
the brother kept in st.anding.
The resolution would, in effect, create a life membership, and we
deem it unwise to enlarge in any way our present system. and the
objects sought to be accomplished by the resolution can now be accomplished by the action of the Lodges under ·the present laws.
