"Past Master.- This title applies only to one who has been' r egularly elected or named in a charter and installed, and has served a
term as Master of a chartered Lodge wit:tJin the jurisdiction of this
Grand Lodge, and who remains a member in good standing of one of
its subordinates.''
This provision is, of course, .controlling as to the meaning of the
term "Past Master" wherever it is used in our Constitution. Only
those who come within its t erms can be held to be entitled· to the
rank and privileges of a Past Master in California, and one whose
only service as Master was in a Lodge of another jurisdiction, is
pl11-inly not within its terms.
we therefore recommend that this decision be modified to conform
to these views.

The Grand Master was also asked as to the status of a Mason
under the following conditions: He is a member of one of ou~
Lodges, and while such member, without first withdrawing from his
Lodge, applies, under Sec. 8, Art I, Part V, for affiliation with another
Lodge, upon a certificate of his standing in the Lodge ·of which he is
a member. He is elected to membership in the Lodge to which he.
applies. When does he cease to be a ntember of his old Lodgef When
does he commence to be a member of the new Lodge to which he is
eiected f when does his liability for dues in the old Lodge end f ,and
when does his liability for dues begin in the 'new Lodgef The Constitution provides in the section just cited: "If such appli~ant be
elected to affiliate with a I,odge, he can become a member thereof,
only by filing with the Secretary, at a stated meeting, the certificate
of his withdr8;wal from the Lodge of which he was last a member.'"

In regard to the question presented to the Grand Master as to the
right of a Lodge. to pay ~rom ~dgf;l funds for services rendeted by a
JNoother in assistmg candidates m the work and. lectures of the first
and second degrees, we are of the opinion that' the Grand Master's
view that no such use can be made of lodge funds, under our existing
law is correct. It is · the settled law of this Jurisdiction that the
fun:ls of a lodge are dedicated solely to charitable purposes, and the
aecessary expenses of the Lodge, the only exception . being that provided by General. Regulation 57, under which not to exceed five (now
ten) per cent of the yearly revenue may be used for purposes of refhshment and the promotion of fraternal intercourse. The proposed
~nditure is not, in our judgment, within any class of expendit,ures
now authorized. It is, of course, within the power of this Grand Lodge
to authorize subordinate Lodges to expend a· portion of their .funds
for 'the purpose, just as it has authorized such an expenditure for
furposes of refreshment and the promotion of fraternal intercourse.
Whether· it would be for the best interests of Masonry that this
should be done is a question of policy for the Grand Lodge . to determine, and as to which we make no recommendation. If it be desired
to do this, it can be done by a regulation authorizing the expenditure,
and it will not be necessary to create any new office in the Lodge or
to amend the by-laws.

It is clear that the mere election of the brother to membership in
the new Lodge under these circumstances in no way affects his standing as a member of the old Lodge. He continues a member of the
old Lodge and liable for all dues that may accrue until such time as
he formally withdraws therefrom, which he may do, undei;. section 6
of 'the same article, by giving notice of his intention so to do at a
stated meeting, whe.n , he being· in good standing, and his dues being
paid, he will receive a certificate of withdrawal or dimit. From that
moment he is not a member of any Lodge until he becomes a member
of another Lodge, and he can become a member of the new Lodge to
which he has been elected only upon filing such certificate of withdrawal or dimit with the Secretary thereof at ~ stated ·meeting. :ijis
dues in the new Lodge. do not commence to accrue until such filing of
the certificate. During the time that may elapse before his withdrawal from the old Lodge and the filing of his certificate of withdrawal o.r dimit in the new Lodge, he, not being a member of any
Lodge, is not liable for dues to any L~dge. The certificate of standing or membership contained in the Grand Master's decision, and
taken by him from Anderson's Manual, at page 77, we find on investigation has never been adopted as a part of our Constitution or law,
and is no part thereof . As we understand the Grand Master's decision, he ruled that the ·brother was liable to the old Lodge for such
dues as might accrue to the time when he formally withdrew therefrom, and such ruling is strictly in accord with our law, and we recommend that it b e approved. We have discussed· this matter .at
length for the purpose of making clear the status of the brother from
the time of his withdrawal to the time of filing his certificate of
withdrawal with the Secretary of the new Lodge, a matter that does
not appear to be explicitly covered by the decision of the Grand
Master.

The decision of the Gi.-and Master relative to the right to use wine
at a banquet held outside of the lodge-room, where such wine is paid
for otherwi1le than fro~ lodge funds, is in accord with our existing
written law on the subject. The only written prohibition now in our
law is as to the payment for spirituous, malt or fermented liquor from
lodge funds. It has also been decided that it is contrary to Masonic
usage to serve such liquors in a Masonic hall. If it be desired to
prohibit the use of such liquors at any Masonic banquet or ·gathering,
wherever held, a regulation to that effect will accomplish the desired
purpose.
The various other decisions rendered, including that in regard to
life membership, are clearly in accord. with our law, and do not
tequire special mention. W e recomin:end that they be approved.
Bespec~fully submitted,

FRANK M. ANGELLOTTI,
WILLIAMS. WELLS,
JAMES B. STEVENS,

T.o the M .:. W.:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee have had under consideration the recommendation of the Grand Maste.r that our Constitution be amended so as. to
authorize the issuance by him of a dispensation for a new Lodge
without the r ecommendation of the nearest or most convenient chartered Lodge, when such Lodge, aft er request, refuses t o grant such
recommendation, and the Grand Master, after investigation, considers
it· proper ·that such dispensation should issue. The restriction. upon
the power of the Grand Master to issue a dispensati<in for a n ew
Lodge without the recommendation of the nearest or most convenient
chartered Lodge, has been a part of our fundamental law for many
years, and has always been considered a wise and necessary provision
for the protection of existing Lodges. Doubtless, t h ere may have
been cases where the recommendation of the nearest or most convenient chartered L odge has b een withheld without good r eason, but we
do n~t think that this demands the practical abolition of what was
considererl a necessary safeguard by the framers of our Constitution,
and this would be the effect of the amendment recommended. It
often happens that a good and necessary 1aw works injustice in 11.
particular instance, but this is not a good r eason for the practical
repeal of the law. On the whole, doubtless the provision in question
has worked for tne general good of Masonry in this Jurisdiction. If
any change at all in the direction suggested is to be made t o meet
exceptional cases, w e are of the opinion that the change should not
authorize the issuance of a dispensation without the consent of the
nearest or most convenient chartered Lodge, except under direction
of the Grand L9dge itl!elf, given aft er notice to such Lodge that such
relief will be sought and an opportunity to such Lodge to be heard
thereon. ·
R espectfully submitted,
FRANK M. ANGELLOTTI,
WILLIAM S. WELLS,
JAMES B. STEVENS,
THOMAS FLINT,
CHARLES W. NUTTING,

The M. :. ·w. :. Frank M. Angellotti, Chairman of the
Committee on Jurisprudence, presented the following:To the M.:. W.:. Grand Lodge of Califomia:Your committee have had under consideration that portion of the
Grand Lecturer's report· recommending legislation whereby Inspectors
may be clothed with authority to forbid and prevent further work
in a Lodge when satisfied that the L~dge from carelessness or lack
of interest is not ·able to confer any or all degrees in a cr~ditable
manner.
An Inspector has, of course, no such power under existing law.
His powers are d'e:ftned by express premises, and we find no such power
•xiywhere conferred.
Nor do we think it advisable that any legislation of the nature
proposed should be adopted. The power of suspending any function
of a Lodge is an extraordinary one, to be exercised only where the
necessities of the case clearlf demand it. That, however, is now
vested exclusively in, the Grand Master, and we deem it inexpedient
that it should be exercised, in whole or in part, by any other officer.
If for any reasol!- whatever a Lodge should not be permitted to con-·
trnue to exercise any of its .f unctions, it is clearly the duty of the
tnspector to immediately acquaint the Grand Master with the condition. The Grand Master can at any time take such action in this
direction as is for the best interests of Masonry. ·

480

481

PROCEEDINGS OF THE.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

We therefore recommend that no· legislation of the character
be adopted.
· Respectfully submitted,
FRANK M. ANGELLOTTI,
WILLIAR S. WELLS,
JAMES B. . S'fEVENS,
THOMAS FLINT,
CHARLES W. NUTTING,
Committee.

Lecturer, which recommJlnds that the Junior and Senior Wardens-elect
be required to perfect themselves in the Entered Apprentice and Fellowcraft Degrees before installation, has been referred to this committee and they report as follows:

The R.:. W.:. Reuben H. Lloyd, of San Francisco, was unanimously elected Senior Grand Warden.

That at the last Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge a
proposed General Regulation, to be known as "General Regulation
No. 82," was referred to them. This General Regulation is found on
page 154 of the Proceedfogs of 1905. Your· committee at that time
reported that they found that the proposed regulation in no way conflicts with any constitutional provision and reported it back to the
Grand Lodge without any recommendation as to whether it be adopted
or rejected, as it involved quite a radical change in existing methods,
they recommended that the same be referred to the next Annual
Communication. This recommendation was ado:pted and the only
thing to be done at this time is to determine as to whether or not they
desire to adopt such r£gulation, and the proper way to dispose of this
matter would be to either adopt or reject the General Regulation
No. 82, as presented last year and found on said page 154.
Respectfully submitted,
F. M, ANGELLOTTI,
W. S. WELLS,
J. B. STEVENS,
T. FLINT,
C. W. NU'fTING,
Committee.

Which was concurred in and the proposed Regulation
No. 82 was adopted.

Bro. Henry M. Owens, presented the following:To the M.:. W.:. Grand Lodge of Califomia:Your committee to whom was referred that part of the Grand
Master's address which contained the communication from the Special Representative of "Manila" Lodge, No. 342, requesting this
Grand Lodge to define our Masonic relations towards other Masonic
powers in the Philippine Islands, to wit: The Grand Orients of Spain
and France.
·From a lack of information and the limited time at the command
of this committee, it recommends that the final disposition of this
question be referred to the next Communication of this Grand Lodge,
and in the meanwhile (the regularity of the afor13said Masonic bodies
being discussed by other Masonic powers), that no Masonic communication be held with said Masonic bodies or their subordinate bodies.
Respectfully submitted,
W. FRANK PIERCE,
H. M. OWENS,
R. M. MEEK,
Committee.

Which was concurred m.

AMENDMENT

TO

THE

CONSTITUTION.

Sec.. 2, Art. I, Part III, adding, after the words, ''the lectures
thereunto appertaining'':
Provided, always, that whenever the nearest or most convenient
chartered Lodge refuses to grant its recommendation, the Grand
Master may, if after full investigation he deems it to be for the best
interests of Masonry, grant such dispensation without any such recommendation having been given.
AMENDMENT TO GENERAL REGULATION No. 57.
Substitute, after the words, '' sultl not exceeding,'' the word ''ten''
for the word ''five.''
NEW GENERAL REGULATION.

No. · 82. No Junior Warden of a Lodge shall be installed until be
shall have produced to the installing officer the certificate of the
Grand Lecturer or of the Inspector of the district in which his
Lodge is situated, certifying that he has personally examined such
Junior Warden-elect · and that be is qualified to give the work and
lecture of the First Degree; and no Senior Warden shall be installed
until be shall have produced a like certificate of his qualification to
give the work and lectures of the First and Second Degrees. Such
eertifica tes shall be sent to the Grand Secretary and filed in his office.

REPORT
OF THE

Committee on Correspondence
, FOR THE YEAR 1906

To THE M. ·. W. ·. GRAND LoooE,
F. and A. M. of CALIFORNIA:
The strenuous season through which we have passed, and from
which we have hardly yet emerged, is. a good reason for the brevity
of this Report, were it not for the additional and more weighty
reason, the wish of the Grand Lodge, as expressed in its action of
the preceding session, when it not only cut off the nub of the story
and denied it publication, but expressed its opinion of the value
of the work by an appropriation of fifty dollars for the present
R,eport.
But as time is money, and money is scarce, without wasting more,
we will take up our friend, Bea.uchamp of Alabama, to stand at the
head of the line and ask him to lend us his countenance in the making up of a brief Report.
ALABAMA.
The Grand Lodge of Alabama held its Eighty-fifth Annual, December 5, 1905, under the direction of the M. ·. W. :. Henry H.
Matthews, Grand Master; R.·. W.~. Geo. A. Beauchamp being Grand
Secretary, and Judge Wm. I. Titcomb, Chairman of Correspondence.
Three hundred and fifty Lodges were represented. Eleven new
Lodges were instituted, several weak Lodges were consolidated, eight
corner-stones of public buildings were placed, and five ReRresentatives
near other Grand Lodges appointed.

ARIZONA.
The Grand Lodge of Arizona held its Twenty-fourth Annual in' the
town of Flagstaff, November 14, 1905,_:_The M.·.
Grand Ma~ter,
George Shand, being absent;· the R. ·. W. ·. Edwm Seymour Miller,
·Deputy Grand Master, presided; the V.-. W.:. George James Rosk~uge ·
being Grand. Secretary.
.
Arizona has nineteen Lodges on the Roll, of which number fifteen
were represented, together wit~ twenty-one other Grand. Jurisdictions.
The M.-. W. :.- George Shand, Grand Master, sent hlB Address. by
mail and it was read by the Deputy Grand Master. H~ sent affectionate greeting to Grand Lodge, regretting his unavoidable absence,
caused by ill-health, obliging him to leave the Jurisdiction for an
indefinite period.
.

· "Permit m~, sir, a few words as Grand · Representative of the

formation of this Grand Lodge those who were active in the work,
desiring to compliment California, which was the Masonic home of

Masonry into Arizona, adoptec'J. her Constitution, By-Laws, Rules,
Regulations and even decisions and Work as our own. Since that time
whenever any doubt or difficulty ·has arisen in our minds over Masonic
matters, it has been promptly settled by asking, 'What would California do in a like case f '
''Following Califo_rnia 's example, we exchanged Grand Representatives with the Grand Jurisd_ictions which acknowledged and accepted
us as a sovereign Grand Lodge. In °1904, at its 55th Annual Session,
Grand Master Nutting delivered his Annual' Address, in _which not a
word was written referring to the Representative system. His
Address was referred to the usual committee for distribution and reference. When this committee reported, at the close of the Report it
said:
" 'It will be pate.at to any one who will give the matter of the
appointment of Representatives to and from other Grand Lodges
prop~r consideration that this custom . is as useless as the "appendix
1
vermiform is ' in the human body. It seems to us that the custom
must have originated in a desire to decorate members with a mere
title. The only proper way· for one Grand Lodge to communicate with
another is through the Grand Masters. Your committee can see no
necessity for the continuance of the custom and therefore recommend that it be abolished.'

"The report of the committee was adopted. It was afterwards
said that this was done without consideration, the members supposing
it was the usual stereotyped report, and paying no attention to its
contents. The Grand Secretary of California took this action, however, as conclusive, and, I understand, notified many Grand Representatives of it, and discontinued to publish the list. · I did no~ receive
any notice, nor did I receive any copy of the Proceedings. When my
· attention was called to the matter I wrote to Grand Master G. W.
Hunter, ~nd asked him if I was or was not the <Jrand Representative
of California. In his letter of October 2d, conveying his good Wishes

''The action taken at the Grand Lodge Session of 1904° c~used

" 'The Grand Representative is not appointed for business purposes-he merely rises, if you will, as an evidence, a tangible symbol
expressive of the friendship and fraternal relations which exist between the Bodies-a link in the chain of unity--oneness-identity
-of being and purpose of all the Masonic Bodies on earth.'
"I have gone into this affair at some length, as it is probably the
last time I shall answer the roll call as the Representative of Cali-.·
fornia. I shall not resign, I hope I shall not be called hence; but I
presume that those who began the crusade will continue their efforts
~mtil California discontinues the system. When that time · comes I
trust that the Grand Lodge of Arizona will disregard precedent and
not follow in California's footsteps. When that day comes, and we
call the roll of Sister Jurisdictions, when California is reached our
Grand Pursui~ant will answer, 'Non est inventus, I and I will add,
'Farewell, farewell, the pride, pomp and circumstance. Othello's
occupation's gone.'
"It is hard to conceive of· the reasons which induced the California
Committee to make its remarkable report. But, sir, when you look at
the brethren before you, bedecked with the jewels which are indicative of th~ir. years of service to Masonry, it will not require much
stretching of the imagination to hear the small, envious voice misquoting Scripture and E<aying_: 'Consider the. ''daisies'' of the Lodge,

The Grand Lodge_ of Connecticut held its One Hundred and Eighteenth Annual in the City of H artford, Je.nuary 17, 1905,-The M.·. W.:
Asa P. Fitch, Grand Master; the Veteran Bro. John H. Barlow being
the Grand Secretary.
An Emergent Communication was held in the City of Danbury,
September 5th, for the dedication of the new hall of ''Union'' Lodge,
No. 40, a Lodge holdi:n"g. a Charter under the Seal of the Grand Lodge
of Massachusetts, dated March 23, 1780. There are ,many items of
interest in this history of this Veteran Lodge of "ye olden tyme,"
which would be voted decidedly out of order in many of our modern
Jurisdictions. As the record evidences:
"In 1785 a worthy .Brother was helped to the value Qf :five qollars.
Instead, however, of giving him the money, some of the Brethren
were empowered to sperid it in buying small shoes for his children.
In aiding a poor woman, who· does not· appear to have been a relative ·
of a Mason, one Brothar agreed to board one of her children for one
quarter of the school year and another assumed the expense of the
tuition of one ·of the children for the same time. It is shown from
the records that it was the · custom of the Lodge to buy a cow occa: sionally and to pass her around from time to time to Brethren who
were .in need of lacteal sustenance. Whether the benevolence of the
Order extended so far as to appoint a Brother to milk the cow does
not appear. There are one or two instances where the l.odge ·voted
to buy lottery tickets. In 1801 three tickets to the Episcopalian
church lottery were purchased. But, alas! they proved to be blanks.
"In 1779 a vote a.ppears authorizing the purchase of 'a 11h-gallon
or 2-gallon stone jugg for the "use of the Lodge.' One Brother was
charged with the duty of :filling the jug; The names of the Brethren
who assisted in emptying the jug are not recorded. Probably the
jug contained only milk from the Lodge cow, although I confess·
that this charitable e.onclusion is a little beclouded by a vote of the
Ledge accepting a bid of one of the Brothers . to supply the Lodge
with liquors at prime c_ost."
The roll shows 110 Lodges, with a membership of 20,087. All the
Lodges were represented. Bro. John H. Barlow, Chairman of Correspondence, submits an excellent Report of 200 pages, and the Journal
is enriched with a fine portrait of the late Grand Master, M.:. W.:. Asa
P. Fitch.

One of the Grand Stewards, Bro. W.·. M.:. Burbank, was ill. A
Committee was appointed to wait upon him,. and convey to him the
sympathy of the Grand Lodge. That Committee, ili its Report, called
upon a friend and Brother of the Steward, who had accompanied
. them to point the way to Brother Burbank's home, to supplement
their Report, which he did in the following words, which so impress
us that we place them on record· here. The chaperon in this case,
Bro. Edward Cook, said:

''I don't know that I can add anything to the very touching and
appropriate Report that has been made by the Committee.·
''It is perhaps proper to give a little further information as to
the conditions in this case.
"The Brother's office and home have long been at 3035 South
Park avenue, at the corner of Thirty-first ·street, where he and his
wife grew old together, until two or three years ago, when she went
to visit a son in California, and died there, since 'which time this
dear Brother, who is nc,w approaching his eighty-fifth birthday, has
lived alone. The growing years have made it impossible for him to
remain in the active practice of his profession as a physician. J!:is
income has dwindled. But the officers and members of 'Lakeside'
Lodge, No. 730, of which he is a Past Master, and its most honored
member, have been true Brethren to him. They have looked after
his wants. They have seen to it that he was provided for. He has'
been kept in his dear old home to which he is much attached. The.y
have engaged the services of a capable and kind woman of mature .
years, who spends her time in caring for him. All this the Brethren
of 'Lakeside' Lodge, the Chapter and Commandery have provided for.
.He is in comfortable circumstances so far as environment and daily
wants are concerned, and. he has the attention and heartfelt love and
sympathy of his Brethren-all of which he abundantly appreciates.
"I feel constrained, Most Worshipful Grantl Master, to say a
word further. At the solicitation of the Committee which you ap.p ointed, they not being particularly familiar with that portion of
the city and its means of transportation, I went with them on th~s ·

chaperon," and they being rather young ( f) needed some one to guide

upon a mission such as rarely falls to the lot of man.

who have not been honored be~ause of their appointment to a place
in the official roster ~f this Grand Lodge, but who have honored us
and our institution by accepting the position of Grand Stew&rds,

16

17

. REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

''The Grand Representative system was abolil!hed on the recommendation of the Co=ittee on Address, who say that it ·is as useless
as the appendix vermiformis in the human body, a remark whereat
we protest because the Almighty may not have yit disclosed to the
California Committee the last word concerning the appendix against
which they take up the hue and· cry. · To vindicate the truth of
history we are also compelled to take exception to the statement
that many of the Grand Lodges are dispensing with the system, as
only a few of them have done so. For a more weighty reason we
desire to recur to an evil which this incident serves to illustrate
just as well as though something more was at stake than the unill}portant question whether a Grand Lodge should keep up the simulacrum of a diplomatic court or not. We refer to reporting by the
Committee on Grand. Master's Address of recommendations j.nvolving
final legislative action. This is outside the proper function of such
a Committee, whose sole duty it should be to recommend the proper
reference of the various topics treated in the Address, that each
subject· requiring action may be presented separately and in a digested
form to the Grand Lodge. This incident illustrates the widest possible
departure from their proper sphere of action by the Committee, because they dealt with a subject not referred to them, the Grand Representative system not being so much as alluded to in the Address.''

''The ·Grand Secretary then presented the A11nual Reports of the
Grand Secretary and Librarian, together with the Financial Reports
of Grand Master, Grand Treasurer, Grand Secretary and Lib:r:arian,
in printed form.
"Ordered, That the Report of .Grand Secretary be referred to

M.·. W.:. Sumner Miller, Grand Master, the R.:. W.:. Newton R.
Parvin being Grand Secretary. The Grand Officers were all present,
with the exception of the Senior Grand Steward, and there was a_
large attendance of Past Grand Officers, and 454 of the 502 constituent
Lodges were represented.
The portrait of the Grand Master, Sumner Miller, on the opening
page of this fine book, is, in our opinion, a splendid portrait of a
handsome man, and, in. fact, the book, as a whole, is a thing to bl!'
admired.
. ·

year's business, advisi:a.g no radical departure from present progress. ·
The Grand Master of Iowa may be content with present conditions, when his Army rolls show a membership of 35,729 Master
Masons, of which total 1,146 were the accredited net gain of the year..

as of interest to our l·eaders:
~'We noted last year a recominenda tion, among others, of. the
then Grand Master for the abolishing of the system of Grand Representatives as a 'useless, cumbersome custom and promotive of inharmony.' No action was taken last year, but the Grand Secretary

20

~1

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

GRAN:D LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

brought up this year the recommendations of the Grand Master as
'unfinished business.' The Special Committee on the Address of the
Grand Master and the Report of the Grand Secretary take charge of
the questions of unfimshed business, and recommend their reference
to the Committee on jurisprudence, but in the ne.xt paragraph say:

Officer in . some other Masonic Gra:ad Bodies, and our experience has
b11en that some of the most pleasant correspondence in the office is
with our Grand Representatives.

" 'It will be patent to any one who will give the matter of the
appointment of Representatives to and from other Grand Lodges
proper consideration, that this custom is as useless as the appendix
vermiformis in the human body. It seems to us that the custom must
have originated in a desire to decorate members with a mere title.
The only proper way for one Grand Lodge to communicate with an~ther is through the Grand Masters.
Your Committee can see no
necessity for the continuance of the custom, and. therefore recommend
that it be abolished. Many of the Grand Lodges are dispensing therewith, and we think the Grand Lodge of California should do likewise. '

'' 'The record states that the Report was concurred in and the
recommendations accompanying were unanimously adopted.
"We do not find any record of Report on this matter by the Committee on Jurisprud,ence, and our guess would be that the adopting of
the recommendations of a Special Committee of reference would
have no legislative force, especially in view of the fact that the office
of Grand Representative and the power of the Grand Master to appoint and accredit such Grand Representatives is recognized in the
Constitution of the Grand Lodge of California.
''Our attention, however, has been called to an official communication received by our Grand Secretary from the Grand Secretary of the
Grand Lodge of California, in which this recommendation is quoted as
the action of the Grand Lodge, and we therefore take it that the
Grand Secretary at least is treating the system as legislated out of
California.
"We admit that we like the Grand Representative system and
are not in sympathy with this expression of the Special Committee
out in California. Of course, the system makes some additional work
for a Grand Secretary, and, if properly conducted, it costs a Grand
Lodge something to maintain it, but we are constrained to believe that
it is worth all it costs. It is possibly true that the custom originateq
in a desire to decorate some Masons with a title, but many Masons
appreciate it, and the natural effect is to create and foster a strong
feeling of interest and fraternity in the accredited representative
toward the Grand Lodge he represents. This in itself is worth the
work and the expense. The writer has the honor to be the Recording

''The argument of the Committee that the 'only proper way for
one Grand Lodge to communicate with another is through the Grand
Masters' is amusing. The same argilment might dispense with Grand
Masters, as every practical Grand Lodge man knows that ninety per
cent of all the correspondence between Grand Lodges is conducted
through . the offices of the Grand Secretaries.
"It may be that t1;te office of Grand Representative is as useless
as the vermiform appendix in the human body, but we are skeptical
as to the wisdom of many so-called medical authorities upon this latter proposition. We are just old-fashioned enough to prefer the judgment of the Creator, .who placed that little sac in our body, and no
meilical carver gets ours without a fight.''
A feature of this number of the Journal is the photographic group
of appointed Grand Officers, every one a future Grand Master.
M.·. W. :. Thomas L. Bond was chosen Grand Master; R.:. W.:.
Albert K. Wilson was re-elected Grand Secretary, and Past Grand
Master William M. Shaver was CQntinued as Chairman of Correspondence.

"In compliance with the order of the Grand Lodge and of the
Grand Chapter and Grand Commandery, I contracted with the W. G.
Sharkey Stone Company of Atlanta, Ga., to make and up set a suitable
monument to John Logan Power, where he- is interred in the cemetery
at Jackson, after a design, which was kindly drawn for me by
Worshipful Bro.ther William A. Stanton, of Vicksburg, at a cost of
nine hundred and ninety-five dollars. It is to be in the form of a
Masonic Altar and I think is very chaste and elegant, as well as
appropriate. I regret that owing to the disturbing conditions caused
by the prevalence of the yellow fever in the summer and fall months,
I was unable to procure the plans until it was too late to make the
monument and have it set up in time for the dedication by the Graml
Lodge at this Annual Grand Communication, but an engraving made
from a photograph of the monument, fUTnished by the contractor, will
be ready for distribution and show its beautiful proportions. While if .
we were to buil-d a monument, measured by our affection for Brother
Power; it would tower higher than the Capitol at Jackson and cost
as much, I f elt that it would be more in accordance with the simplicity
of his noble character to set up a monument of moderate cost and
proportions, but which would be as enduring as our love for him will
be lasting.''

NORTH DAKOTA.
The Grand Lodge. of North Dakota held its Sixteenth Annual
Communieation in the eity of Grand Forks, June 28, 1905,-The M.·.
W.:. James W. Foley, Grand Master, presiding, the R.·. W.:. }'rank W.
Thompson being the Grand Secretary. Sixty~six of the seventy-two
chartered Lodges were represented, with two under Dispensation, together with twenty-seven other Grand Jurisdietions. Eight Past
Grand M~sters were in attendance. The Grand Master in his Address
reported the granting of Dispensations for the forming and opening of
two new Lodges, 3fld the constitution of three heretofore ehartered.
No important deeisions were reported.
The Grand Seeretary submitted an exhaustive Report, in whieh
he reports the year as progressive and prospe:rtms. The Jurisdietion
having a membership of 5,153 Master Masons, the transactions of the
Session were entirely routine, requiring DO comment. Grand Lodge,
however, broke some new ground in the matter of defining the duties
of Fraternal Correspondent. We quote the action and will await
results:
''The matter of what should or should not be incorporated in the
Review of · Fraternal Correspondence was brought.. up by M. ·• W. ·.
Bro. Robert M. Carothers,· writer of the Correspondence Report. The
question was discussed, pro and con, and the consensus of the mem.bers present was in favor of confining the Review to the reporting· of
approved decisions made by the Grand Masters of the several Grand
Lodges. It was believed that the space which could be allotted to a
review of any one Grand Lodge was too small, the expense of preparation and .printing too _great, and the readel'll of the Report too few, to
ZT

34

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.
GRAND LODGE OF .0.A.LIFORNI.A.

make it worth the while. It seemed that with f ew exceptions the
greater number of Fraternal R eviews were largely devoted to complimentary remarks among Correspondent writers, or criticisms. which
served no practical end; 'that through the reporting·of approved decisions, or making syllabi thereof, each year's Review would be of
practical value as showing the true trend of Masonic thought and
the molding of Masonic law and precedents. · Therefore,
"M. ·. W. ·. Bro. Robert M. Carothers moved:
'' 'That the work of the Correspondent be modified and limited
to a compilation of the approved tlecisions and important legislation
of the various Grand Lodges. ' ''
The election of 0.fficers being in order, the M. ·. W. ·. Louis A.
Jacobson was chosen Grand Master, and R.:. W.·. Frank J. Thompson
was re-elected Grand Secretary. ·
The Grand Master made his appointments and all were installed
by Grand Master Foley, Past Grand Master James McDonald acti.fig
as Master of the Ceremonies.
The' Grand Orator M.:. W.:. Bro. Walter L. Stockwell delivered an
Oration before Grand Lodge for wh_ich he received a vote of . thanks.
''Acacia'' Lodge, No. 4, was tendered a vote of thanks for its
courtesy and hospitality in the entertainment of Grand Lodge.
We quote the following as one of the events of the Sixteenth
Annual of the Grand Lodge of North Dakota. ·
"Just as the tellers had finished counting the ballots for Bro.
Grant S. Hager, Depu~y Grand Master, an awful hail storm broke
over the city, destroying all of the windows at the Grand East, and
the wind scattered the Grand Secretary's papers and the ballots
promiscuously over the Lodge room. The brethren rushed to the
dining room for tables and barricaded the windows of the Lodge toom
with them, holding them in place through great efforts. The streets
were filled for the time being with runaway horses, it being impossible for the drivers to live in the fusillade of hailstones which f ell.
The' Grand Secretary had fortunately made a memorandum of the
ballot which he preserved from the ravages of the storm. Some were
unkind enough to· say that the storm came as a result of Brother
Hager's election, but Brother Hager declared that it was the applause
of Heaven. Whatever the cause, it was an event which the members
of the Grand Lo.dge will not soon forget. It is needless to say that
confusion prevailed among the Workmen, and the dignity of the
occasion was forgotten in the excitement of the moment. In due
time order was restored, none of the brethren were injured, and
Peace and Harmony prevailed.''

'l'he Grand Lodge of North Carolina h.eld eight Special Communications during the year, of which number six were for the placing of
corner-stones of public buildings, one for .t he installation of Officers

The One Hundred and Nineteenth Annual was held in Raleigh,
January 9, 1906,-The M.:. W.:. Walter S. Liddell, Grand Master, presidl.ng, the R.:. W.·. John C. Drewry being Grand Secretary. Of the
338 chartered Lodges, 182 were represented, together with thirty-two
other Grand Jurisdictions. Twelve Past Grand Masters were present.
Th~ 338 Lodges register a membership of 15,813.
The Grand Master in his Address referred feelingly to the death
of Bro. William Simpson, Past Grand Treasurer, paying an eloquent
tribute to his memory. No import~nt decisions were reported and
no business out of the usual routine submitted for consideration.
The Grand Secretary reported sixteen new Lodges under Dispensation. The Superintendent submitted a detailed Report of the administration of the Oxford Orphan Asylum. The asylum had on its Roll,
November 1, 1905, 131 boys, 135 girls; a total of 266.
A stirring Address was delivered by the Grand Orator Bro. Andrew
J. Harris for which he was thanked by a rising vote of the members.

R.·. W.:. Bro. Wm. Simpson, and the veteran, learned and zealous
Mason Bro. Bernice Walker, who died in Granville county in 1904 at
the age of 87 years, appear in this number of the Journal. The Committee on Charters recommen<).ed and Grand Lodge ordered the issuance of sixteen Charters to the new Lodges, numbered from No. 417
·to No. 53it, inclusive.

M.-. W.:. l!'rancis D. Winston was chosen Grand Master, and the
R.-. W.·. Bro. John C. Drewry was re-elected Grand Secretary.

by Past Grand Master Charles H Robinson, M.·. W.:. B. S. Royster
acting as Master of the .Ceremonies.

NEBRASKA.

Past Grand Master Charles J. Phelps submits an excellent Report
of one hundred pages, wherein he ·reviews the Masonic World as it is
of record up to the prese.n t time.

The Grand Lodge of Nebraska held an Emergent Communication in
the City· of Lincoln June 4th, 1905, for the observance of the last sad
rites to the remains of Past Grand Master Robert Wilkinson Furnas.
The Grand Lodge held its Forty-eighth Annual in l'reemasons'
Hall, Omaha, June 6, 1905, the M.:. W.:. Charles E. Burnham, Grand
Master, the R.:. W.:. Francis E. White being Grand Secretary.
The Grand Lodge has enrolled 233 chartered Lodges on its Roll, of
which 213 were represented at th13 present Annual. Twenty-five Past
Grand Masters were in attendance.
.
Grand Lodge Roll shows the number of Master Masons, 14,190.
The Grand Master's Address was a lengthy paper, full and elaborate. ·
as to all matters treated but requiring no special comment.
From the following item we fear our representative near the Grand
Lodge of Nebraska, Past Grand Master Daniel H. Wheeler, is in allhealth.
"A Committee consisting of Brothers, Cheney, 100, Richards, 43,
and Murch, 46, was appointed to visit Past Grand Master Wheeler, and
present him with a bouquet of flowers in token of the sympathy of
the Grand Lodge, and to express the hope for his speedy recovery to
health and strength."
The election of officers ~eing in order the M.:. W.·. Bro. Melville
R. Hopewell was chosen Grand Master and R.·. W.:. Bro. Francis E.
White was re-e~ected Grand Secretary. '
.
Many amendment.a to the organic law were considered. The several committees presented their reports, and Gra~d Lodge procfeded
to the installation of the Officers-elect. We read the following with
interest:
"Past Grand Master Lininger proceeded to install the Grand
Officers, selecting Past Grand Master Burnham to act as Grand
Marshal. In presenting the officers for installation, Brother Burnham
briefly recorded their services to the Grand Lodge, making special
mention of their assistance to him during the past Masonic year, Past
Grand Master Lininger following with words of commendation, and
admonishing the several officers as to their duties, ·a nd pointing out
how much the future success and prosperity of the Grand Lodge depends upon those whom it had so highly honored. While all of the
ceremony was informal, it was the unanimous opinion that it was the
most interesting and impressive ever witnessed in the Grand Lodge
of Nebraska.
A very useful member of the Fraternity, to the Grand Lodge of
Nebraska, is Past Grand Master Lininger.

NEVADA.
The Grand Lodge of Nevada held a Special Communication for
the purpose of paying the last sad tribute to the remains of Past
Grand Master Tremnor Coffin, in Carson City, August 28, i904, also
on the 3d of June, 1905, for the purpose of placing the corner-stone of
the Nye County Court House. The Forty-fust Annual Communication
was held in Carson City; June 13, 1905.
The M.:. W.·. George Gillson, Grand Master, presiding, V.:. W.:.
C. N. Noteware being Grand Secretary.
Tliere are twenty-two co~stituent Lodges on the Grand Lodge Roll
of which nineteen were represented, together with twenty-one othe;
Grand Jurisdictions. No important business presented itself and the
. .nsactions were of the usual routine. The M.:. W.:. Charles· A.
Beemer, of Spar~s, was chosen Grand ·Master, and the R:-. W.:.
"1launcey N. Noteware was re-elected Grand Secretary. Our W.·.
Bro. E. D. Vanderlieth was continued as Correspondent, under the new
and more elaborate title of "Co.mmissioner of Review."
We expect to see Nevada, in the near future, '·'shake herself" and
take the place appointed for Nevada in the Masonic column;· with her
almost unlimited territory and the wonderful inducements pr~sented
to populi;ition by the development of her electrical, mineral and agricultural industries the result must be more people, progress and prosperity.
Bro. Vanderlieth submits another excellent Report of more than
two hundred pages, wherein he reviews the proceedings of the various
Grand Bodies composing the Masonic World, extracts the meat and
serves it up for the use of his brethren of the Round Table.

Bro. S. A. Brown, Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence,
submits a Report of unusual excellence. In his conclusion he enunciates so forcibly to Masons, the duties of the hour, that we take it
as a whole:
''The startling increase in numbers which is apparent in Masonry
everywhere, being no less than fifty thousand in the United States
alone, must give thoughtful Craftsmen food for serious reflection. It
shows that men are seeking Brotherhood in its unmodified characterBrotherhood! and that alone. And it behooves us to see that they get
it; for if they do not, shall we not see the ebb which followsf Is not
Brotherhood the one thing needed in this world whereby we may
withstand the destructive forces which instantly originate to undermine every new development of human progressf Great prosperity is
upon us, and the mischiefs 'that come with it-are they not also apparenH Masonry, Brethren, must be the true Brotherhood. All othe!
societies have some divergence which makes them fail of the ideal of
Universal Brotherhood; and the danger is that we also shall fail, for
it may be that our Brzthren will not exemplify our noble principles.
Now is the time for every true Son of Light to bestir himself and be
in his place in Lodge to show the seekers that which is being sought.
Many societies seek to cultivate the mind; it is ours to cultivate the
heart. Great is the glory of the mind; but the heart-that is the best.
The great mind may do great harm; but the great heart-it can do
naught but good.

The Grand Lodge of Texas held its Seventieth Annual Communication in the city of Waco, December 5, 1905,-M.·. W .:. A. W.
Campbell, Grand Master, presiding. The registered Lodg~s on. the
Roll number 723. Of these 464 were represented, together with thirtyfive other Grand Jurisdictions. Twelve Past Grand Masters, all the

tricts were present.
The Grand Master's Address was a lengthy paper of nearly forty
pages, necessarily so, perhaps, from the extent, territorially, of the
Jurisdiction, and the immense amount of business to be supervised by
tho Executive Head. Many decisions were . solicited in the ·form of
questions and answers, of which the Grand Master reports thirty-five.
From the Report of the Grand Secretary we learn there are_ on the
Roll of Membership, 38,270 Master Masons. Charters were granted
to twenty-one new ~odges at the present Session. The Committee
on the Masonic History of Texas presented a deeply interesting Report
of sixteen pages, in the present number. The present chapter brings
the record down to about the year 1850. Plans are provided and the
necessary funds in a great part contributed for the building of a
Home a~ Fort Worth for the Widows and Orphans of the Masons of
Texas.
The routine business of the Session being completed by the. reports
and consideration thereof, of the reports of the various Committees,.
the election of Officers for the ensuing year was in order.

Farewell.
But the hour is at hand. Brethren of the Guild, I shall be with
you no more. In spirit I pass silently around th.e table where you sit
and tender to each of you the warm grasp of a hand that never knowingly did any man a wrong. May the work which we have all been

the good of Masonry; may you long be spared to continue that work;

The retiring Grand Master was presented with a Past Grand

Past Grand Master and Chairman of· Correspondence Bro. Aldro

the present conclusion, the subject whereof is "The Recognition of
Grand Lodges and Their Effects," a generally neglected subject in
Masonic jurisprudence.
WYOMING.
The Grand Lodge of Wyoming held a Special Communication in
the town of Thermopolis, july 25, i905, for the purpose of placing the
corner-stone of the Masonic Temple in course of erection .for "Malta"
Lodge, No. 17, and in the to~n of Douglas, Augu.st 2d, in the Hall of
"Ashler" Lodge, No. 10, for the placing of. the cQrner-stone of the
Converse county 1:ourthouse; and, again, in the town 'of Sheridan, assembling in the Hall of "Sheridan" Lodge, No. 6, to place the
corner-stone of the Sheridan county courthouse.
The Thirty-first Annual Communication was held in Laramie, September 6, 1905,-The M. ·. W. :. Frank A. Luckfield, Grand Master,
presiding.
There are twenty-three Lodges in this Grand Jurisdiction, with a
membership of 1,819 Master Masons. Of these seventeen Lodges were
represented at tlie present Annual. Seven Past Grand Masters were in
attendance.

63

"In concluding this, my nineteenth Report as your Grand Secretary, it may not be out of place 'to say that in the roll of Grand
Secretaries I 'now rank as number twelve in length of service. My
name as Grand Secretary is attached to every Lodge Charter in the
State except the first six. During my service membership has increased from 493 to 1,809, and I have received in Grand Lodge funds
altogether the sum of $25,600.94, every cent of which has been
promptly paid to Grand Treasurer, as printed Annual Proceedings
show. Of this record I am, as I believe, entitled to here say that I am
proud; and yet I am prouder still of the long-continued confidence I
have enjoyed at your hands, for which I thank you.
· ' Respi::ctfully submitted,
'' W. L. KUYKENDALL,
' 'Grand Secretary. ''

L. Kuykendall was re-elected Grand Secretary and Corresp.ondent.

page of this number of the Journal. The .Grand Master made his
appointments and all were installed by Past Grand Master J. M. Rumsey, Bro. Hugh Hynds acting as· Master of the Ceremonies. The
Standing · Committees were appointed and after prayer by the Grand
Chaplain the Grand Lodge closed in Ainple Form.
Bro. Kuykendall submits his usual review of other Grand Jurisdictions composing· the Masonic World. That the Report is an excellent review of the transactiosn in Masonry for the. year 1905 goe~
without saying. Masanry is both prosperous and progressive. "So
say we all of us.''

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.
CONCLUSION.

GRAND OFFICERS

We submit the foregoing as our Report on Correspondence. We
had not intended to write it, but the Grand Master, having thought
proper to name us again for the work, and in delaying the e:xplanation
to him of our reasons for not wishing to discharge the duty until too
late to give him a fair chance to select another, we have written
the paper we submit herewith as our final Report.
Respectfully submitted,
WM. A. DAVIES,
Chairman.

set forever upon the past; it never rises upon the future, for what
we call future is forever resolved into an eternal present.
The
:fl.o"{ers, therefore, of happine!IB, anil the fruits of achievement, if
gathered at all, are gathered only in the present moment, the one
shining jewel from the exnaustless stores of eternity that is absoi.utely
ours. The best things of this world, it has been said, are the things
that lie nearest-lig·h t in our eyes, breath in our nostrils, violets at
our feet-Masonry is proud of its past, of its deeds, its deyotion to
humanity, to liberty and to truth; but Masonry does not exist upon
the past, it lives to-day, it exalts the present, it means Development;
it builds up, it does not tear down; it conserves, it. does not destroy;
it raises and supports, it does not condemn or consign; it brings its
candidate from darkness to light, it says to him: "let not him that
seeketh cease from his search until he find.'' Masonry is as a seed
which grows, not as a diamond cut and :fixed, it does not profess
infallibility, nor even to be a system or perfected truth, it is a search
for truth; it is tolerant, it sees a soul of goodness in things evil,
a soul of truth in things erroneous, it holds that if perfected truth
were offered. in one hand and the search for truth in the other, it
would be the higher course to choose the· search for truth; it holds
of itself, as of nature, that there is no life without growth, and that
as the plant must either grow or die, so must Masonry, in its principles and teachings and purposes, either broaden and deepen, or
.p erish. The to-day of Masonry is the greatest of all the days which
have gone before, the greatest in the scope of its beneficences, richest
in the quality of its brotherhood, broadest in its ever widening circle
of human consideration and kindness, and more vital in its potentiality
and growth.
During the past year no ·Lodges have surrennered their charters,
and none have lost their' identity through consolidation. Dispensations have been issued to form eight new Lodges, and the net gain
in membership within the jurisdiction has been 2357, the greatest
within the State since the formation of the Grand Lodge, fifty-seven
-y ears ago, and exceeded only once by 33 ~hen the 11ewly formed
Lodges in the Orient added a considerable number to the net' gain
of the whole jurisdiction.

those changes let us read hope, not sadness; light, not darkness, for
hope is the keystone of human life-all pow~rs, even love and fait.P,
rest finally upon hope; it iii that which tells us that love and friendship
are immortal, and that the threads which are lost from our grasp
in the shadows of the receding world are found again in the beauty

Some of Our Honored Dead,
In 1857 Samuel Prager was Seni6r Deacon of Los · Angeles Lodge,
No. 42, and for fifty years thereafter was an active and conspicuous
member of the Grand Lodge of California. He was with us,. as we
all remember, one year ago, rarely missing an Annual Communication
of the Grand Body,: and, having held various appoi:i'ited offices therein
almost continuously for probably more than thirty years; he was
also, for many years, the highly efficient president of the Los Angeles
Masonic Board of Relief, and at all times and in all place11. was
conscientious· and capable and a Mason tried and true.
Brother Prager is missed to-day from his accustomed haunts.
The standard of the Grand Lodge, which it was his office to bear, i1
now entrusted to other hands, a~d the places which have known
him here on earth will know him no more forever. The Grand Lodge
was called in special communication for the purpose of conducting
the funeral, R.'. W.''. Oscar Lawlor, Junior Grand Warden, presiding,
and all that remains to us now of Brother Prager is the memory of
bis kind an'd amiable personality, his genial presence, his soft ' and
sunny disposition; his genuine manhood and worth, his love for family and friends, and his lifelong loyalty and 'devotion to Masonry.
It was our privilege and pleasure one year ago to reappoint
to the chairmanship of the important Committee on Grievances in the
·Grand Lodge, on which committee he had served as chairman with
marked ability for a number of years, Brother John A. Hosmer, of
King Solomon's Lbdge, No. 260, and it is difficult now to realize that
Brother Hosmer can never perform the duties of that-· office again;
he has gone from us in the :flower of his strength and usefulness in

Brothe'r Hosmer , was for many ye~rs active in Masonry; filling
many offices of honor and responsibility , an<} always with COJlSpicuous fitness. In 1901 he served the Grand Lodge as Grand Orator
leaving upon the minds of those who were privileged to hear him ~
deep impress of his research, his learning and his ability.
As
a citizen he was exemplary, and throughout his life' did well whatever duty he was called upon to perform. As Judge of the Superior
Court of the City and County of San Francisco, whieh position he
occupied when his summons came, he manifested those qualities
which make ·.a jurist great; he .p ossessed the judicial temperament,
and the inherent sense of justice; he was scholarly and .thoughtful
and in his resea~ches thorough and exhll-ustive; hi13 mind was logical:
his grasp ~omprehensive, and his powers of discrimination and ana.l y-,
·si!I exceedingly .high, and as the foundation of it all, his character
for integrity and honor was absollltely without spot" or blemish.
Let us yield to him that greatest praise which was accorded to
the noblest Roman, and say of J:iim, as w~s said of Brut~s, ''that
nature could stand up and say to all the world, this was ,. man."

MISCELLANEOUS.
In the Grand Secretary's report will be found full and complete statements covering the matters of Lodges constit~ted, dispensations granted for new Lodges,. special communications of the Grand
Lodge for the purposeg of laying corner stones, dedicating Masonic
halls, etc.; special dispensations issued, lists of representatives received and appointed and amendments to By-Laws; and the only
reference to thesP subjects needed from the Grand Master is to the
matter of dispensation granted to form Dinuba Lodge: At the Annual
Communication of 1906 an amendment of the Constitution was adopted
vesting in the Grand Master the discretion ·of issuing dispensation
to form a new Lc;>dge, if in his judgment it appeared proper to do so,
notwithstanding the refusal of the nearest existing old Lodge to
give consent thereto. The occasion which guve rise to the discussion which resulted in the adoption of the amendment above referred
to, was the refusal of Reedley Lodge, No. 304, to yield its permission to the formation of the proposed Lodge at Dinuba; and
after the adjournment of the Annual Communication one year ago,
the brethren at Dinuba began anew the proceedings to form the desired new Lodge, and in due time application was again made by
them to Reedley Lodge for its acquiescence and consent, which
was again denied, and appeal was made by the brethren at Dinuba
to the Grand Master, who, accompanied by the Grand Lecturer, proceeded, early in February, to the scene of the disagreement, and
made an exhaustive and comprehensive investigation of the situation, including, within the scope of his inquiries, not only the
brethren at Reedley and Dinuba, but those also in such surrounding
towns as Visalia and Fresno, and as a result of that investigation
the Grancl Master was persuaded that the best interests of Masonry
would be subserved by granting the dispensation prayed for, which,
accordingly, was done. In our opinion the brethren at Reedley, in
their refusal, were actuated only by worthy motives, being apprehensive, as tl1ey no doubt were, that the formation of the new Lodge
would most seriously impair the strength and usefulness of the old, but
in our judgment they were in error, and the activity shown by both
Lodgl!s, as disclosed in their reports to the Grand Secretary, since the •
dispensation was granted, and the good will and amity which we arJ
assured exist between them, .afford convincing evidence of .the soundness of our views.

At the Annual Communication of 1906, the general direction
of relief necessitated by the Great Calamity of April, 1906, was, by
virtub of his office, and resolution of the Grand Lodge, continued in
the hands of the Grand Master, and in rendering final report thereon,
we would state that the organization, ·with its several branches, specially established after the catastrophe for handling the details of
the work, was carried forward with one or two changes in the
official staff, and a high order of efficiency distinguished the administration of both the San Francisco and Oakland Boards. Brothers
W. Frank Pierce, President of the Board in this city, and Rodolph
W. Meek, President of the Board in Oakland, are especially de~rrv­
ing of the unqualified praise .and thanks of the fraternity for t-Lir
unselfish devotion to the cause of ·the needy and distressed, serving
without one farthing of compensation, and surrendering almost their
entire time for a whole year to the exacting duties of thei1' positions,
performing arduous toil, actuated only by the love of humanity and
Masonry, and with no thought of reward except the approval of
conscience and the generous approbation of their brethren..
Final balance sheets of the San Francisco and Oakland boards,
also general balance sheet of the Grand Master, are presented herewith, together with certificates of expert accountants as to the accuracy of the several statements; the final report of the San Jose
Board is also given.
Early in June the following communication, which is self explanatory, was audressed to all the Masters and Secretaries of the Lodges
of San Francisco, and a similar communication to other brethren,
conversant with the situation here and at Santa Rosa and at San
Jose; the response to the letter, sometimes V!Jrbal, more frequently
in writing, was very general and painstaking, and on the basis
of the information afforded thereby, some of the most valuable work
of relief was rendered. The following is a copy of the communication referred to:
June 6, 1907.
"Worshipful Sir and ,B rother:
''The Special Masonic Reliaf Bureau organized in this city immediately after the catastrophe of one year ago to take charge of
Masonic Relief incident to the conflagration, has closed its affairs
and has been dissolved, and the few ordinary cases remaining will
be attended to by the regular Masonic Board of Relief of this city.
''As a result of observation and experience during the past year,
we are constrained to believe, and in this view are supported by the

567

.
"You, as Master of your Lodge, may know of certain such
mstances among your members, and I would ask you to kindly take
t~e roster ~f your Lodge, and carefully scan its membership and
give me a list of names of such members as in your judgment may
be worthy of true Masonic charity. We would not wish any of
them to know the source of our information, and whatever is done
will be done quietly and without publicity, and in such a manner a~
to avoid humiliation to the recipient . In this list, the widows of
Masons may be included, provided their widowhood, or present distress has some reasonable connection with the disaster of one year
ago. We would ask you to make the list in the order of merit be·
ginning with the most deserving and arranging them in order t; the
close, and the two conditions to be observed in preparing the list are
as follows:
"First-The distress must have been occasioned in some manner
eithet directly or indirectly by the earthquake or
of April 1906

''Second-There must be distres.s at present existing.

together and is now faidy prosperous, he will not come within the
scope of our intention. Give me the name and correct address and
full particulars as to each case that you may mention and if the
relief should not be given directly in any case, but s~ould be entrusted to some one of judgment for his or .her benefit so state and

for, as you know, it is not unfrequently the case that the mos;

is the class that we desire now to reach.

amount, we have a balance of $301,986.16, upon which, if 20 per cent
were returned to the donors, it would amount to $60,397.23.

be returned to the donors, it will leave a balance of $1,681.42 re·

maining on hand.

An examination of . the above statement discloees the fact that
on .September 6, we had on hand an unexpended balance of $62,078.65,
and the work having been practically completed; the serious question
was presented as to the proper disposition of this balance on hand.
The Grand Maater, desiring to act in harmony with the wishes and
desires of the Masons of California, on September 12 called a conference of elective Grand Officers, such as could be brought together
and other representative men of the fraternity, and after a com'.
prehensive discussion it was decided with absolute unanimity that
if approximate accuracy could be arrived at, the only just and prape;
course to pursue would be 'the pro rata return to the donors of the
excess contributed over the amount needed.
The Grand Master
had already, through the exhaustive analysis of an expert accountant, determined that this could be done, which action accordingly
was forthwith taken, and the sum of $60,397.23 ·returned to generous
donors. Each remittance was accompanied by a letter expressive of
the. thanks and appreciation of the Fraternity of California copy
of which is as follows:
'
SAN FRANCISCO, September 12, 1907.
Dear SirWben the great calamity of Apr.il, 1906, befell San Francisco
and vicinity, the Masons from all over the world, with spontaneous
generosity, poured forth upon the stricken district their offerings of
love and sympathy, and the financial aid thus r endered made it
possible to prevent the untold suffering which must othei:wise have
ensued.
.
:he a_dministration of the trust imposed upon the chosen officer15
rn disbursmg the funds thus freely given, has been, we believe, careful and judicious, and yet no worthy case, so far as we know, has
been overlooked; and now, as we are about closing the wor'\t. of

relief, we find a considerable balance of the fund which was contributed, unexpended.
·

to any purpose other than that for which it was intended: viz., the
relief of suffering growing out of the great ·disaster, and it is the
judgment of the Fraternity in California that the unused balance
should be returned pro rata to the donors.
We therefore are able to return to you $ ........ ·i check for

Thus is closed in MaSQnic history the greatest episode of its
kin'd that has occurred in the centuries of the existence of Freemasonry; it has reflected honor, and only honor, upon the Craft,_
and has placed a living crown of light µpon the teachings and prof ,siomi of our Fraternity.
Man's hand· is powerless against na.are 's 1·.;~idtlesf! sway, and it was in consequence thereof, our unhappy fate to raise perforce the signal of distress, to cry help for
the Widow 's Son; the cry was heard, and Masonic precepts burst
with splendor into life; overflowing bounty poured forth upon us,
and while the offerings of love from the entire world were spontaneous and free, uninfluenced by any consideration as to how our
Masonic duties might in times past have been discharged, yet, there
is to us a measure of compensation in the records made by our Boards
of Relief since the system was established by the Grand ~odge sonte
fifty years ago; for direct appropriatioll'll from the Grand Lodge for
their support, amounting to more than $300,000, have been made,
every dollar of which has been devoted to the relief of distressed
sojourning brethren, their widows and orphans, from other jurisdictions, and no fraction of which has been returned, and this amount
has been very largely increased through the per capita assessments
contribu·~ed monthly by the Lodges tributary to the several Boards.
Our capable Grand Secretary informs us, that after careful investigation, he has found that, owi,Il'g, no doubt, to our geographical position and benign climate, California's expenditures of this character
have been, not only more than similar expenditures of any other
American jurisdiction, but possibly nearly as large as all others
combined. This work has truly been a work of love, no sordid thought
has ever <'.ast a darklinr Rhadow, the only consideration has b!len a
high and worthy purpos·e to exemplify Masonic truths, yet when
our hour of tribu1'1ltion came, which chilled our hearts with distress

generous glow of sympathetic love of ~ur brethren throughout the

DECISIONS.

Early i n the year numerous requests were received for an inter·
pretation of the Resolution adopted at the last Communication of th~
Grand Lodge concerning committees of in'Vestigation on petitions for
degrees, and ~pplications for membership, and in response thereto, we

594

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALlFORNIA.

construed the resolution as follows, which construction is submitted
for your approval:
Our interpretation of the resolution adopted at the last Annual
Communication of the Grand Lodge of California in reference to
keeping secret the names of brethren appointed on Committees of
Investigation on petitions for degree1• and a{>plications for membership, and our judgment as to the pn per method of procedure, are
as follows:
The intention of the resolution being to secure absolute secrecy,
the names of the brethren appointed on these committees should
not, in our opinion, be given by the Master to · the Secretary, to
enable him, as formerly, to notify the brethren of their appointment, neither should. their reports be returned to the Secretary; but
the Master himself should severally notify the members of the committees of their appointment, not revealing to one the identity of. the
' others, and their reports should be rende~ed by them directly to
him, and when practicable, should be given verbally, and if in writing, after having subserved the purpose of informing the Master of
the results of the investigations, should be by him, destroyed, and
his simple announcement to the Lodge of such results, will be all the
information concerning these reports conveyed by him to anyone.

Gardena Lodge was situated in a territory a few miles outside

a portion of Los Angeles County, which resulted in the annexing to

"GARDENA, CAL., Aug. 1, 1907.

312 Frost Bldg., Los Angeles, Cal.Dear Sir and Brother: Your favor of the 8th ult. in reference
t to. the question as to whether or not Gardena Lodge is properly within
the joint jurisdiction of the Los Angeles Lodges and hence included
in the membership or the Masonic Board of Relief of Los Angeles,

The charter to Garden!l Lodge, No. 372, was issued. to a Lodge in

its By-Laws, raising its fees .for degrees tl;i the minimum allowed by

No amendment of this character· was ever presented to me for ·my ...

And my reply thereto was as follows:
August 12, 1907. .
Dear Sir and Brother: Your favor of the 30th ult., propounding to us question relating to waiver of jurisdiction, came duly to
hand.
In reply to your question as to whether a request for a waiver
of jurisdiction should be acted upon by the Lodge at the same meeting when presented, I won.Id say that it should not be so acted upon,
but should lie over for one month, and a Committee should be appointed to investigate, first as to whether the Lodge to whom the request for waiver is addressed, actually possesses jurisdiction, and secondly if the rrnsons alleged by the applicant as to why a waiver is
desired, are good and sufficient. This report can only be rendered at
a stated meeting succeeding the one when the request is received,
and the Lodge can only act intelligently in the light of the information afforded thereby.

Iii addition to the reasons above set forth it is, we believe, impracticable for the town of Gardena to hold concurrent jurisdiction
with the Lodges of the city of Los Angeles, and we hardly think
that Gardena Lodge is open to criticism for moving its Lodgeroom
into the town of Gardena, and out of the so-called "Shoestring
Strip.''
Yours sincerely and fraternally,
,EDWARD H .. HART,
Grand Master of. Masons of California.

'

If the Lodge to whom the request for waiver of jurisdiction has
been made refuses to grant the waiver asked for, another Lodge
holding concurrent jurisdiction, cannot, within twelve months, receive and act upon a request from the same' applicant.

Yours sincerely and fraternally,
EDWARD H. HART,
Grand Master of Masons of California.

A Vouchment.

A Past Master of one of our Lodges addressed to us t he following communication:
September 4, 1907.
Mr. E. H. Hart,
M.'. W.'. Granu MasterDear Sir and Brother: A Lodge in this city acting upon the
autllority of Section 935 of Decisions as given in Anderson's Manual, page 389, admitted a sojourning brother on a vouchment of one
oi its members, who had recently sat with him in a Chapter of
Royal Arch Masons.
A few days thereafter the visiting brother·
was taken sick and was cared for by the Board of Relief. A . brother
who attended him, wishing to notify his Lodge, asked the name. of
the Lodge and the address of its Secretary. It developed that the
brother had been dimitted from a Lodge in one of the Eastern States
for n68.rly four years.
It seems to me that the decision quoted is doubtful authority. I
therefore ask you to decide as to the necessary prerequisites for a
vouchment.
Yours fraternally,
My answer was:
No Mason can rightfully vouch for a visiting brother unless he
shall have sat with him in open Lodge, or have examined him under
proper authority.

n99

To this I an.s wered:
The same reasons which impelled the Grand Lodge at the Annual
Communication of 1906 to adopt the resolution providing for secrecy
of committees of investigation, clearly indicate that voting upon
objection to advancement, as set forth in the above letter, should be
by secret ballot, and not by show of hands, for by show of hands
the brothers voting would be obliged to expose their ballots. Owing
to the impracticability of voting by ball and cube, the ballot should
be taken by slips tJf paper on each of which should be written "yes"
Or ''no.''

THE MASONIC HOME.

The great monument of Masonic beneficence within our State \s
the Masonic Widows' and Orphans' Home at Decoto, or, according ·
to th~ new By-Lawe adopted during the past year by the Board of

GRANI) LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

Trustees, to conform the name more nearly to the true character of
the ins titu tion, "'l'he Masonic Home of California," and it is a
monument of which every Mason in the jurisdiction may justly feel
proud.

need of a Superintendent could be put aside no longer, but demanded
present action, it came as an inspiration to the Grand Master, that
the one man in California suited in every respect to the requirements
of the responsible and trying position, was that same man, William
Harvey Edwards; and this conviction was deepened and confirmed
in our knowledge, because of personal acquaintance, of the eminent
fitness of his gracious an~ talented wife, to fill with absolute perfection, and overflowing measure of equipment, the high and important
position of matron. We doubted, however, that it would be possible to persuade Brother Edwards to give up all other interests and
assume charge of this great work; he yielded, however, to the
appeal 'of the Grand Master and the unanimous and urgent request
of the Board of Trustees, and on October 1st took the helm at
Decoto, and every Mason in California knows into what safe and
sure hands that helm has passed.
We have taken from our Grand Jurisdiction a Grand Lecturer,
who during his incumbency of ten years in office, has wrought into
harmony the "work" throughout our commonwealth; he has carried
the standard upward to so high a level of efficiency that a successor
may, we believe, be chosen who will hold the results which he has
achieved; and in transferring him to a bigger, better, broader
field of usefulness, we have, we believe, bestowed upon the fraternity
the most beneficent act of our administration.

The sad and untimely death of Past Grand Master Hiram N.
Rucker in December, 1905, who was at that time the Superintendent
of the .Home, left that institution withou.t a. chief administrative
official. The noble and superior woman, who had been for so many
years Dr. Rucker 's companion and helpmeet, and who had during
his incumbency as superintendent at Decoto, ably assisted him as
matron, consented to remain and perform the duties of that office
until such a time as she could be relieved without serious detriment
to the Home, and for nearly two y.ears the chief responsibility of the
internal direction of our cherished institution rested upon Mrs.
Rucker, and to say that she discharged that responsibility with a
high order of ability, winning the unstinted appr9val and commendation of the Board of Trustees, is to accord to her but a faint measure
of the praise to which she is justly entitled. Her administration was
full of excellence and order, she endeared herself to every resident
of the Home, and in the hearts of the children, as seen in their daily
attitude towards her, she is enshrined with a richness of affection
and tenderness that will ever remain a priceless tribute to her gentleness, her character, and worth.
·
For several reasons the Board found it difficult to secure a suitable successor to Dr. Rucker; men possessing the proper training and
adaptibility for the work being by no means numerous, and besides
this, the remuneration attached to the office is not attractive to men
of ability, except by combining in husband and wife, as in the case
of Dr. and Mrs. Rucker, the two positions of superintendent and
matron with the. salaries pertaining thereto, and the incidental privilege of a family residence at the Home free of expense. Early in
the year the conviction was borne in upon the Grand Master that
what was needed at Decoto was not only a competent matron, which
we had, but a competent superintendent as well, which we had not;
a man fitted not only to take supreme direction of the internal
affairs of t~e Home, and exercise a watchful care over the residents,
especially the boys, but one also qualified, under direction of the
Board, to assume a large part of the responsibility of the business
administration of the institution.
·

VISITS.
A tour of visitation thrdughout the Masonic districts of California impresses most forcibly upon one the immensity of our wonderful
land. California is an empire covering an area more extensive than
the States of Maine, New Hampshhe, Vermont, Massachusetts, Connecticut, Rhode Island, New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania
combined, with a coast line, if measured upon the Atlantic seaboard,
extending from the coast bf Maine to that of South Carolin-a. There
are in California fifty-four regular, and four special Masonic districts, making fifty-eight in all, and the Grand Master has, during
the past year, visited officially and held district meetings in all of
these fifty-eight districts, omitting none, and in several of the larger
and more important districts, we have visited nearly every individual
Lodge therein. He has extended his tour of visitation over the seas,
exchanging fraternal greetings with our Lodges in the Hawaiian
Islands, more than two thousand miles fro~ our shores-the so-calle1
Forty-ninth California Masonic District; and the only district within
the broad sweep of the embracing arms of the mighty jurisdiction
of California not visited by the Grand Master during the past year,
