is the so-called Fiftieth District, comprising the Philippine Islands,
and the only reason why he failed to call upon this far away district was that the year contained only twelve months, instead of
fourteen.
The distance traveled on land by the Grand Master in his tour
of visitation was more than twenty thousand miles, and the distance
traveled by sea nearly five thousand miles, together being ·sufficient
to encircle the globe.
During this grand tour of visitation, many notable Masonic
incidents came along our pathway. In the city of Porterville, in
December last, at a meeting of Porterville Lodge, No. 303, we were
present at the raising at one meeting, to the sublime degree of
Maste;r Mason, of a father and fo.ur sons, an incident of this kind
which we believe is absolutely the world's record.
We were also present in the month of July in the city of Santa
Cruz at a meeting of Santa Cruz Lodge, No. 38, at the raising to the
degree of Master M~~on of one Hiram Abif. The young man, who
had just passed thP age • •w enty-one, had still another name, Lorenzen, we believe; but until that night he had never fully understood the significanee of the name he bore, and it is needless to say
that his father, who was present that evening, an earnest Mason,
was also an enthusiastic member of the craft, something like twentyone years ago.
It has not been uncommon during the past year for us to be
present at meetings where fathers have raised to the sublime degree
their own sons, and one of the rare and delightful privileges, which
came to the Grand Master during his year of office, was that of
conferring, on September 12th, in California Lodge, No. 1, upon his
own son this crowning degree of Ancient Craft Masonry.
This simple recital of visitations during the past twelve mont.h s
might seem sufficient, but the personal contact by the Grand Master
with the Masons of our vast jurisdiction, in their own homes, means
more to him than a plain recital of the facts; it means meeting
with Monroe and Richards and their men in the shadows of the
giant redwoods of Humboldt and Mendocino counties; it means
gathering with the Masons under Dr. Nutting and Judge Sweeney
in Siskiyou and Shasta at the base of that lofty and silent sentinel
at our northern portal, the eternally snow crowned king of the
Sierras; it means exchanging fraternal greetings with the brethr~n
assembled from mountains, meadows, lakes and timbered slopes m
. far off Lassen and Modoc counties, with Christie and Bonner; it
means the hand grasp with those big hearted men living next to
nature, above the strife and turmoil, up near the sky, where the stars

shine at night, and where the mountains lift in majesty their
chaste and encircling crest, the counties of Mono and Inyo, led
Masonically by such true men as Judge Murphy and Dr. Doyle;
it means the unfeigned, joyous welcome of Arbogast and Case of
Coats and Moncur and May, and of those brave and hardy mountaineers and mining men of Sierra and Plumas and Nevada counties, that have poured into the open lap of the world the fabled
wealth of Midas; it means traversing timbered heights, and following between jagged walls, tossed and turbulent streams, to the
historic town of Downieville, located on a shelf in the canyon walls,
with its aptly named Mountain Shade Lodge of Masons, here to seize
the outstretched hand of welcome; it means gathering about the
banquet boards with Dye and Clough and Larew and the strong
brave men of Amador and Calaveras, of Tuolumne and Mariposa
counties, within the sound of the falling stamps of quartz mills,
making music, to ears inured thereto, sweeter than the cadences of
falling waters, or the liquid note of the shepherd's lute; it means
Masonic reunions with Leininger and his men, in that ruitful foot·
hill country, more beautiful than the poet's Auburu; our Auuurn,
our rolling, sun colored, rainbow tinted Auburn, our peaceful, picturesque, pleasing Placer County; it means the gatherings. with
Mierson and the Masons of El Dorado County, within the circle of

we have met within ·the sacred precincts of the tyled Lodgeroom, as

CONCLUSION.

THE GRAND LODGE.
This is what our year of visitation has meant to us; it has
emphasized to our mind what we imperfectly appreciated before, the .
greatness and wonder of California, the magnificenee of California
Masonry, and the splendor of our superb strength, gatbued here in
this grand and sui:reme Masonic body of our mighty State.
The spectrum separates a beam of sunshine into its component
parts, individually of varying degrees of brilliancy and beauty, yet
each, so intimately dependent the one upon the other, a:s to necessitate the complete and harmonious union of all t~ produce a .r ay
of light; so of our organization: the harmonious blending of all our
factors and forces, of Lodges, of officers, of individuals, combinll
to give us the one unclouded flood of light, the Grand Lodge, Free
and Accepted Masons of California.

607 .

Only a word remains:
"Keep on striving" is the secret of success in life. What has
be:n done moves rapidly. into the region of the past. The brightest
shield, neglected, soon gathers rust, and the fairest memories of
worthy deeds are soon forgotten in the shadows of subsequent sloth
and abandoned ambition. Memories are treasures of the soul to
bri:qg com.fort and consolation in moments of reverie and reflection
but memories do not win battles, and neither individuals nor na'.
tions, nor institutions, can live on memories, but as inspiration to
stronger effort, ·and to point the way to other victories memories
are of priceless value.
'
The keynote of the past century bas been evolution and this is
the d~min~nt note of the present hour. The cardinal 'principle of
evolut10n is struggle--struggle for life, the survival of the. fittestor, as has been indicated by an · eminent thinker, in a farther and just
as t~ue. a sense, struggle ~or the life of others; in any event, struggle is inseparable from life, and is the very manifestation thereof
it is the st~mu~ant .of the race, ~nd the cessation of combat, of struggl~
and of aspirat10n, is the cessation of life itself.
Forward was the watchword of creation when, "In the begin-·
ning God created the heaven and the earth, and the earth was without
form and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep.''
Forward has been the watc.h word of the world ever since, and is
the watchword of success to-day, in every undertaking of life; and
. Forwar~, awa~en~d by a <lesire for light and truth, by a conception of the ideal, inspired by love of humanity and enforced by undeviating purpose, will ever continue to be the watchword of the
human ra~e, so long as man shall live upon the earth, so long as he
shall be mflueneed by ambition and hope, and so long as he shall
strive to gain the standard of HIGHER THINGS.
EDWARD H. HART,
Grand Master of Masons of California.

A petition for restoration from Joseph Daniel Jourden of Mission
Lodge, No. 169, suspended by Abell Lodge, No. 146, January 5, 1895,
has also been received and transmitted to that committee.
Of the proposed amendments to the By-Laws of Lodges which
have been received, the approval of the Grand Master in thirty-six
cases has been filed in this office. Of these, thirteen being from
Lodges Nos. 38, 123, 193, 200, 224, 226, 269, 279, 309, 310, 313, 328, 363,
and 380, proposed changes in time for stated meetings; nine being
from Lodges Nos. 35, 38, 61, 104, 147, 193, 215, 268, 335, 360, and 375,
proposed to increase the fee for the degrees; nine being from Lodges
Nos. 1, 30, 35, 44, 181, 248, 320, 324, and 364, proposed adopting the
life membership system; three beihg from Lodges Nos. 78, 161, and
287, proposed increasing dues; one being from Lodge No. 320, proposed
creating an affiliation fee; one being from Lodge No. 248, proposed
decreasing dues, and one from Lodge No. 209, proposed decreasing
fee for degrees.
The approval or disapproval of the Grand Master being but
temporary, the foregoing amendments, as required by our laws, have
been placed in the hands of the Chairman of the Committee on ByLa ws of Lodges, and will be submitted to the Grand Lodge for final
action, as have the books of By-Laws of the Lodges now working
under dispensation.
At the last Annual Communication, the surrender of the charter
of "Ionic" Lodge, No. 121, was accepted, and Brother Michael
Lininger, Inspector of the Fourteenth District, was authorized to
wind up its affairs. He reports the collection of dues and payment
of debts and has transmitted to this office the sum of $109.35.

In addition to the foregoing report, the M.".
Grand Master
transferred $2,000 to this Board on September 4th from the General
Funds in his charge for the purpose of relieving sufferers from the late
calamity. Of this amount $661 50 have been expended, leaving still a
balance of $1,338 50 on hand.
A close and careful study of the conditions surrounding the poor
unfortunates of the la~e disaster gives convincing proof that the amount
set aside for the purpose of their relief is entirely inadequate to cover
the demands to be made upon it within the very near future.
The depression in business and the local labor and political disturbances have caused many of our brethren to look for assistance. Especially is this the case with professional men who faithfully expected to
outlive their misfortune under ordinary, prosperous conditions.
The rainy season, now rapidly approaching, will add another
misery to those of our brethren inhabiting refugee cottages, many of
which are in need of repair at no little expense.
As the funds of the General Board of Relief are now exhausted, the
matter of assisting the sufferers of the late calamity will fall upon the
local Board and a year of exceptionally large demands upon its funds is
·
confidently expected.
Respectfully submitted,
J. B. Rm:BEN, Secretary.

In glancing over this report it will be observed that the calls for
relief have been far greater this year than heretofore, probably owing to
the continued suffering resultant from the San Francisco disaster of
1906; yet with the general assistance of Past .Grand Master Brother
Motley Hewes Flint, we have been able to weather the storm. Had it
not been for this aid, we would have been several thousand dollars
overdrawn, or the suffering brethren could not have been relieved. As
it was, however, we were able to rent cottages, buy furniture, sewing
machines, tools for mechanics, provisions, clothing, medicine, artificial
limbs, etc., and thus place deserving brethren in position to become
self-supporting. All this costs money, but the recipients do not lose
their manhood and self-respect. This we deem true charity.

MASONIC EMPLOYMENT BuR£Au.
The Masonic Employment Bureau, established sixteen months ago,
has proved a decided success. It has been the means of securing more
than seven hundred positions since its organization. We cannot commend it too highly.
DEATH OF OUR PRESIDJ!:NT.
Saddened, indeed, were the hearts of the members of this Board 'of
Relief when, on the sixth day of Jui~e, 1907, the spirit of our Honored
President, Brother Samuel Prager, "Took its flight to that unknown

j

628

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

world whither our fathers have gone before us." While his death was
not unexpected, it has left a vacancy among us which will be hard to
refill. No words can be more fittingly spoken of him here than the
resolutions adopted by this Board of Relief. They· are as follows :
WHEREAS, No higher recommendation can be given any one than·
that we can truthfully state that our beloved brother was a MAN and A
MASON, and as a Mason he was one to whom the world well knew the
burdened heart could' pour out its sorrows ; one to whom distress could
prefer its suit; one whose hand was guided by justice, and whose heart
was expanded by benevolence.
Brother Samuel Prager was an active worker in the Masonic
Grand Lodge of California for over fifty years, and his loss wiU be
keenly felt by all the breth~en composing that organization, more particularly his kindly face, his genial words of greeting, and his able advice
on all important questions.
WHEREAS, As President for many years of the Masonic Board of
Relief, Brother Prager has relie°ved the distress of thousands of worthy
distressed brethren, their wives, widows and orphans, and in the performance of this duty has devoted practically all of his time for this
true Masonic Charity; listening patiently, and with deep sympathy, to
the sorrows of the widowed and fatherless, and giving wise counsel and
assistance to the distressed brethren, so' that after a life ·o f great usefulness, not only to his beloved home city, but also to our Great Fraternity,
we can and do state in this, our hour of bereavement, "Well done, thou
good and faithful servant."
Be ft Therefore Resolved, That .in the death of Brother Samuel
Prager, the entire Masonic Fraternity, and the City of Los Angeles,
have met with an irreparable loss, and in the Masonic Board of Relief
a vacancy w}tich never can be filled ..
Be It Further Resolved, That to the family. of our deceased friend
and brother dp we express our deep sympathy in this . their hour of
trouble; but we feel that their burden may be lightened by the enduring
monument that Brother Prager has erected on the "sands of time," and
the thought that the world has been better and brighter by the examples
he has set.
Be It Further Resolved, That a copy of these resolutions be spread
upon the minutes of the Masonic Board of Relief, and a copy be sent
to the family of Brother Prager.
Fraternally submitted,
}
M. H. FLINT,
D. R. . WELLER,
Committee. ·
ASHTON A. WELLS,

We are sor~y to note that some jurisdictions seem to consider that
they are under no obligation to relieve the distress of their members
when they go beyond their threshhold, and even decline to reimburse a
sister Lodge or Board of Relief for aid extended in emergency cases.
Perhaps they do not realize the vast number of calls upon the Fraternity
on the Pacific Coast, and especially in Southern California, which is
undoubtedly the Hospital for the world.
I publish herein a letter or two, which are on file with this Board
of Relief, which show different Fraternal feelings in two jurisdictions
with the hope that the TRUI! Fraternal spirit manifested in the one, may

(The Worshipful -~foster's Letter.)
CHARLESTON, S. C., March 7th, 5907.
Dl!AR BROTHER RHETT: Yours enclosing statement from Dr. J. M.
Dunsmoor has been received. The payments made Mrs. N. on July
13th and September 13th were unauthorized by me, or our Lodge, as
far as I can remember. I have written to Dr. Dunsmoor for information as to his authority but have received no reply. Of course Orange
Lodge wishes to pay all its just debts, but cannot undertake to reimburse the Masonic Fraternity of Los Angeles for money which . their
own generous impulses have prompted them to give to a woman in
distress, and which was charged against our Lodge as an after thought.
Until further notice from me, send $5.00 directly to Mrs. N. on the first
day of each month. Write Dr. Dunsmoor of these instructions. I have
no authority to exceed the amount granted by the Lodge.
The transactions of July 13th, and September 13th, were personal
matters between the Masonic Board of Relief and Mrs. N. They can.
perhaps arrange the matter on a satisfactiory basis.
Very truly,
K. TAT!!,

(Our Reply.)
Los ANGEELES, CAI.., March· 18th, 1907.
Mr. !' on L . Rhett, Secretary Ora1ige Lodge, No. 14, F. & A . M.,
.
Charleston, S. C.
DEAR SIR AND BROTHtR : Yours of March 8th, containing check for
Mrs. N. has been received, and the same has been transmitted to Mrs.
N . I heartily approve of your decision that in the future you will deal
directly with Mrs. N. in person, and not through our Board of Relief.
Our offer ·to act as your agent at this point was only done in the spirit
of true brotherly love and Masonic courtesy. Our advancements to
Mrs. N. were made at a time when the wolf stood at her door; sickness
and destitution were within. We acted as we would have you act
towards one of our worthy members or their families should they be
at your threshold and in like condition, and we would certainly be very
willing and glad to reimburse you for any reasonable outlay which you
might advance to relieve their immediate distress when waiting for a
letter or even a telegram for instructions would increase their distress
and physical suffering. However, as you take the technical point of
view that you did not autho1-i:te the two payments which you specify, our
President directs me to state to you that that account is donated to your
Lodge as a charitable gift from this Board of Relief.
Fraternally yours,
J. M. DUNSMOOR, Secretary.

(Letter from San Francisco, Cal.)
OccIDENTAL LoDGE, No. 22, F. & A. M.
SAN FRANCISCO, CAL., March 26th, 1907.
Dr. !. M. Dunsmoor, Secretary.
DEAR SIR AND BROTHER: Your letter of the 19th informing me that
Brother A. was ill with rheumatism and unable to work; that his wife
was also sick, came duly to hand, and I referred it to the Worshipful
Master who ·directs me to say that he would particularly appreciate it
if the Masonic Board of Relief will continue to advance to Brother A.
all in your opinion you consider necessary and just. We know that
this is a very worthy case, as Brother A., some three years ago, was
seriously ill with this same complaint, and at that time we took care of
him and his family and sent him to Arizona where he finally recovered.
Brother A. has endeavored to return some of the money we advanced
to him for the care of his wife and himself at that time,, and has done
all that his means permit, and we are confident that if he had the

GR.A.ND LODGE OF CALIFORNI.A..

633

money he would refund all. We return to you herewith by check the
$~5 you gave to him, and w~uld particularly thank you for relieving his
distress, and would esteem 1t a favor .if. you will. continue to see to the
wants of himself and wife, and upon receipt of :word from you .notifying
us of the amount expended during the month, we will be pleased to mail
you our check. Again permit me to extend you our thanks for the
attention given to Brother A., and any further kindness and consider~tion you can extend to him will place us .under. additional obligat10n to you.
Yours truly and fraternally,

A Code of By-Laws was adopted, a copy of which is hereto annexed. It will be seen, in the organizing of the corporation, ·that all the
directions given by the Grand Lodge have been carefully observed and
carried out.
·
At a subsequent meeting a committee was appointed to select and
recommend a suitable site for a Masonic Temple, and to that ·c ommittee were given a large number of proposed sites for consideration, .After
careful and thoughtful investigation, and a number of me~tings, the
committee came to the conclusion that as the fire had disrupted the
business and other centers of San Francisco, it would be very difficult
to determine which would be the most available and suitable. place for
a Temple, and they came to the conclusion it would be better for the
interests of the Order to wait until these centers were definitely fixed,
which is now being rapidly done, before choosing a final site. They
further found on investigation that the price of property was much
higher tha~ it would probably be in the near future, an~ it was prudent
to await the settling of values before purchasing.
By direction of the members of the corporation, at a full meeting
held in the office of the corporation, on October 1st, A. D., 1907, your
committee was directed to report the progress made to the· Grand
Lodge and request the approval of its action.
By the Organic Act, it is provided that the number of directors
shall be twenty-five, who shall be chosen from among the members of
the Masonic Order, and . shall be members in good standing of the
Grand U:>dge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California;
and to further safeguard the corporation from the influence ·o f any but
Masons, and to always keep it 'entirely under the control of the Grand
Lodge, it was provided in the By-Laws that no person shall be elected
a director of the corporation unless he is the owner and holder of at
least five shares of the capital stock thereof at the time of his election,
and a resident of the State of California, and a ~ember in good standing of the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of
California.
And by Article XIII. of the By-Laws it will be observed it is also
provided that the Board of Directors shall have the power to declare
the seat of.any member vacant who shall absent himself from the State
of California for more than three months, or who shall be absent from
six consecutive metings of the Board without leave of absence from

653

BY-LAWS
of
MASONIC TEMPLE ASSOCIATION OF CALIFORNI..\ .
Article I.
The name ·of this Corporation is and shall be MASONIC TEMPLE
ASSOCIATION OF CALIFORNIA.
. Article II.
·
The office of the Corporation is and shall be in the City and County
of San Francisco, State of California.
.
Article III.
The annual meeting of the c~rporation shall be held at the office
of the Corporati·o n .in said City and County on the third Tuesday in
October at ten o'clock A. M. in each year, and all special meetings of
.the Corporation shall be held at the office of the Corporation.
Article IV.
The annual and all special meetings of the Corporation shall be
called by publication of notice of such meeting, stating the time and
·.p lace thereof, signed by the . President, and published in some daily

654

6n5

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

newspaper published in the City and County of San Francisco, for two
weeks next before the day fixed for said meeting.

directors; having been duly served, or published in a newspaper in said
City and ~ounty for ten days before such meeting.
At all meetings of the Board of Directors seven members of the
Board being present shall constitute a quorum for the transaction of
business.
Adjourned meetings may be held in pursuance of a resolution of
the Board, adopted at any meeting by vote of a majority of the direc·tors present on a motion to that effect.

Article V.
At the annual, and all special meetings of the Corporation, the
presence of the holders of a majority of the shares of the ciJ.pital stock
thereof shall constitute a quorum.
Article VI.
At the annual, and all special meetings of the Corporation, stockholders may be represented and act by proxy. No person can hold the
proxy of a stockholder, or vote or act for him, unless he himse}f be a
stockholder of the Corporation. The right of the person clai~ing to
vote or act by proxy for another shall be evidenced by a written cer- ·
tificate of appointment, signed by the stockholder delegating tpe, power
to vote and act, and shall be filed with the Secretary of the Corporation, or the Secretary of the meeting a't which he offers to vote. ·
Article VII.
The annual election of directors of this Cor-poration shall be hel.d
at the annual meeting of stockholders, as provided for in Article III.
No person shall be elected a director of this Corporation unless he is
the owner and holder of least five shares of the capital stock thereof
at the time of his election, a resident of the State of California, and a
member in good standing of the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons of the State of California.
Article VIII.
The officers of this Corporation shall be a President, Vice President, Secretary and Treasurer.
Article IX.
The pay and salaries of all officers, agents and servants of the
Corporation shall be determined from time to time by the Board of
Directors.
Article X.
The regular meeting of the Board of Directors shall be held on the
second Tuesday in each month at two o'clock P. M., and notice of all
regular meetings of the Board of Directors is hereby dispensed with:
Special meetings of the Board of Directors shall be held on the
call of the President, or by notice issued by authority of the President,
personally served on each director, or published in a newspaper of general circulation in the City and County of San Francisco, according to
law. Special meetings may also be held upon notice signed by three

Article XI.
The President, Vice President, Secretary and Treasurer shall be
elected by the Board of Directors at their first meeting after the annual
election of directors, and such officers shall hold their office for one
year and until their successors are elected and qualified.
The President and Vice President must be selected from members
of the Board of Directors; the Secretary may be so selected, or the
Board may elect any resident of the State of California who is the
holder and owner of five shares of the capital stock of this Corporation,
and is a member in good standing of the Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted Masons of the State of California. The Treasurer need not
be a member of the Corporation.
Article XII.
If, during the term of his office, any director or officer, other than
the Treasurer, shall cease to be a resident of the State of California,
or cease to be a holder in his own right of at least five shares of the
capital stock of the Corporation, or cease to be a member in good
standing of the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the
State of California, then his office shall, ipso facto, become vacant.
Article XIII.
The Board of Directors shall have power to declare the seat of
any member vacant who shall absent himself from the State of California for three or more months, or who shall be absent from six
consecutive regular meetings of the Board without leave of absence
from the Board, or who does not own five shares of the capital stock
of the Association standing in his name on the books of the Association
or who ceases to be a member in good standing of the Grand Lodge
Free and Accepted Masons of California.
Article XIV.
Vacancies from any cause in the Board of Directors may be filled
for the unexpired term by the remainder of the Board at any regular
meeting.

permitting such transfer.

The funds of the Corporation shall be kept by the Treasurer of

The Secretary shall keep .the books of the Corporation, the minutes
of the meetings of the Corporation, and perform such other duties as
the directors may from time to time require.
Article XVIII.
Dividends fron:i the net profits of the Corporation may be declared
and paid by order cf the Board of Directors in accordance with the
law.

out of the funds of the Corporation in his hands; taking a proper

he shall submit a statement of the finances of the Corporation with a

satisfactory to the Board of Directors in such sums as they may from
time to time determine.
Article XXIV.
Other officers and employees of the Corporation shall perform such
duties as appertain to their respective positions or as may be required
by the Board of Directors or the President.

Article XXVII.
If the President, Vice President or Secretary shall be absent, or
otherwise disqualified, the Board of Directors are empowered to appoint temporary substitutes for any or all of said officers.

Article XXV.
The number of Directors who shall manage the affairs of the Corporation shall be twenty-five, and shall be elected at the annual meeting of the Corporation as herein provided.
No one shall be eligible to be elected or appointed or act as a Director unless he is the owner of at least five shares of the capital stock
of the association, a resident of the State of California, and a member
in good standing of the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of
the State of California.
Article XXVI.
It shall be the duty of the President at the first meeting of the
Board of Directors after the annual meeting of the stockholders to
appoint a Finance and also an Auditing Committee consisting of five
members each.
It shall be the duty of the Finance Committee to examine the books
of the Secretary and Treasurer and report thereon in writing to the
Board at each regular monthly meeting and to verify all financial statements submitted by the officers of the Corporation, and to recommend
from time to time what dividends, in their judgment, should be declared.
It shall be the duty of the Auditing Committee to examine all bills
against the Corporation and report thereon.
The President shall appoint such other committees from time to
time as he may deem necessary for the best interests of the Corporation, and such committees as the Board of Directors may designate, and
under. the direction of the Board shall define the duties and powers of
such committees.

Article XXVIII.
These By-Laws may be altered, amended or any of them repealed
and new By-Laws adopted at any regular meeting of the Board of
Directors by a vote of at least fifteen Directors; or they may be so
amended, altered or repealed at any general or special meeting of the
stockholders of this Corporation, or by the written assent of two-thirds
of the capital stock of the Corporation.

ARTICLES OF INCORPORATION
of
MASONIC TEMPLE ASSOCIATION OF CALIFORNIA.
KNow Au. MliN Bv THllsll PRllSllNTs:
That we, the undersigned, have this day associated ourselves together for the purpose of forming a Corporation under the laws of the
State of California.
AND Wll HllRllBY CllRTIFY:
FIRST :
That the name of said Corporation is MASONIC T'JlMPI.ll ASSOCIATION OF CAI.IFORNIA.
SllCOND:
That the purposes for· which it is formed are :
1. To purchase and own a lot of land in the City and County of
San Francisco, State of California, and erect and maintain thereon a
Masonic Temple, with halls, Lodge-rooms and apartments therein for
the meetings and accommodation of the several Lodges of the Masonic
Order, and all the branches thereof; said Order and all its branches
being benevolent and charitable societies and organizations; and also
to construct, maintain and have stores, halls and offices in said building, and let and lease the same for other purposes.
2. To buy, sell, deal in, improve and use real and personal property
and let and lease the same.

Bro. George F . Rodden presented the following report:
To the M :·. W.". Grand L odge of California:
Your Committee, to whom has been assigned the pleasant duty of
reporting upon the Address of the Most Worshipful Grand Master,
annourn;es the completion of its task
In reviewing this most excellent article, we can only record our
unqualified commendation of the sentiments and ideals contained in the
document and congratulate the Grand Lodge upon hay.ing selected as its

highest officer a man who has occupied the exalted station with so much
grace, dignity and ability.
We recommend that the action of the Most Worshipful Grand
Master with regard to the General Masonic Relief Fund, be approved
and especially commend the return of the moneys not needed for the
relief work to the various generous donors. In an age that has been
denominated an "Age of Money" it is at least an indication from this
Masonic Body that commercialism has not invaded our sacred precincts,
and this act of our Most Worshipful Grand Master will exemplify to
the world that we do not merely profess great principles, but that we
put into active practice the teachings of our Craft.
We recommend that a special committee of three be appointed on
Necrology, that the memories of our departed ones may , be more
particularly honored by this Grand Body.
We recommend that the portion of the Gran·d Master's address
dealing with decisions be referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence.
We desire particularly to call att~ntion to that portion of the
Address under the head "Visits." It is a record which clearly demonstrates his conscientiousness in the discharge of every duty and ·should
call for special commendation on the part of this Grand Lodge. It is
a fitting cc·nclusion to an introduction which breathes the noblest
thoughts and in hearing it one can only feel the pulsations of a true
~fasonic heart.
Brother Hart's address is Free Masonry from beginning to end and
will occupy in the minds and hearts of all who heard or may read it,
a lasting place.
The Grand Secretary's report which was also submitted to this
Committee is, as his preceding ones have been, a model of clearness and
conciseness and . is a lesson in precision. The knowledge that its
clerical affairs are in such truly diligent and efficient hands, must" be
very comforting to this Grand Lodge and is in itself a cause for much
congratulation.
We recommend that the section referring to dispensations be
referred to the Committee on Charters.
Respectfully submitted,

The M:. w:. Edmund C. Atkinson, Chairman of the
Committee on Jurisprudence, presented the following

To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee have had under consideration the communication
of the Grand Lodge of Saskatchewan asking for recognition from the

681

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

Grand Lodge of California and now beg leave to report that this new
Grand Lodge is an outgrowth of the Grand Lodg!! of Manitoba and is
located in the province of Saskatchewan.
The Grand Lodge of Saskatchewan was duly formed by the
requisite number of subordinate Lodges which had wi:hdrawn from
the Grand Lodge of Manitoba, and as it has received the approval of
the last named Grand Lodge, as evidenced by the fact that its first
Grand Officers were installed by the Grand Master and the Grand
Secretary of the Grand Lodge of Manitoba, it is apparent that said
Grand Lodge of Saskatchewan is regulady constituted.
We therefore recommend that fraternal recognition be extended
by the Grand Lodge of Califotnia, and that a representative of 6e
Grand Lodge of California near the Grand Lodge of Saskatchewan be
named.

In the matter of a trial transferred from San Bernardino Lodge,
No. 348, to Phoenix Lodge, No. 178, the Grand Master says : "The only
important question of procedure involved is the decision of the Grand
Master which is. submitted for approval-That San Bernardino Lodge
had by virtue· of its action in ordering its Junior Warden to prefer the
charges disqualified itself from trying the same."
While your committee are not willing to establish the general rule
that a Lodge by ordering its Junior Warden to prefer charges thereby
renders itself disqualified from trying the case, yet in this particular
instance your committee find good and sufficient reasons in the correspondence of San Bernardino Lodge with the Grand.Master to justify
the transfer of the trial to Phoenix Lodge, No. 178, and commend his
wisdom in so acting.
All which is respectfully submitted,

In the matter of the communication addressed to this Grand Lodge
by the Grand Secretary of New York, your Committee are pleased to
report that the invasion of the jurisdictional rights of the Grand Lodge
of New York bv the Grand Lodge of Hamburg, on account of which
all Masonic co~munication between the Lodges and Masons of this
jurisdiction and those acknowledging allegiance to the Grand Lodge of
Hamburg was forbidden in the year 1855, having now ceased, fraternal
relations can be restored, inasmuch as the Grand Lodge of Hamburg has
within the past year recalled tlfe charter of the Lodge established by
it in New York City.
We therefore recommend that friendly relations be entered into
with the Gr:and Lodge of Hamburg.
Respectfully submitted,

Edmund C. Atkinson, Chairman of the
Committee on Jurisprudence, presented the following report:
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee have under consideration the following decisions
made by the Grand Master and beg to report as follows :
The question was asked: "When an ·objection has been made to
the advancement of an Entered Apprentice or a Fellow Craft and the
Committee has reported, how should the vote of the Lodge be taken?"
To this the Grand Master answered substantially as follows:
"The same reasons which impelled the Grand Lodge at the Annual
Communication of 1906 to adopt the resolution providing for secrecy of
Committees of Investigation clearly indicate that voting upon objection
to advancement should be by secret ballot and not by a sh.ow of hands,
for by a show of hands the brothers voting would be obliged to expo~e
their ballots. Owing to the" impracticability of voting by ball and cube,
the ballot should be taken by slips of paper on each of which should
be written 'Yes' or 'No.' "
10

682

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

A Past !v1aster addressed a letter to the Grand Master in substance
as follows:
"A Lodge in this city, acting upon the authority of Section 935
of Decisions as given in Anderson's Manual, page 389, admitted a
sojourning brother on avouchment of one of its. members wjio had
recently sat with him in a Chapter of Royal Arch Masons. A few days
thereafter the brother was taken sick and was cared for by the Board
of Relief. A brother attending him wished to notify his Lodge and
asked the name of the Lodge and the address of the Secretary. It then
developed that the brother had been dimitted from his Lodge in one
of the Eastern States for nearly four years.
"It seems to me that the decision quoted is doubtful authority and·
I therefore ask you to decide as to the necessary prerequisites for
avouchment."
The Grand Master answered as follows :· "No Mason can rightfully
vouch for a visiting brother unless he shall have sat with him m vpen
Lodge or shall have examined him under proper authority."
A Lodge Secretary asked the following questions :
"When should a request for a waiver of jurisdiction be acted upon:
at the same meeting when presented, or should it lie over until the
next stated meeting? If it should lie over should Committee be appointed? If the Lodge refuses to waive jurisdiction can another Lodge
holding concurrent jurisdiction receive and act upon an application
from the same applicant ,within one year from the time the former
Lodge rejected the application?"
The Grand Master answered :
"In reply to your question as to ~hether a request for waiver of
jurisdiction should be acted upon by the Lodge at the same meeting
when presented, I would say that it should not be so acted upon, but
should lie over for a month and a committee should be appointed to
investigate; first, as to whether or not the Lodge to which the request
for waiver is addressed actually possesses jurisdiction, and secondly,
if the reasons alleged by the applicant as to why a waiver is desired
are good and sufficient. This report can only be rendered at a stated
meeting succeeding the one when the request is received, and the Lodge
can only act intelligently in the light of the information received therefrom. If the Lodge to which the request for waiver of jurisdiction
has been made, refuses to grant the waiver·asked, another Lodge holding
concurrent jurisdiction cannot within twelve months receive and act
upon a request from the same applicant."

STATUS OF PAST MASTERS OF 0cltANIC Looot.

The question was asked, "If the Past Masters of old Lodge Le
Progres de I'Oceanic, No. 124, A. and A. S. R., are to be considered as
Past Masters within the meaning of that term as defined in onr
Constitution?''
His reply thereto was to the effect that inasmuch as Oceanic Lodge,
No. 371, is in every sense of the word the successor under a new name
Masters by service in the old Lodge are to be regarded in the light of
Past Masters by service in Oceanic Lodge, No. 371, and as such are
entitled to all the rights and privileges as Past Masters of the
jurisdiction.
GARDENA LoDGE AND THE Los ANGELES BoARD oF RELIEF.

Early this year an election was held by the qualified electors of the
City of Los Angeles and a portion of Los Angeles County which
resulted in the annexing to the City of Los Angeles of a portion of land
one-half mile wide and some twenty miles long, known as the "shoe
string strip." This strip severed the township and village of Gardena
and included the Lodge-room of Gardena Lodge, No. 372. When this
"shoe string strip" was declared a part of the municipality of Los Angeles, the Los Angeles Board of Relief sent a communication to
Gardena Lodge, asking that it appoint a committee of representatives
on the Los Angeles Board of Relief and hold concurrent jurisdiction.
It seems that Gardena Lodge did appoint such committee and after two
or three meetings with the Los Angeles Board of Relief protested
against being named as a City Lodge, and evidently acting upon Grand
Lodge Decision No. 482 :
"A Masonic Lodge cannot hold it!! meetings in a hall situated in a
town or village other than that in which it is sought by dispensation to
establish the Lodge,"
And realizing that it was within the city limits of Los Angeles,
moved into another block beyond the line of the "shoe string strip-";

684

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

whereupon Los Angeles Board of Relief asked the Grand Master to
·state whether or not Gardena is properly within the joint jurisdiction of
the Lodges of Los Angeles and included in the ·membership of the
Masonic Board of Relief of that city.
The Grand Master's answer was as follows: "The charter to
Gardena Lodge, No. 372, was issued to a Lodge in the town. of Gardena,
and in moving its Lodge-room into the town of Gardena it committed,
in our opinion, no infraction of our ·law. Gardena Lodge could not
have acquired joint jurisdiction with the Lodges of the City of Los
Angeles and have become a member of the Masonic Board of Relief of
that city without first amending its By-La.;,.s and raising its fees for
degrees to the minimum allowed by our Constitution where joint
jurisdiction is held with other Lodges. No amendment of this character
was ever presented to me for my official approval, without which it
would not become effective, and for this reason, if no other, Gardena's
attempted recognition of the jurisdiction of your Board was premature
and _improper.
In addition to the reasons above set forth, it is our belief that it
would be improper for the town of Gardena to hold concurrent jurisCJ.i.<;tion with the Lodges of the City of .Los Angeles, and we hardly
think that Gardena Lodge is open to criticism for moving its Lodgeroom into the town of Gardena and out of the so-called "shoe string
strip."
All these decisions are approved by your Committee.
Respectfully submitted,
EDMUND c. ATKINSON, }

RESOLVED, That Section 11, of Article III, Part III, of the Constitution be and is hereby amended to read as follows :
Sec. 11. No Lodge shall expel a member for the non-payment of
dues; but, in case an( member shall have refused or neglected to pay
his regular dues during a period of twelve months he shall be notified
by the Secretary, either by registered letter or by actual service of

notice, duly certified by the Tyler, that unless at the next stated

Provided, That should any member suspended for non-payment of
dues neglect for the period of two years to pay said dues or have the
same remitted by his Lodge, said member shall not be restored except
by a three-fourths vote by ballot of all the members present at the next
stated meeting after the petition for restoration is presented.
Any Secretary failing or neglecting to comply with the require~ents
of this section relative to notifying delinquent~ shall be subject to
discipline by his Lodge for neglect of duty.

The accused was suspended on September 28th, 1906, for Unma. sonic conduct in applying opprobrious epithets to a Master Mason in
good standing and a member of said Lodge. . The time for appeal not
having expired, your Committee took no action upon the record at the

Resolved, That the action of Vacaville Lodge, No. 134, in suspending Brother John James Hagerty from all the rights and privileges of
Masonry be affirmed.
Respectfully submitted,

It is unnecessary to say that if he was suspended he should have
applied for reinstatement to the Lodge which suspended him, in accordance with our law.
It mt1st be admitted that he has failed to furnish proper proof of
having given notice to Abell Lodge of his intention to apply to this .
Grand Lodge for restoration, t1nless his own statement in his petition
can be regarded or accepted as such proof.
Section Six of Article Five of the Constitution of the Grand Lodge
provides that "before such petition shall be considered by the Grand
Lodge, proof of the giving of such notice to said Lodge shall be
furnished."
It might be assumed that had such notice been given, we should
have been furnished under the S'eal of said Lodge, information or proo"f
of some action favorable or unfavorable, taken by said Lodge in this
matter.
We have been informed that such action was taken, but that for
some reason the result of that action has never been communicated to
this Grand Lodge. Had it been, and had Abell Lodge thereby admitted
having received such notice, . it should no doubt be regarded as
sufficient.
In view, therefore, of the want of sufficient proof that such a notice
was ever given, and further in view of the many conflicting statements
that have been made to your Committee, touching this matter, we can
only recommend that the petition be laid over until the next Convocation of this Grand Body, that the record may be made more complete
before final action.

Your Committee, to whom was referred the record and transcript
of the trial of Brother Charles McGill Figeley (presumably a member
of Suisun Lodge, No. 55, F. & A. M. of California), tried by a Commission elected by Suisun Lodge on charge of Unmasonic conduct, in
this, "that during the year 1905 he embezzled moneys of his employer,
the Pacific Portland Cement Company," beg 'leave to report as follows :
It does not appear from the record so far as the charge is concerned, whether Charles McGill Figeley was a member of any Lodge.
The evidence produced shows that said Charles McGill Figeley had
confessed that the charges made against him were true, but that he
made such confession on the promise that he would not be prosecuted,
that he should be immune from prosecution by virtue of this alleged
confession.
. The record does not show that the alleged confession was made
free and voluntary on his part and without promise of reward, and
before the confession can be used against him as evidence, this must
affirmatively be shown or independent evidence other than the confession .should be produced; if, however, the accused takes the stand in
his own behalf and testifies under oath that he did take money at
different times, as was done in this case, and there had been no promise
made to him by the Commission or any member thereof or by the
Accuser, that if he confessed he would be immune, his own admissions
would be sufficient evidence to warrant the Commission in finding him
guilty.
The record shows that on May 15th, after several continuances
had been had at the request of the accused, that on motion the Commission adjourned sine die, which action at once dissolved the Commission and rendered any subsequent action of the Commissioners
absolutely void.
Your Committee therefore, in view of the necessity of a re-trial,
deems it advisable to point out as hereinabove set forth, in what .
manner the evidence should be produced on a new trial, in order to
prevent any further mistakes.
We therefore submit the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:
Resolved, That the action of Suisun Lodge, in expelling Brother
Charles McGill Figeley be and the same is hereby reversed and that a
new trial be had therein.
Respectfully submitted,

"WHF.IU:AS, It appears from the statement of Brother Hubbard and
the report of Bro. N. A. Bailey, who has examined Bro. Hubbard's
books, that Bro. Hubbard is now indebted to the Lodge in the sum
of $874.57, and
"Wm!RF.AS, On account of Bro. Hubbard's long and. faithful services
in the Lodge, and also because of the belief that said indebtedness is
not the result of any criminal intent on his part, 'it is not the desire of
the Lodge or members thereof to proceed against Bro. Hubbard on
account of such in~ebtedness;
"Tm:R£FoRE DE IT Resolved, That Bro. Hubbard be requested to file
with the Treasurer of this Lodge his written acknowledgment of said
indebtedness ; that it is the sense of this Lodge that Bro. Hubbard repay
said amount, and the whole thereof; that no objection be made to his
installation as Secretary of this Lodge for the ensuing year, but that
he ·be required to pay his salary as Secretary as it accrues towards the
satisfaction of said indebtedness."
This resolution certainly exhibits highly exemplified true Masonic
Charity and follows out our beautiful lessons tqught us in the several
Degrees of Masonry; the evidence, however, shows that Bro. Hubbard
had had sickness in his family, that he had been out of employment and
needed money, but he never asked the Lodge to assist him financially
or otherwise,, hence his talcing of the money was cl~rly unlawful and
could not be j us~ified' under any circumstances ; the Commission found
him not guilty on the first specification, which was the only sp~cification
in the charge.
The evidence is clear and convincing that the accused was guilty of
Unmasonic conduct and should have been found guilty and then the
Commission could have taken into consideration his former good
character in fixing the punishment.
The Lodge could not condone the offense by agreeing to let him
repay the money, the crime had already been committed, a crime which
this Grand Lodge has repeatedly held inexcusable.
We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption :

Resolved, That the action of San Bernardino Lodge, No. 348, be
and the same is hereby reversed and 'the case remanded for a new trial.

J. D. MURPHY,
H . M. OwENs,

The Grand Lecturer presented his Annual Report to
the Grand Lodge as follows :
To . the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
I beg to submit this, my annual report for the Masonic year now
closing:
Another year has sped its course into the forever past. It has been
for Masonry in this Grand Jurisdiction one that will live in happy
memory through all the years that are yet to conie.
Great progress has been made. Increase . in membership has been
unprecedented, and the earnestness and enthusiasm manifested everywhere speaks eloquently for the future of our great fraternity.
Our lodge work throughout the Jurisdiction is done in a most
creditable manner, and though it be true that in remote places where
the membership of Lodges is widely scattered and where it is almost
impossible for Masters to have full and proper assistance, yet in these
places we find that effort to emulate the more fortunate Lodges and
to do the full and perfect work. There is a pleasing exactness and
uniformity in the rendition of . the work that is truly as wonderful as
it is delightful. Go "!W'here we may, whether to the snowy crests of
our great Sierras, or to the fragrance-spreading groves of our orange
section ; whether to the mines or to the vineyards, everywhere we will
witness the same correctness, of execution, the same rendition of the'°
ritual. and the same spirit of devotion to the great truths which
underlie and form the foundation of our beloved Fraternity.

696

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

I have visited nearly every Masonic ·district in California since the
last communication of the Grand 'Lodge, and have conducted Lodges
of Instruction in many of the Lodges, and have given individual instruction to many brethren. It has been a great pleasure to feel that
my visits and work have done some good-that I have contribute<j. my
mite.
The office with which the Grand Lodge in its kindness has honored
me for the past ten years is in most respects a very delightful one. It
gives the opportunity for acquaintance and fellowship with the truest
and best men of every section of our great commonwealth. It enhances our appreciation of those Masonic words: "Brotherly Love,
Relief, and Truth."
·
This office also has its worries, its labors, and its trials. No
occupation requires more patience, more care, more concentration. ' To
suffer one's self to cease vigilance for one moment is perhaps · to leave
an error in the mind of him one teaches that will be hard to eradicate.
It is the experience of all, that it is harder t~ unlearn what js wrong
than to learn it right in the first instance.
Of the Inspectors of the several Masonic districts of this· Jurisdiction I beg to repeat what I have said in the reports of last and
other years, that in the discharge of their official duties they have
proven their sterling worth and competency. They have been faithful
to the trust committed to their care and have by their works endeared
themselves to the Lodges of their districts and to the Fraternity at
large.
It has been my very great privilege and pleasure to have traveled
almost throughout the entire. State in company with our Most Worshipful Grand Master. I have sat spellbound in crowded halls and listened
to his matchless oratory. I have sat beside him in the silent watches
of the night and drun.k the gentle influence of his sympathetic nature.
I have watched the trend of his daily thought and act, and I pay to
him the homage that every Mason owes to one whose life is pure,
whose thoughts and deeds and words, warmed by the sunshine of his
genial soul, bring delight to all who meet him.
·
I regret that I may never more be so close in my daily life to .that
distinguished man and Mason, our beloved Most Worshipful Edward
Henry Hart. Long may he live to honor himself, his family and the
great Fraternity over which he has so ably presided.
And now, my brethren of the Grand Lodge, it is with feelings
akin to grief that I bid you farewell as Grand Lecturer. Nevermore
can I expect to travel from Lodge to Lodge and meet you in your
homes as I have done in the years that have now gone forever.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

697

From the deep recesses of my heart, I thank you one and all for
the many courtesies and honors I have received at your hands, and I
thank the Most Worshipful Grand Master and the Directors of the
Masonic Home for the confidence they have manifested by placing me
and mine in charge of the Masonic Home at Decoto. We shall do the
best that in us lies to make the aged brethren, the widows and the
orphans who are placed in our care feel and know that Masonry is indeed the greatest and best Fraternity on the face of the earth.
WILLIAM HARVEY EnwA&ns, Grand Lecturer.

. All beginnings are difficult, but I can imagine few beginnings more
difficult than formulating the introduction to an address designed for
this Grand Body.
.
When one. remembers that seated as his audience are not only
men of educat10n, culture and refinement; men of discernment and
discretion, skilled in worldly matters, able to sit in judgment and to i'
dete~i~e upon the exact value of each word, phrase and sentence, and
to crittc1se every thought and sentiment; but men who know the ritual
and with whom its language is so fluent that they find it impossible to

keep it out of their ordinary conversation, he becomes convinced that
mere perfervid oratory, a flight of winged words will never do. Here
are men of thought-and that which is offered them must not only be
the result of mature thought, but must possess the additional quality
of being able to engage their most serious attention and lead them by
logical paths to a logical conclusion. I might enunciate a problem or
suggest hypothetical questions and reasoning upon them, endeavor to
educe some thought that might commend itself to the imagination, or
I might proceed to discuss definitions and by thus limiting the breadth
of discussion narrow down my argument to a few generalities. ·

utterly fall to comprehend that they were deprived of their liberty, a
few stout hearts that, with fearless minds, were willing to undergo
martyrdom stood forth to champion the cause of liberty.

But in the stead of all these expedients it is my purpose to pro- ·
pound a question and in the course of my attempt to solve that question or answer it, to engage your thoughts and your most serious attention, to. enliven your sympathies and sentiments and . to lend wing
to your imagination .. The question I am about · to discuss is, "What
makes a man a Mason." I k~~~ th~t · ~ost of my friends here assembled would solve the question immediately by responding, his obligation makes a man a Mason, and that position I am about to contest.

An

obligation no more makes a man a Mason than does subscribing to the creed of a particular church make one a true follower of .
the doctrines inculcated by that church. One may attend church every
day and be conversant with every ceremony and be no Christian, or
attend the Temple and repeat every prayer and be no Jew. Similarly
a man may be present, whenever his Lodge convenes, know the work
perfectly and be only a lodge Mason. Like some frequenters of
churches and temples, ~hose religion never strays beyond the confines
of the religious edifice, his Masonry may be and is confined to lip service and ritual work. Such men are never Masons and no amount of
obligations can make them Mason~. Men whose hearts do not realize,
and whose minds cannot comprehend the real usefulness of Masonry;
men who cannot apply the teachings of the Craft to their lives and to
the practice of their daily existence, and feel their Masonry only within
the precincts of the lodge roo'm ; such men are a detriment and a
hindrance to the cause that Masonry represents.
·
When men originally banded themselves together under the name
of Masons, it was the espousal of a sacred cause and a desire to
promulgate the doctrines of that cause that impelled them to combine.
Jn. an age when ignorance among the masses was promoted and encouraged for fear that men might realize that freedom, their inalienable right was denied them~ when factional feud and sectarian strife
was fostered and stimulated by designing rulers that men's minds,
divert~d by the non-essentials represented by dogma and f?rmula, should

Collecting about them men of like calibre selected from all sorts
and conditions of men they constructed a society that would, by destroying the stumbling blocks so adroitly placed in the path of human
progress, render it impossible for men, through ignorance of one another, or bigotry, to retard the growth of that spirit of brotherly·
love that alone could cement the men who desired to serve the Grand
Master of the Universe mto one common band. Hence no restriction
as to calling or creed was imposed upon those who, seeing thfl light
and desiring to aid in spreading i~ volunteered their services to the
holy cause.
Each one thereafter undertook to individually manifest in the pursuit of his own existence, and to demonstrate in ·his personal life, the
great beauties conceived and promulgated by the Fraternity.
The Holy Bible, the rule and guide of his faith, was the source
from which shone the light which was thenceforward to be reflected .in
his own actions and words, in his demonstrations to his fellow men,
in his companionship with his family and his comradeship with his
friends. It is to the Bible then that we must look for the light that
we are to absorb and then to disseminate that we banded together for
the promotion of all that is best and noblest, may fit ourselves as mas- •
ter workmen proficient in the knowledge of our Craft and competent
for the performance of our work.
The fifteenth Psalm gives us . the picture of an honest man, the
man whose soul is above untruth, and who finds no joy in gaining
wealth through the misfortunes of others. He never forgets nor does
the true Mason that the mistakes of others are contributary to his own
good, and often their failure means his success. He therefore deems
it his duty to attempt equalization by proffering the unsuccessful aid
and encouragement to prosecute his vocation. . The psalmist speaks of
God as mighty, just, powerful; but he is full of goodness; he is merciful, long-suffering and slow to anger too, and in the highest concept
of the psalmist, God's most exalted function is described in the words,
"Father of the Fatherless and Vindicator of the Widow." Brethren,
do you realize what this meant, pronounced as were these words at a
time when money had corrupted men's minds and the weakest and most
helpless were prey to the strong and the rich ? Or can you conceive
the conditions that prevailed when that grand orator-poet Isaiah denounced his generation, berated them for the uselessness of their assemblies convened or convoked for personal gain or aggrandizement?

700

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

When he characterized their holy convocations and fasts as · farces and
their unmeant devotions and supplications as blasphemies, and when
he declared the acceptable day of God as one in which you break the
yoke of servitude, free the enslaved, feed the hungry, clothe the naked,
shelter the homeless and cease pointing the finger of scorn. Do you
understand what pointing the finger of scorn means? . You know the
difference between insinuated insult and the affront conveyed in definite
terms. The one is deadly because indefinite, and cowardly because undeterminable. The insinuated insult leaves a man helpless and denies
him the human and natural desire to be avenged because it is not
stated; it leaves him defenseless. So it is with pointing the finger of
scorn. There is a pointing of the finger which is only mental, and
.men have been thus only mentally exposed to scorn because of their
religious beliefs. But this is wrong in a society where men _o f all
faiths are banded together for the prosecution of a common cause.
To obviate all this when man's freedom was assailed on all sides,
our Fraternity strove to disseminate the light which is of the eternal coeternal and like a glory ·did invest the rising world of waters dark and
deep. We are still banded together for the enlightenment of mankind
and any danger that menaces humanity must engage our most serious
attention. Individually each of us is under obligation to eradicate tg
the best of his ability any disease or distemper that threatens to infect
men's minds, and destroying their reverence for God and righteous• ness cause crude forms of thought to hold sway.
Today there is a disorder which is not local, a malady which is
not national, but epidemic the world over. Money fever, the greed for
gold is a disease that has infected mankind, not only here but everywhere and nothing seems to have any value except it has a price in
mone;. Today, when men of high repute and standing have their
price in gold, and high officials become traitors to their trust for so
much money, it becomes the duty of every Mason to lend his aid to"
battling against Mammon. In his service neither mercy or kindness,
love nor sympathy finds a place; all things must subserve him. But we
who serve God as our master must be up and doing. Gold will not
unbolt the portals of heaven; money will not unbar the gates of Paradise. Money is not the standard by which we measure men; we judge
by character only. Who is the most honored of our three first most
excellent grand masters? Solomon, king of Israel, with gorgeous
panoply of kingly raiment, or Hiram of Tyre with his wealth of stone
and timber? Neither ! but the humblest architect of the work who forfeited his life rather than his integrity, and whom neither persuasion
nor force could induce to prove traitor to his trust. The simple, honest
mind, great in its simplicity, drinking into his soul the lessons symbol-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

701

ized in the tools of his trade is the greatest exemplar of Freemasonry
known to man. Neither his obligation nor a knowledge of the work
made him a Mason; but his unswervable honesty, his piety, his fidelity,
his putting into practice the principles of his art, made him the noblest
of all Masons. Our most ancient teachers inculcated morals by means
of parable and allegory a:nd, following their noble example, I will with
your forbearance granted, attempt to compose one for you.
My soul was once granted leave to stray away from my body, that
unobserved I might note the ways of . men, entering into their secret
thoughts without fear of detection. Accordingly my soul did stray
away one night to a large and thriving mining camp, where the moral
law is put aside and men carry legal decisions in their hip pockets.
Among those most unfortunate there was a sturdy and strong young
man who, to quote him, had been "lucky-fortune had smiled upon
him," he said. He had dug in many a claim and found many a pocket
which he had transferred to his bank account. Amongst those who
had dug down into the earth, he had been most successful, and now
grown rich he hungered to go home, not to do good 'tis true, but to
show the villagers, his early companions, what he had done and how
rich he had grown. He boarded the train, and in a short while fell
asleep and dreamed. My soul kept company with his thoughts and
dreamed his dream with him. He dreamed that he had died and the
funeral o'er, his soul began its journey heavenward. On a rough and
rugged road he found himself, trudging and laboring onward, his feet
all cut by the projecting rocks and his frame borne down by the weight
of gold. But as he labored painfully along other spirits passed him by
whose feet seemed scarce to touch the ground, much less to suffer by
the contact. And he looked and wondered and anon, as his strength
waxed weak, he queried of a passing spirit the cause .why he so painfully trudged along and they passed, experiencing no pain at all. "My
good deeds have lightened the burden of my sins and I feel their weight
no more," was the response, but still he labored on. Soon he came to
an iron gate against which he pressed with might, but no strength of
· his could move those gates, so he stood aside to observe. Anon there
came several souls that knelt them down and prayed and arising did
pass through as though no gate were there. And there came a voice
from out the heights that uttered the mandate, "Pray." Pray? Why,
he had not prayed for years. In the busy life he lead he had no
time for such a thing. Even the prayer he lisped at night a,t his
mother's knee had from his memory passed clean away, and neither
the memories of his childhood, nor the soft and refining influences
that home recalls had entered into his life for many a year. Pray?
Who prayed out there where he lived? But anon, like the cool breath
of a heavenly wind, it came back to him again, and kneeling there at the

had taught him, he toQ knelt at the gate and as from the depths of
sincerity rang out the words, "Oh, God, I have sinned; forgive me."
The gates flew wide open and he, like the others, passed through. And
now he stepped upon mossy grovnd with paths moist with heaven's dew
and toiled along till he came to a golden gate as slight as a spider's

gate. So again he waited in order to observe how admission could
be here gained. And as he waited there passed him by an aged and

through you of God and human love, enter thou most deserving one."

heard in accents full of love: "Oh, thou blessed one, long has thy love
been known; thou hast earned heaven's most cordial welcome. Hungry
yourself, you shared the little you had with those who had nought."
And the golden gates parted for her.

The history of Masonry in Spain and the Philippine is not complete
in any of the works that have been published. Gould's History of
Masonry does not attempt to report authenticated information on this
matter; it is mostly rumors and hearsay evidence.
This Grand Lodge should not use any but the most positive information as to the regularity of Masonry in the Philippines. The best
information that we have is that the' records of the so-called Grand
Bodies in Spain are very incomplete as to their Lodges, if any they
have in the Philippine Islands.
As this Committee has been unable to get full information on the
matter, we deem it advisable and recommend that it be continued,
with power to add to its number in order that they might obtain
the fullest information possible and that this matter be continued
until the next Communication of the Grand Lodge; that in the meanwhile we recommend that no Masonic communication be held with said
Masonic bodies or their subordinate Lodges.
Respectfully submitted,

Bro. Henry M. Owens presented the following:
To the M:. W.~. Grand Lodge of California:
Brethren :-Your Committee, to whom was referred that part of
Grand Master Motley H . Flint's address at the Annual Communication
of this Grand Lodge in October, 1906, which contained the communication from the Special Representative of Manila Lodge, No. 342, requesting this Grand Lodge to define our Masonic relations towards
other Masonic bodies in the Philippine Islands, to-wit: The Gra.nd
Orients of Spain and France, beg leave to report:
That at the meeting of this Grand Lodge, one year ago, we reported that from a lack of information and the limited time at the
command of this Committee, it recommended that the final disposition
of this question be referred to the next Communication of this Grind
Lodge, and in the meantime (the regularity of the aforesaid Masonic
bodies being discussed by other Masonic powers) that no Masonic communication be held with said Masonic bodies or their subordinate
bodies.
Since making the above report, your Committee has personally
interviewed representative from the Philippine Islands, have had correspondence with others, and one member of this Committee has attended the Masonic Conference held at Brussels, Belgium, at which
conference twenty-one Masonic Powers were represented; this matter
was discussed at that conference and a final determination of the standing of the Grand· Orients of Spain and France was not determined.
The matter was at that conference continued in order that further
information might be obtained.

These are serious accusations and when established to ·the. satisfaction of a Trial Commission after a fair trial in conformity with our
laws and usages merit the severest penalties imposed by our laws upon
its offenders. The man who is permitted to participate in the privileges of Masonry and so far forgets his solemn engagements as to attempt to disrupt his Lodge through malice and bigotry was never 1l
Mason in spirit or in fact, was never worthy and well qualified, but was
an imposition upon the Fraternity when he crossed our threshold.
This case appeals to us as one in which there was a strong feeling
in the Lodge that,. the accused, in violation of his obligations, was disposed to arbitrarily override the will of the majority whenever that
expressed will ran contrary to his opinions and convictions. The evidence, however, presented to the Commission is not convincing as to
any of the specifications and totally wanting as to some of them. Generally speaking, each specification is supported by the testimony of one
witness, and the statements of each are specifically denied by the accused and his denial is supported by the fact that a large number of the
most prominent and respected members of King David's Lodge testified
to the excellent reputation of the accused for honesty and integrity.
The accused was found guilty upon all of the specifications, notwithstanding that as to one, at least, there is not a suggestion of evidence to support the finding. However, if the record did not show
fatally defective errors in the proceedings, your Committee would
not be disposed to interfere with the conclusions of the Trial Commission on questions of fact alone.
In this case the special meeting of the Lodge for the election of
Commissioners· was held on the 15th day of August, 1906. The Master
then appointed the 19th day of September, 1906, as the time for the
first meeting of the Commissioners and gave proper direction for procuring the attendance of the necessary parties at that time. Upon convening for the trial the Master announced his disqualification to preside
at the trial and stated that he had requested the Most Worshipful
Grand Master to designate the Master of some other Lodge to act in

Sec. 585.
We might pr<;>pertly leave the matter here, but as the case may b~
again tried we will notice other errors on the face of the. r~co~d. Th • .
Commission was continually adjourned by the Master; t~1s 1s irre!'111ar
and improper. The Commissioners are the proper parties to a:l1ourn
the Commission, and not the Master.
The Commission found upon all the specifications named in the
charge, but failed to find upon the charge ; this is ~atal error. Unless
the records' of the Commission show that the findmgs are upon b?th
the specifications and the charge they failed to find the accused gmlty
of any offense to which a penalty can be attached.
A finding upon the charge separate an~ dis~inct from the specifications is as necessary as a finding upon specifications.
The record clearly discloses one other serious and fata_l error. The
accused objected to all of the Commissioners upon sufficient grounds.
The examination of two of the Commissioners showed. them to have
been unquestionably disqualified and they should not have b~e~ permitted to participate in the proceedings. One of: the Comm1ss1oners
stated that he had conversed with many of the witnesses, had so~ght
to discover evidence against the accused, and had formed an unq~ahfied
opinion as to his guilt. He then said that he could and would give the
accused a fair and impartial trial. Notwithstanding this statement, upon ·
the showing made, he was disqualified.
The Commission should be so constituted as to be reasonably free
from any suspicion of unfairness, bias, prejudice or. partiality. A Commissioner who has conversed with nearly all the witnesses and formed

The examination of one of the other Commissioners and evidence

These two Brothers participated in the trial up to the· time of balloting on the specifications, and the record shows that they withdrew

after their withdrawal a majority of the Commissioners still remained
and as such would proceed to dispose of the case. We cannot sanction
this view.
All the Commissioners who participated in the trial should be
qualified, and the withdrawal of a disqualified Commissioner at the
close of a trial and after participating in all the proceedings, comes too
late to cure the error of his retention.

Bro. Henry M. Owens, from the Committee on Grievances, presented the following report:
To t,he M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Brethren :-Your Committee having considered the report on the
transcript of the trial of Brother Hugh Spencer Breszee, of Manila

711

We have carefully examined the records of both of these cases
and find that all of the purported evidence which was used at each of
the trials was that of affidavits, which this Grand Lodge has repeatedly
held is not evidence upon which a Mason can be convicted of any
offense.
The reason why affidavits can not be used as evidence:
"Affidavits is a statement or declaration reduced to writing, and
sworn to before some officer who has authority to administer an oath
or affirmation; it differs ·from a deposition in this, that in the deposition
the opposite party . has an opportunity to cross-examine the witness,
whereas an affidavit is always taken exparte."
By general practice affidavits are allowable to present evidence
upon the hearing of a motion, but they are not allowable to present
evidence on the trial of an issue raised by the pleadings. Here the
witnesses must be produced before the adverse party in order that such
party may have the opportunity to cross-examine the witness; a witn~ss
can truthfully make an affidavit and tell truthfully of facts which
standing alone would tend to convict, but not tell all of the facts, which,
if told, would tend to acquit, and if .the adverse paro was present and
had a chance to ask about the antold facts he probably would bring out
the truth but if he was present or had an opportunity to be present
and failed to take advantage of his right to cross-examine the witness,
then he can not complain for the reason that he has had his day in
court and by his own negligence he must suffer the consequences of
his acts.
While this may seem to many members of this Grand Lodge as
elementary law, yet we have had so many Brothers ask us why an
affidavit can net be used as evidence we have deemed it proper to give
a full definition of the word and point out the difference between an
affidavit and a deposition which is the proper mode of taking the testimony of witnesses when living at a distance and can not conveniently
attend before a Commission.
Article IV., Part VI., of the Constitution of this Grand Lodge
points out the . way evidence should be procured and does not need any
explanation.
The only question not covered is where a deposition is desired
when the tdal proceeds e.xparte and the residence of the accused is not
known, in which event we are of the opinion that if the record shows
that the residence of the accused is unknown, the accuser should apply

The Grand Master early in the year had numerous requests for an
interpretation of the resolution adopted at the last annual communication of the Grand Lodge · concerning committees of investigation on
petitions for degrees and 'applications for membership, and in response
thereto he gave his construction of that resolution as follows:
'(l)ur interpretation of the resolution adopted at the last Annual
Communi<;ation of the Grand Lodge of California in reference to keeping secret the names of brethren appointed on committees of investigation on petitions for degrees and applications for membership, and
our judgment as to the proper method of procedure are as follows :
"The intention of the resolution being to secure absolute secrecy,
the names of the brethren l/.ppointed on these committees should not,
in our opinion, be given by the Master to the Secretary, to enable him,
as formerly, to notify the brethren of their appointment; neither should
their reports be returned to the Secretary; but the Master himself
should severally notify the members of the committees of their :.11.1pointment, not revealing to one the identity of the others, and their .
reports should he rendered by them directly to him, and when practicable \hould be given verbally, and if in writing, after having subserved the purpose of informing the Master of the results of the investigations should be by him destroyed ; and his simple announcement to
the Lodge of such results will be all the information concerning these
reports conveyed by him to anyone.''
The foregoing decision is approved by the Committee.

Cr.AIM oF Tuor.UMNE LoooE, No. 8.

Your Committee to whom was referred the petition of Tuolumne
Lodge, No. 8, asking for the remission of its Grand Lodge dues for this
year, have considered the same, and we find as follows:
That during the past year said Tuolumne Lodge, No. 8, has been
called upon to render financial assistance to a number of its members
who were taken seriously ill while absent from home; that during this
year said 'Lodge has lost several of its older-members, thereby entailing
upon the Lodge a large funeral expense. That these expenditures
together with the usual charity claims paid by it, have amounted to
approximately $1,350; that by reason of these facts said Tuolumne
Lodge, No. 8, should have its Grand Lodge dues for this year .remitted.
we therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:

Resolved, That the Grand Lodge dues of Tuolumne Lodge, No. 8,
for this year be and the same are hereby remitted.
